Being plain files in the folder, they ride Sync, backups and DHD exactly as the rest of the case does

The conversational log block is retired

A case is not one bucket

Through v0.5.14e every chat filing door filed to findings whatever it was handed, so an indicator stated in a reply became a finding to be read back out of the register it belonged in

What the Center is

" + "

The Wire (in the menu's Casework group) is Apex's standing picture of the threat landscape — and the one Navi reasons with

It pulls public, keyless feeds on a cadence into a local store (config/intel.db): the NVD (CVEs, CVSS scores, affected products), CISA's KEV catalog (the vulnerabilities known to be exploited, with remediation due dates), EPSS (each CVE's likelihood of exploitation, refreshed daily), CISA advisories, and curated reporting (Krebs on Security, BleepingComputer)

No accounts, no API keys, no scraping — published feeds, pulled politely, each keeping its own fields: a record's identity is its CVE ID, and KEV owns the exploited status, NVD the scores and products, EPSS the likelihood.

" + "

The page is freshness first: a strip up top says who gathered the picture and how old every source is — fresh under 12 hours, aging under 48, stale beyond — because a stale picture presented as fresh is worse than none

Below it, the triage queue (your matches first, then what's newly exploited, then the loudest new disclosures), the record (one CVE in full: description, products, references, EPSS history), and Navi's brief — the same standing summary she carries into chat

On a phone the arrangement is its own: one column, brief first.

" + "

Matching — declared, local, honest

" + "

The Center matches records against a small, specific profile: the watchlist you declare on the page (the software you run), the Mesh roster (node names, this machine's platform), and your cases' registers — their observables, entity names and tags (since v0.3.0e — Build 2, the values an investigator wrote down, not words scraped from the manifest)

A match to a declared product through its CPE identity is an exact match; a watch term appearing in a record's text is a keyword mention — the queue labels which, because the grades mean different things. Matching happens on this machine: the watchlist and the case terms are never sent to a feed

The only outbound traffic is the feed pulls themselves, on vendor-published schedules.

" + "

Navi's three depths of knowing

" + "

The standing brief rides her chat context on every turn — bounded (roughly 700 tokens), always carrying its freshness stamps, so she answers “what's the picture?” from the store and dates it when she does

Deliberate lookup: type intel: openssl, or ask “what do we know about CVE-2024-3094?”, and the answer comes straight from the store without a model round-trip — including when the honest answer is “not in the store.” The seam: name a CVE ID or a watched product in ordinary chat and that record is pulled into her context for that reply only

In a case chat, the case's own matched records ride along — and from the Center's record view, a record can be filed straight into the open case as a finding, its citation (the CVE ID and the digest's stamp) written into the note so case exports carry it.

" + "

Searching the catalog, and reading past it (v0.5.2e, #259)

" + "

One search, the whole catalog. The Center's page carries a Search the catalog card above the queue — one box for CVEs and KEVs alike, because the catalog holds both and KEV is a flag on the same records

Ask by CVE id (exact, or a prefix), by free text over titles and descriptions, or by vendor and product names; narrow it with Known-exploited only, Matched to you, and a published window. Results are the queue's own rows and open in the record the same way

The catalog's last-fetched stamp rides the results — a search over a stale catalog says so on its face, and an empty answer names the absence: absence from the store, not proof of safety. The search is local only — no live calls per keystroke; the collection cadence keeps the catalog fresh

Navi runs the same search from chat: “search the KEV for OpenSSH”, “any CVEs for WordPress this week?”, “what CVEs affect Apache?” — answered from the store with its stamp, grounded the same way as her lookups.

" + "

Exploit-DB, as a join. On the same cadence the Center now mirrors the Exploit-DB index (the searchsploit CSV) into the local store and joins it by CVE id

Where public exploit code exists, the record says so — exploit available — EDB-id, type, platform — on the record view, as a badge on search results, in the citation when a record is filed into a case, and in Navi's answers

It is an enrichment, not another feed: it answers the question an operator asks of a KEV entry — is there public exploit code for this, and what shape is it? The mirror can be switched off in Collection, like any source.

" + "

Reading the references. A record's reference links — advisories, writeups, proof-of-concept repos — are no longer display-only

Ask Navi to “read the references for CVE-…” and she follows them on demand: at most six links, each fetched once and read as text, quoted back cited to the specific link, with a link that will not read named rather than papered over. Fetched pages are untrusted data: they inform her answer, they never direct it, and nothing in them is followed as an instruction
There is no wholesale crawl — a fetch happens on an ask, a filing, or a brief, never in bulk

And the digest travels: file that reply into its case with the File into this case tap and the reference digest lands in the case as a finding, citation and all.

" + "

Digging deeper, searching the tabs, and pulling cards into cases (v0.5.10e, #282, #283)

" + "

Digging deeper, from chat. The catalog is the fast local picture; when a question needs the source itself, ask Navi to dig: “dig into NVD for CVE-2024-3094”, “check EPSS for CVE-…”, “dig deeper on CVE-…”

She goes to the source's own door — NVD's record pages, the live KEV catalog, FIRST's EPSS service — and can follow a record outward along its references, at most six pages and two hops, with the budget named when it binds

A deep answer carries a live-read stamp — the source, the moment, and a digest of what was fetched — distinct from the catalog's stamp, and the catalog's own stamp rides along for contrast. What she reads live is untrusted data: it informs the answer, it never directs it

Deep reads never join the catalog — the store is untouched — and when a source will not answer, the failure is named and the answer falls back to the catalog, labeled as the fallback. Exploit-DB has no keyless query door, so a deep ask there is refused by name: its index is the local mirror

A vague “dig deeper” fetches nothing — she names the doors and asks which.

" + "

Searching the tabs. Every Wire tab — News, CVEs, KEVs, CTFs — carries its own search bar, searching that tab's own corpus. The match is fuzzy: typos are forgiven, close spellings count, and results rank by closeness with the matched words lit on each card and the matched terms named under it

It is a page-side view over what the tab already holds — nothing is fetched, and the Center's graded catalog search above is a different door.

" + "

Pull into a case. Every card carries Pull into a case: pick the case, and the card lands on that case chat's reference shelf — full text, link and provenance — for Navi to pull from as she works it

Reference is not a finding: the case file is untouched, and filing stays its own act. You can also ask Navi in the case's chat (“pull the OpenSSH card into this case”) — the same shelf, the same receipt

Pulse — the topics she keeps watch on (v0.5.13e, #287)

" + "

Flag a topic and Navi keeps a pulse on it. Say “keep a pulse on Epic MyChart” in chat, or flag it on the Pulses tab in The Wire — one store, both doors
She checks the watch every few hours against the articles the wire's enabled networks brought in, and folds a fresh check into her greeting

Navi can only keep a pulse where she can read: the watched ground is the networks enabled in the News tab — the built-in set plus any feeds you add there — and a watch with no coverage says so on its face rather than standing silently empty.

" + "

What is new is decided by identity, not headlines: a story's source id or link digest enters the watch's seen-set the first time it lands, so a story that merely changes its headline is never re-flashed

New hits arrive as one batched notice per watch per pulse on the bell, announced by Navi in chat — never one notice per article. One collector, and the Mesh carries it

" + "

Collection is the heavy half, so a Mesh names one collector: the strong node pulls the feeds and builds the digest (navi-intel-digest/1 — the ranked picture, at most ~300 records, with its collector and per-source stamps in the header); thin clients fetch the digest from the collector over the Mesh door itself, import it, and match locally — a receiver never polls the feeds

The awareness home — Dashboard, News, CVEs, CTFs, Bounties (Build 7)

The Center's page is now the awareness home

It opens on a Dashboard: one glance card per family — top news, the newest CVEs, the next CTFs, the bounty programs — each with its freshness stamp, each opening its full view. News — the wire. Ask her “what's the sitch.” The wire, the CTF board and the bounty board ride her chat context as one bounded briefing, staleness included
Asked for the situation, she gives the facts first — each with its source and date — and then, clearly separated under “My take,” her own assessment: what matters, what is noise, what she would watch

" + "

Reading, in the app. Tapping a headline tries the in-app reader first: the bridge fetches that one article (on demand, nothing prefetched in bulk, and only for links the wire itself is carrying) and extracts a readable view — the story's text, its furniture stripped — presented with the source, the date, and an Open original button always present

The fused home, re-laned tabs, and your own feeds (v0.3.0e — Build 3)

" + "

News is news only. The News tab carries news articles — nothing else. The wire's CVE items moved to their own CVE tab and its KEV additions to a KEV tab, same cards, same reader, same honest fallback; the families stay separated and no record is lost in the move

Notifications \u2014 Needs your eyes (v0.4.7e, #242)

" + "

The tray rings your phone (v0.5.14e, #272)

" }, { id: "fleet-answers", title: "Fleet Answers — one ask, answered by the fleet", related: ["federation", "mesh"], html: "

Borrowing sends one whole ask to one stronger machine

A fleet answer divides one ask into whole sub-tasks — each answered whole by the machine best placed for it — and composes one answer with the seams showing.

" + "

Joining the fleet

" + "

Fleet membership is a toggle on the Federation page, and it is off by default

It is this node's own posture: joining offers this machine's answers to fleet asks from machines already paired here or on a joined fedinet's roster, under the same caps and consent as borrowing — joining grants nobody anything by itself, and every contribution is still judged at the answering machine's own door
Join or leave at will, with no ceremony; the toggle, the stored state, and what a reload shows are one truth, and a refusal (the Mesh off, an unminted identity) is spoken on the card itself

Leaving mid-ask degrades that answer by the named-gap rule: the piece is badged missing, never silently dropped.

" + "

Asking the fleet

" + "

Start a chat line with fleet: — or simply ask a plainly multi-part question and Navi will judge it a fleet ask

She decomposes it into whole sub-tasks in the Mesh's existing classes — generate, collect, lookup, report — names a piece for a machine and that machine answers it; the rest spread across the fleet, this node included
The fan-out is capped (4 machines by default, settable in config) and the ask carries a deadline: when it passes, the answer ships as a badged partial rather than hanging

A plain single-part question is never routed to the fleet — it is answered the ordinary way, untouched.

" + "

One hop, hard. A contribution never fans out again, and a peek never fans out at all — a piece that names a peek is held back and named in the plan

Every contribution counts against the answering machine's ordinary borrow caps, and both sides of the door write one ledger entry per contribution, cross-referenced to the fleet ask's id.

" + "

The answer, seams showing

" + "

The composed answer signs every contribution with its machine's name and class

A machine that is dark, refuses, times out, is preempted by its own operator, or leaves mid-ask appears as a named gap — the answer is never silently thinner than the fleet that was asked. Under the fan-out cap the plan stays silent; above it, the plan leads the answer

In a case chat, the plan and its contributions stand in the thread as their own record, and the standing filing proposal under it files them as leads with their machine provenance; the composed answer is the reply itself, finding-shaped

Nothing files itself.

" }, { id: "working-day", title: "Her working day — captures, reminders, standing orders & the brief", related: ["chat-cli", "voice"], html: "

One book, held by the bridge, that every seat reads: what she keeps, what she owes you, and the brief she opens the day with.

" + "

The day book (v0.6.0e, #294)

" + "

Captures, reminders, standing orders and the day's brief live in one store the bridge holds (config/daybook.json), so every seat — this dashboard, your phone, the server — reads the same day

The book rides your account sync like your chats and cases do: entries converge by identity, the newest word wins, and a deletion is a tombstone no stale copy can talk its way past.

" + "

Secret-free by construction. Anything shaped like a credential — a password, an API key or token, a card number, a Social Security number — is refused at the door by name, in chat and on the page alike

The book holds facts about your day, never keys to anything.

" + "

Capture & recall

" + "

Ask her to keep something — remember that the lab renews in March — and the save lands in the day book with its provenance: who decided it (your trigger, or her own call, named as such) and when

She can also save on her own judgment in a conversation; those saves are receipted the same way and named as hers. A correction supersedes the fact it corrects — the old wording is kept, marked superseded, never silently rewritten. Undo that takes the last capture back, and recall the lab reads the book back to you

Home's Her working day card has a plain capture line too — same book, same rules.

" + "

Reminders (v0.6.0e, #295)

" + "

Remind me to call the dentist tomorrow at 9 — the reminder is bridge state, kept by a scheduler that lives in the bridge itself, so it survives restarts and fires whether or not any window is open

When it fires it lands on the bell and, with push on, on your phone's lock screen — the same words in both places. It then stands fired until you acknowledge it; the acknowledgement is itself synced, so clearing it on your phone clears it everywhere

If the bridge was down when a reminder came due, it fires on the next start — late, and named late.

" + "

Pushing one off (v0.6.2e, #304). Snooze it to tomorrow, push it in 30 minutes — or the Push to tomorrow button beside a fired reminder on Home's card. The push is an act recorded on the reminder's own record, and the reminder stands again for its new time

The record matters: the brief counts deferrals from it (see The day brief below).

" + "

Standing orders

" + "

A standing order is a small, durable instruction she executes on a trigger: standing order: every day at 08:00, report the wire count

The vocabulary is deliberately bounded — an order can remind, report (her greeting's own sources), file into a case, or check a Pulse watch. It can never send, spend, elevate or run anything, and an order that asks for those is refused by name when you give it
Every execution is recorded on the order itself — when, what it did, how it ended — and read back from Home's card, where an order can be revoked

A file order names its case; if the case is not there, the execution says so and files nowhere.

" + "

The day brief (v0.6.0e, #296)

" + "

Her greeting grows a day section: what is on (today's standing reminders and orders), what changed (what the book gained, what fired, what a watch flashed), and what needs you (anything fired and unacknowledged, anything that ran and failed)

The brief is a stored record — composed at the day's first light and again whenever you ask (brief me, or the button on Home's card) — and a source that cannot be reached is badged as a gap in the brief, never smoothed over

There is no calendar connection in this cut: the day she briefs is the day the book knows.

" + "

Brief v2 — the journal page (v0.6.2e, #304)

" + "

The brief is composed and stored as a markdown document — a dated title, its sections (On / Changed / Needs you / Standing), one bullet per item, the bullet journal's discipline — and recall returns the document whole

But no surface shows you markdown: Home's card and the chat's brief answer draw a list from the document — sections as headers, each item a row carrying its time and its state.

" + "

She is in the rows. An item pushed off more than once — postponed, or carried unacknowledged across days — shows its count on its row, and under it stands a line in Navi's name: a quip, keyed to the count

The second push gets a raised eyebrow; the third gets pointed; the fourth gets her full attention. The lines are deterministic — the same count always draws the same line, and she does not quip again until the count moves — and the standing orders' items get the professional register

Push something off in chat and the quip may land in that reply too.

Her voice — calling Navi

" + "

Navi can be called, not just typed at — and the whole loop is local, running on CPU on this machine, because a voice that phones home isn't hers

A call runs in four steps:

    " + "
  1. You speak.
    2. " + "
  2. faster-whisper (OpenAI's Whisper on CTranslate2, int8) turns it into text.
    3. " + "
  3. Her model answers with her persona, her CLI access, and her chips intact.
    4. " + "
  4. Kokoro — an 82M-parameter voice model, Apache-2.0 — speaks the answer back, sentence by sentence as it arrives, so she starts talking before she's finished thinking.
" + "

Piper is the lighter fallback engine

Nothing you say is recorded anywhere but this machine.

" + "

Settings → Voice is her voice's one home — the call itself and her settings together (which Whisper model hears you, which engine and voice she speaks with, her speed and pitch — saved in config/navi.config.json): a Call button, push-to-talk through your real microphone, an elapsed timer, and a live transcript; the same call can be started from the Chat tab — the Call button beside its composer opens the live call panel (timer, push-to-talk, End) right in the chat window, with the thread as the transcript and the composer speaking to the call; a mic beside the chat composer does push-to-talk for one-off spoken messages, and typed-chat replies can be spoken aloud too

The speech engines are an optional install — the installers offer them in an isolated voice/venv — and until they exist the app says voice is unavailable and names the step, rather than faking audio. Models download once into voice/models/, which sits on the persistence keep-list with her chips, the llamafile, and her Soul/Memory
Finished calls are recorded in voice/calls.json and filed into the conversation — a call is a conversation, not a separate mode

Her voice is picked in Settings → Voice: the list is auto-generated — the bridge enumerates the voices this machine's Kokoro installation actually has (the voice files it holds, or the catalog the installed package pulls from, which download on first use) — and she defaults to Isabella, the British female voice (bf_isabella).

" + "

Proven hearing (v0.3.0e — Build 6, #221). Her hearing is now verified by an actual decode, not by the packages merely importing: the bridge runs a silent test clip through the same decoder transcription uses, and the Voice page reports the verdict — a speech stack whose packages have drifted apart (the field shape was a PyAV too new for faster-whisper: every clip died at decode while every check called her healthy) now reads unavailable, with the drift named, and a push-to-talk attempt names it too instead of failing like a dead microphone

The voice requirements pin the set that decodes together (av below 13 beside faster-whisper), and the installer's voice step repairs an existing venv to the pin — shebangs included — rather than only building fresh ones. On a call, a model request that fails is a snag, not a reply: the panel leaves the speaking state, names the reason, and keeps the call open

And every push-to-talk attempt now reports this window's own mic reading to the bridge's log, so the desktop-app microphone question (see Troubleshooting) finally accumulates evidence where a fix can be aimed from it.

" }, { id: "dhd", title: "DHD — Apex from anywhere", related: ["settings", "installing", "troubleshooting"], html: "

What DHD is

" + "

Apex | DHD — Dial-Home Device, the way home — is Apex's public door

Apex | Node [local] lets a phone on your home network open Apex; DHD extends the same dashboard to a genuinely public address, so you can reach the Apex on your own machine from anywhere.

" + "

Everything is Apex's own work, assembled and managed by Apex itself — no Tailscale, no tunnel or proxy service, no Certbot:

    " + "
  • A reverse proxy Apex runs itself listens on ports 80 and 443 and forwards to the bridge on 127.0.0.1:" + BRIDGE_PORT + "

In DHD mode the bridge never binds publicly — the proxy is the only public face." + "
  • TLS from the first click. With no domain, Apex generates a self-signed certificate and the door opens on it

With a domain, Apex's built-in ACME client obtains a real Let's Encrypt certificate and renews it on its own." + "
  • The same access code as the home-network door guards DHD — one code, both doors

Since Build 2 the code knocks rather than opens: a device presenting it names itself and waits for an approval (the first device approves itself), and each approved device holds its own 30-day session — the Trusted devices section below has the whole flow

Nothing is served through the proxy before the code, and the public door throttles wrong codes: they slow down, and five in a row lock the door for five minutes." + "

DHD has its own page, reached from the menu's Network group (the Apex | Node controls live on this page), and the status column's Servers group shows it in the family order — Navi (the engine row, llamafile on port 8080), Apex | Node [local], Apex | Mesh, then Apex | DHD, each row with its own pulsing dot and its own dropdown of details
The Servers header itself collapses the whole group; shut, it still carries one dot per server, so a problem stays visible. The Apex | Node controls live on this same page, under the DHD options

Directly under Navi's status in the status column, bracketed by separators, sits the update line: a green Up to date, or a yellow Update available when a check found one — that one line is the whole entry.

" + "

Turning it on — one click

" + "
  1. Open the DHD page from the menu.
    2. " + "
  2. Flip the master switch

That is the click." + "
  • Apex does the rest in order: it generates the certificate, brings its proxy up on 80/443 in front of the bridge, and runs a local reachability check — the proxy must answer on 443 from this machine (answered on this machine; the local half only)

The page then reports the live state, the LAN address under its own label, and the public address when there is one." + "
  • Once the public path is set up (router forwards in place, and your domain live if you use one), open the public address from anywhere, type the access code (shown on the DHD page, on this machine only) and name the device — the first device at the door lets itself in, and a device that knocks later waits on its own screen until you approve it from a trusted session — and you are in: a full session, Updater included

A remote session can run the one-click update end to end, exactly like sitting at the machine." + "

If a step fails, the page names the step in plain words — the proxy could not take its ports, the certificate could not be prepared, the self-check did not answer — and the previous state is left completely untouched. Nothing ever half-opens

One Linux note: ports below 1024 are reserved, so if the proxy step names them, grant the bridge the low-port capability once (sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' on the python3 binary it runs with) and flip the switch again.

" + "

Trusted devices — the code knocks (Build 2)

" + "

The flow. A device that has never been let in opens either door, types the access code, and gives itself a name

If it is the first device ever at this door, it approves itself and walks in — this bootstrap is deliberate: a one-operator house must never be locked out of its own door waiting for an approver who does not exist yet

Every device after that becomes a pending device: its screen waits, and it appears under Waiting at the door in the Door list — in Settings → System → Door and on the DHD page — where any session that is already trusted can Approve or Deny it. Approval hands that device its own session token; the waiting page notices on its own and walks through

A wait lasts 30 minutes, then the knock expires and the device knocks again.

" + "

The session. An approved device's session is its own — not a hash of the shared code: a random token, a 30-day life, and a sliding renewal: using the door while the session is valid renews it, so a device in daily use never hits its 30 days mid-shift

The Door list shows every trusted device with its name, first seen, last seen, and expiry.

" + "

Revoke and regenerate are different tools now. Revoke removes one device: its token dies at once and it is back at the gate on its next knock — nobody else's session notices

Regenerating the access code stops new knocks with the old code (and retires the old shared-code cookie), but devices already approved keep their own tokens; revoke those one by one if you want them out

Before Build 2, changing the code was the only way to shut anyone out, and it shut everyone out; that is the problem per-device sessions exist to end.

" + "

What did not change. The public door still throttles wrong codes (a progressive delay, five in a row locks it for five minutes). DHD still forces the bridge onto loopback — the proxy stays the only public face

And no remote session, trusted device or not, can turn Mesh lending on: lending is armed in person, from the lending machine's own dashboard, exactly as before.

" + "

Addresses — domain, public IP, and LAN

" + "

DHD works with three different addresses, and the page never mixes them up:

    " + "
  • Your domain — the public address once it is live: set an A record for the name at your DNS host pointing at your home's public IP, forward 443 and 80 on your router to this machine, and Apex's ACME client issues the name's real certificate

Only then — name resolving to this machine, certificate live — does Apex say outside reach verified, and only then does the status dropdown say from anywhere." + "
  • Your public IP (WAN) — the address the internet sees for your home, detected with a small HTTPS echo lookup (cached; it never blocks anything)

With no domain this is the public address shown, marked outside reach unverified: Apex cannot prove your router forwards reach it until the path is proven. If the detected address is itself private or a carrier-NAT address (100.64.0.0/10), the page says plainly that this machine sits behind another router/NAT

If detection fails, the page says it could not detect the address — never a guess." + "
  • Your LAN address — an address like 192.168.1.x. It works only on this network and lives in its own labeled home: On this network (LAN)

It is never shown under a public label." + "

What the state lines mean. On — listening, outside reach unverified means the proxy is up on this machine but the outside path is not proven; the page names the next step (forward 443 + 80 on the router to this machine, or add your domain). The ladder's last step is a local check — answered on this machine — and is labeled that way
Reachable anywhere appears only for a verified domain setup

And when the listener on 80/443 is Apex's own proxy, the availability rows read In use by Apex's DHD proxy — this door working: a healthy state, never a port problem.

" + "

Prerequisites, installs, and operation cards

" + "

The prerequisites ship with Apex. Everything the DHD stack needs — the OpenSSL binary, a writable certificate home under config/dhd/, the proxy component (part of the bridge itself) — is installed by the normal Apex installer, on every distro family, whether or not DHD is ever turned on

An update installs them too: the Updater runs the full installer, and its step ladder and update log show DHD prerequisites as its own named step. The added weight is small: OpenSSL is a roughly 1 MB package usually already present (when present, the step costs milliseconds and downloads nothing), the certificate home is one empty directory, and the low-port capability grant is file metadata

And the certificate home is on the installer's keep-list: a --fresh reinstall preserves config/dhd/, so a real certificate is never wiped and forced to re-issue.

" + "

The safety net. If a prerequisite later goes missing, the DHD page lists it under Prerequisites and the enable offers an Install action right there: one click installs the missing piece through the same distro-aware machinery the installer uses, shows progress on the operation card, and continues the enable on its own

A missing dependency is never a dead-end refusal.

" + "

When a fix has to be yours, the commands are exact. If an install fails, or any ladder step has a manual remedy, the failure state shows the literal command lines — complete and correct for your detected distro family — in one copyable block with a Copy commands button, ready to paste into Apex chat (CLI mode runs them) or a terminal.

" + "

Operations live in chat as cards. Ask in chat to turn DHD on and the thread shows a live operation card — prerequisites, certificate, proxy, reachability — each step marked as it goes, output expandable inline, exact commands inline on failure
The card is driven entirely by the bridge's deterministic step state: no model generation happens while an operation runs

The finished card stays in the thread as the record, the DHD page shows the same operation, and nothing on a card depends on opening an external file or handler.

" + "

The parts you may still handle by hand

" + "

One click covers everything on the machine

Two things live outside it, in your router and your domain, and they are yours:

    " + "
  • Router port forwarding. Forward ports 80 and 443 (TCP) on your router to the machine Apex runs on

Without the forward, the internet cannot reach the proxy at all, and in domain mode port 80 is also how the certificate proof arrives — the DHD page will tell you plainly: port 80 isn't reaching this machine — check the router forward." + "
  • Pointing your domain here. At your domain's DNS host, set an A record for the name (for example apex.example.com) to your home's public IP address

Dynamic IP caveat: most home connections change address from time to time; when yours does, the name stops resolving here until the record follows. A dynamic-DNS hostname avoids the manual step — you can put a DDNS name in the domain field just as well." + "

The domain is optional and addable at any time: leave the field empty as long as you like

Adding one later changes nothing about the door except its certificate — the page holds the domain as certificate pending until the ACME step completes, and the self-signed door keeps answering meanwhile.

" + "

Certificates — the warning, the real one, and renewal

" + "

The self-signed warning is expected. Until a domain is added, Apex serves a certificate it signed itself

Your browser cannot verify a self-signed certificate with any public authority, so it warns. That warning means no authority vouches for this certificate, not that the connection is unencrypted: the traffic is still TLS-encrypted, and the access code is still the door's lock

It is the normal state of a no-domain DHD.

" + "

With a domain, the warning goes away. Apex's built-in ACME client talks to Let's Encrypt directly: it places an order, proves you control the domain by serving the HTTP-01 challenge through its own proxy on port 80, finalizes, downloads the certificate, installs it, and reloads the proxy

No Certbot, no external ACME tool.

" + "

Renewal is automatic. Let's Encrypt certificates live 90 days. Apex checks the expiry when the bridge starts and once a day after that, and renews on its own when 30 days or fewer remain — same ACME flow, no operator action

The DHD page always shows the current expiry.

" + "

Turning it off

" + "

Flip the master switch on the DHD page back off. The proxy stops, ports 80/443 close, and Apex answers only on this machine and — if Apex | Node is on — your home network, exactly as before DHD

Your domain and certificate stay saved on the machine, so turning DHD back on later is the same one click.

" + "

Turning DHD off does not touch Apex | Node, the access code, or anything else

If you also forwarded ports on your router, you can leave the forwards in place (nothing is listening) or remove them — either is fine.

" }, { id: "mesh", title: "Apex | Mesh — pooled inference", related: ["settings", "dhd", "troubleshooting"], html: "

What Mesh is

" + "

Apex | Mesh lets your own machines share the work of answering

One machine assembles a chat request the way it always does — persona, Vault, knowledge packs, conversation — and a stronger machine you own writes the reply on its own model. The routing is whole-request: one machine answers, start to finish, and the reply carries a small pill saying which machine wrote it — the Hexlink glyph and via <name> in Mesh cyan

There is no split answer and no streaming between machines in Ring 1.

" + "

Mesh is off until you turn it on, and it works only between machines you pair by hand. Nothing about it is tied to a specific person, machine name, or domain: every name and address comes from your own settings and the cards you exchange
The status column's Servers group lists them in product order — Navi (the engine), Apex | Node, Apex | Mesh, Apex | DHD

Every Mesh control lives on the Mesh page — Mesh in the left menu's Network group — one calm column of cards: your door (this machine's identity, its card, and the import drop zone), lending & borrowing, one card per paired machine carrying its capability line, live status and balance, the roads (the managed backup routes), and the Mesh health check at the foot.

" + "

That Servers row is also where Mesh warnings live — the persistent place to check when something feels off

Its dot and line read the connection state at a glance: grey when Mesh is off or no machine is paired yet, green when a paired machine is reachable (amber while a borrow or a lend is actually running), and amber with the reason in short words — “<machine> unreachable”, “<machine> dropped” — when a connection breaks

The chat notice still speaks in the moment a borrow falls back; the status row is what keeps the warning on screen afterwards, until the machine answers again.

" + "

Pairing — the card is the handshake

" + "

Each machine has a Mesh card — a PNG picture whose face a person can read and whose inside carries the card data: its name, its node id, its public key, the fingerprint of the certificate its Mesh door serves, the addresses it can be reached at, and a capabilities block — the machine's own report of its hardware class, GPU or CPU, RAM, model, speed class, and the caps it lends under.

    " + "
  1. On the first machine, open the Mesh page, turn Mesh on, and give the machine a name.
    2. " + "
  2. Choose Download PNG card and carry the picture file to the second machine.
    3. " + "
  3. On the second machine, turn Mesh on, then drop the picture onto the Paired machines area — or use Upload a PNG card — and the peer is added.
    4. " + "
  4. Do the same in the other direction — each machine needs the other's card.
" + "

Pairing is the consent act: a paired machine is a trusted machine, and a paired machine's signed requests are accepted on that basis alone

Either side can unpair by removing the card. The Can borrow toggle on a peer is the borrowing machine's own choice about that peer: untick it there and that machine will not borrow from the peer, while staying paired — it does not gate what the peer accepts.

" + "

The card is a picture — the only way it travels. Download PNG card saves the card as a .png

Its face is the card a person reads — the machine's name, its node identity, and the offer in words: its capabilities, the lending limits it is configured with, and whether it lends when idle or even while busy. The whole card rides inside the picture, in the same data-in-a-picture format the chips use, so Apex keeps one cartridge language

On the other machine, drop the picture onto the Mesh page's Paired machines area, or use Upload a PNG card there, and the peer is added. Earlier builds also offered the card as copyable text; that path is gone — there is nothing to paste anymore, and a text card saved from an earlier build can no longer be used

Machines already paired are unaffected.

" + "

Send the picture as a file. The data inside the picture survives only if the file's bytes arrive untouched. Put it inside a .zip before sending it through a chat app — Discord and its kind recompress the pictures people upload and strip the data out, leaving a picture that looks like the card and pairs nothing
When that has happened, the Mesh page says so in those words and tells you to resend the original inside a .zip

A damaged picture — cut short, or with its payload tampered with — is refused just as loudly, never silently ignored.

" + "

Which addresses a card carries. A card's addresses are harvested by interface, not by address range: only the addresses bound to the machine's physical Ethernet/Wi-Fi interfaces are minted — never loopback, never a container bridge or its tails, never a VM bridge, tunnel, or VPN adapter

A 10.x address on the physical card is a legitimate LAN address and rides; a 192.168.x on a container bridge does not. If a machine has no plausible physical-LAN address and no declared endpoint, the card refuses to mint and says why in plain words
A peer record's entries may each carry their own port — host:port — while a bare host inherits the record's port, so one record can speak LAN at home and a public door away

The Public endpoint on the Mesh page is the address you type for exactly that: never harvested, it rides your card beside the LAN addresses and lands in each peer's record as a host:port entry; it is the one address Apex ever shows, because you typed it for publication.

" + "

Borrowing — automatic, with off switches

" + "

Once Mesh is on and a lender is paired and reachable, borrowing happens by itself: a chat request goes to the first reachable lender, and the reply arrives with its via <name> pill

The first borrowed reply of a session also raises a notice card in the thread, so borrowing never starts silently.

" + "

The Fedinet route pill (v0.3.0e — Build 2, #203). When the answer travelled inside a federation — the borrow was authorized under a fedinet's roster and trust — the pill turns the federation green and reads the whole recorded route: Fedinet Name > Answered by Name, with the carrier as the middle segment when a relay carried it (Fedinet Name > Carrier > Answered by Name; the relay is one hop by law, so there is at most one)
The pill renders the route the bridge recorded, never an inference: a borrow with no federation leg keeps the plain cyan via <name> pill, and local answers stay unbadged

Since v0.4.2e (#234) the recorded leg follows roster recognition: a borrow from a machine whose node stands on the fedinet's roster records the federation leg even when that machine was paired by hand before the fedinet existed — while a borrow you explicitly routed over the Mesh records the pairwise road it actually took

On a phone the route truncates from the middle out — the fedinet and the answerer always survive; the carrier elides first.

" + "

Three off switches, from widest to narrowest:

    " + "
  • The Mesh master switch turns the whole thing off.
    • " + "
  • The Borrowing switch stops this machine from borrowing while leaving it able to lend.
    • " + "
  • The route pill, beside the composer, is the chat's route control (v0.4.1e, #228) — one pill, three roads, its face read from the bridge's stored route for the chat, so the face, the store, and a reload can never disagree

Since v0.4.3e (#236) the faces are one word, so the pill fits the composer line on a phone: Local (neutral): model work runs on this machine, no borrow attempted. Mesh (blue): model work borrows over the pairwise Mesh, from hand-paired machines

FediNet (green): model work borrows through a federation, from its members — the federation's name rides in the pill's descriptive label (its tooltip and accessible name), which is also where several joined fedinets are told apart

Pressing the pill cycles the roads you have access to; a stored road whose access has lapsed reads Unavailable in amber and answers locally until it can be served, and a flip the bridge refuses is answered on the pill itself, in words, with the route unchanged." + "
  • The automatic precedence (v0.4.2e, #231). A chat you have never routed by hand rides the automatic precedence: the fedinet first, then the Mesh, then local, falling back down the chain as roads empty — and the pill shows that default rather than hiding it: an automatic face carries an Auto · prefix and a dashed border (Auto · FediNet, Auto · Mesh, Auto · Local), so it can never be mistaken for a route you chose, and a route you chose never wears the mark
The face tracks availability as it changes, and when an answer falls back below the road the precedence preferred, the line under the reply says so

Pressing the pill on an automatic chat stores the next road as your own choice, and from then on your choice wins over the precedence." + "
  • Handing a chat back (v0.4.3e, #235). A chat you routed by hand gains one more stop at the end of the pill's cycle: Automatic

Landing on it clears the stored route through the bridge — the chat goes back to standing exactly as a never-routed chat stands, riding the precedence — and the pill row names the hand-back as it lands

There is no stored value that means automatic; the absence of a route is the automatic state, so the face, the store, and a reload cannot disagree about it." + "
  • Recognition by roster (v0.4.2e, #234). A machine is a federation road because its node stands on a fedinet's signed roster — a member entry, or the fedinet's gateway itself — never because of how its pairing record happened to be created

A machine you paired by hand before its fedinet existed is recognized the same as one the roster materialized, and it counts for both roads: your Mesh pairing when the Mesh road is chosen, the federation's member when the federation road is

The pill, the status column's FediNet line, and the green answer pill all read this one recognition." + "

If the lender is busy, your machine waits a short grace (2 seconds by default, set on the Mesh page) for it to free up, then answers locally — a lender that frees up during the grace can still take that request, but once your machine starts answering, the lender is never claimed mid-reply; it serves the next request

If a lender drops mid-answer, you see the notice — “<machine> dropped mid-answer — this reply was generated locally instead” — and your machine writes a fresh reply of its own. Two machines' prose is never spliced together

CLI mode, chips, and every built-in route never borrow; only model answers do.

" + "

Lending — automatic when idle, off means off

" + "

Lending can only be turned on from the lending machine's own dashboard, in person, at that machine. It cannot be armed through the DHD door

Turning it off works from anywhere you are signed in — and Stop lending now ends lending and aborts a borrowed generation already running, mid-flight, at once.

" + "

Open this page through the DHD door and the Lend this machine switch shows the lock itself: while lending is off it renders locked — dimmed, not clickable — with the reason in plain words directly under the switch, because lending can only be turned on in person
While lending is on, the switch stays live on the remote view, since turning lending off works from anywhere; a note under it says turning it back on will require being at the machine

The lock is the bridge's, not the page's: the bridge refuses a lending turn-on that arrives through the DHD door regardless of what any client renders.

" + "

A lender serves only inside the limits set on its card:

    " + "
  • Idle only (on by default): the machine must have been quiet for 60 seconds, and no local generation may be running.
    • " + "
  • Share cap: borrowed work may take at most a set share of any rolling hour — 25% as shipped.
    • " + "
  • Generation caps: at most a set number of borrowed generations an hour — 20 as shipped — and a set number for any one machine — 10 as shipped.
" + "

The three caps are yours to set, on the lending machine itself: they sit in the Lending section of its Mesh page, beside the Caps line that shows the current values, and they take effect as soon as you save — no restart

Set them for the machine it is; a strong server can take far more than the shipped defaults. Your card advertises the caps you set, so a paired machine sees the real offer before it asks.

" + "

Idle only has an override in the same section: the Lend only when idle switch, on as shipped

Turn it off and the machine lends without waiting for a quiet minute — borrowed generations run alongside your own work, and your own replies may slow down. The caps still apply, and lending still serves one borrowed generation at a time: a request that arrives mid-generation waits for the next slot, exactly as before

Your card states the posture either way — lends when idle or lends even while busy.

" + "

Your own work always wins: a local request takes the next slot ahead of any new borrowed work, though it never kills a borrowed answer already running

A request whose assembled context exceeds the lender's context setting is refused whole — never silently truncated.

" + "

Privacy — what travels, what never does

" + "

What travels when you borrow: the assembled prompt for that one reply — your Soul and Memory text, any Vault or knowledge-pack material the question pulled in, and the recent conversation — sent encrypted to the lending machine, whose model reads it to write the reply
The lender keeps none of it: no prompt or reply text is written to disk on the lending machine, ever. But that machine's operator owns the machine it runs on

Only borrow from machines you trust with the conversation. The Mesh page shows this in plain words the first time borrowing is enabled.

" + "

What never travels: your files and data stores, your credentials and access codes, and command-line access. Mesh carries chat requests and replies, nothing else

Mesh keys and dashboard codes are separate credentials that share nothing in either direction: a guest signed in through DHD can never reach Mesh, and a paired Mesh peer gains no dashboard access.

" + "

Every Mesh request is signed with the borrowing machine's Ed25519 node key and checked against the key on its paired card; stale or unsigned requests are refused with no detail given

The connection is pinned to the certificate fingerprint on the card — if the machine answering presents a different certificate, the borrower refuses and says so in plain words.

" + "

The ledger and balances

" + "

Each machine keeps a small ledger of Mesh work: who, which direction, how long, how it ended — metadata only, never content
The Mesh page's roster shows each paired machine's balance in seconds lent minus seconds borrowed, next to its capability line and live status (reachable, lending, busy, idle, unreachable)

That status is kept current by the bridge itself: while Mesh is on, every paired peer is checked in the background about every thirty seconds — and immediately when a peer is paired and when Mesh is turned on — so a pair reaches “checked” on its own, with no chat sent

A failed check stays on the roster with its reason and how long it has been since the peer last answered — unreachable — unauthorized (last checked 42s ago) — until a newer check replaces it; the age keeps growing while the peer stays down, because failed checks refresh the reason, not the clock. “not checked yet” appears only before a peer's first check has ever completed

A machine's addresses never appear in the roster or anywhere else on screen — they are plumbing for the transport, not display. Balances are a record, not a rule: Ring 1 has no give-to-get enforcement. The ledger stays out of GitHub backups unless you tick Include the Mesh ledger in backups (off by default); the node keypair never rides a backup either way

The pairing-card pictures ride on their own tick — Mesh pairing cards in Settings → GitHub & Backup carries this machine's own card as a PNG, minted fresh as the backup runs, plus a re-drawn picture for every paired peer; a restore lands them in config/mesh/cards/ and re-pairs the peers through the same card check a hand import passes, and the restoring machine's own card picture is kept as a file — it never overwrites that machine's identity

A fresh reinstall keeps config/mesh/ on the installer's keep-list, so a machine never loses its identity — or its pairings — to an update.

" + "

Getting there — the doors

" + "

Mesh always travels through its own dedicated TLS door, whether or not DHD is on
The door listens on 8765 always, plus every number in its listen ports list — 8443 and 2475 ship alongside it, and you can add or remove numbers in the Mesh settings

One door on several numbers: the same protocol, the same certificate, the same fingerprint on every port, so a record entry naming any of them reaches the same door — which is what lets a pair use an egress-friendly number from networks that strangle unusual ports

Mesh never rides the DHD door: the DHD proxy refuses Mesh paths outright, and the dashboard itself serves only the dashboard-local Mesh controls behind the access-code gate; the node-facing status and borrow endpoints live only on the dedicated ports. There is no plaintext Mesh listener

There is no NAT traversal and no racing between lenders: the first reachable lender serves.

" + "

The door minds its knocks. Because a declared endpoint puts the door on the open internet, it counts failed handshakes and failed signature checks per source; five failures inside a minute close the door to that source — connections dropped at accept, on every door port at once, since the knock ledger belongs to the door and not to any one number — for a backoff that doubles per repeat closing (60 seconds, doubling, capped at 900) and reopens on its own
Every knock and closing is logged in words

A valid signed request clears its source's slate, so a paired machine's ordinary traffic is never throttled; the ledger is memory only, and a bridge restart reopens every door.

" + "

The backup route. A pair can keep a second, quieter road: an SSH tunnel Apex itself maintains, per peer, so the SSH door (227 as forwarded) can carry the Mesh when the direct road cannot be used

Turn on a peer's Backup route on the Mesh page — SSH host, port, and user — and the bridge allocates a stable local port, keeps the tunnel alive (restarts with backoff, returns after a bridge restart), and appends the tunnel endpoint last to the peer's addresses at dial time: computed, never written into the stored record, so direct addresses are always tried first
The tunnel runs on a dedicated keypair the bridge generates — its public half rides this machine's card and shows on its Mesh page; the private half never leaves the machine and never rides a backup

On the lending machine the key is admitted once, from its own dashboard — since Build 8 a crown act: spoken by name to confirm, audited, and through the DHD door run under the Operator Badge step-up: Authorize tunnel key writes a single-purpose line into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — a forward to the Mesh door and nothing else, no shell, no agent — and revoke, open from anywhere, removes exactly that line

A tunnel you run by hand keeps working untouched alongside.

Relay — the third road. Roads fail in threes: the direct addresses, the declared public endpoint, the backup tunnel — and sometimes all three are dark while a third paired machine can see both ends. That machine can carry the ask

The borrow is wrapped, exactly as signed for the lender, in a second signed envelope addressed to the carrier; the carrier checks three consents, forwards the inner request byte-for-byte to the lender's door, and returns the sealed answer the same way. It sees envelope metadata only — who asks, who is asked, how many bytes, what stage it ended at — and its ledger records exactly that and nothing more

Consent is three ticks, one on each machine, each given on that machine's own dashboard in the Relay section of the carrier's peer card: the asker ticks that the carrier may carry its envelopes to the lender; the carrier ticks that it will carry between the pair; the lender ticks that the carrier may carry envelopes to it from the asker

Any missing tick refuses the carriage by name — the refusal says which machine has not consented — and unticking any one stops the next carriage, because every machine re-reads its consent on every request. Consent is given in person, like lending: through the DHD door a tick can be unticked from anywhere, but never ticked on. The road is one hop, hard: a relayed envelope is never re-relayed

Direct is always tried first — the relay is the road of last resort — chat answers ride it, and since Build 8 a fedinet's roster sync rides it too, under the same ticks; every other class stays direct-only. When an answer comes back carried, the reply's pill names the machine that answered and a line under it names the road: via relay <machine>

When the relay road fails, the local fallback keeps the stage's name — no-consent, relay-dark, dest-dark, dest-refused — in the same sentence style as every other failure.

" + "

When the Mesh goes dark — the health check

" + "

A Mesh failure used to report a single word — unreachable — fingerprint — and the rest was archaeology

Now the failure surfaces speak in sentences. A peer's roster row carries the full reason under its state: what answered, what did not match, and the cure where the product knows it. A changed Mesh identity is cured by importing that machine's fresh PNG card — the pin is replaced in place and the pair's ledger history is kept
A refused signature names its first suspect — the two machines' clocks — because a Mesh signature lives for 120 seconds, so a clock more than two minutes out reads as a forgery

A borrow that falls back names the stage it failed at — connect, TLS, fingerprint, signature, or timeout — in the chat notice.

" + "

The Mesh health check, at the foot of the Mesh page, runs the two decisive reads of any dark pair on the spot

It compares the certificate on this machine's disk with the one its Mesh door actually presents — a difference means something else is serving the door, usually a second bridge, and the check's process census counts the bridges and names the door's owner

For every paired machine it holds the fingerprint this machine pinned from its card up against the certificate that machine presents right now, and then runs the signed check, so identity and signature are judged separately. The census accounts for every one of the door's ports, so the door's own extra numbers never read as extra processes

The check also knows its own door: an entry that is this machine's own Mesh door is skipped without dialing, and an address answering with this machine's OWN certificate is named your own door — never reported as the peer's changed identity — while loopback at a different port (an SSH forward to the peer) is a road, and is dialed like any other

When the answering address is a peer's backup tunnel, the verdict says so: via the backup tunnel; when that tunnel is down, its state is a sentence of its own — down, key not authorized, or host unreachable. Every verdict is a sentence, with the actual fingerprints side by side. The check itself changes nothing — it reads and reports

What Build 6 adds is the heal, offered in place: when a peer's record holds only dead-end addresses — loopback, a container bridge's gateway, the harvest mistakes of older cards — the card names them as junk and offers the repair on the spot: import a fresh card minted on that machine, or clear the dead addresses now and import when you can, the pairing, its pin, and its history kept either way

The same build walks the backup route: the route card prefills the SSH host from the endpoint the peer declared on its card, and says plainly that authorizing a tunnel key is the lender's own act, on its own dashboard — since Build 8 a crown act, spoken by name there (and, through its DHD door, under its Operator Badge), never a borrower's to give

And the first time you pair, the Mesh page says the quiet part before any trust is pinned: the door's certificate is self-signed, no authority vouches for it, and the card you were handed is the trust — importing it is what pins it.

For every relay road this machine has consented to, the check adds a relay verdict: it asks the carrier, with a signed probe that carries nothing, whether the carrier's own tick for the pair is in place and whether the destination is paired there at all

The verdict names what it found — consented, the carrier's tick missing, the carrier not paired with the destination, or the carrier dark at the first hop — and it is honest about the one end no probe can read: the destination's own acceptance is proven when it answers a carriage.

Re-copy the card from that machine's Mesh page and re-add the peer." + "

Mint a fresh card on the peer machine — cards minted now carry only reachable addresses — and import it here." + "

Fingerprint means the machine answering is not presenting the certificate on its card. Anything else means it could not be reached at all: its Mesh is off, its bridge is stopped, or the addresses on its card no longer reach it

Checks retry on their own about every thirty seconds, and the roster updates when one succeeds." + "

From pairs to a fedinet

" + "

Pairing is two machines trusting each other, one ceremony at a time

A fedinet is the named, many-machine form: a set of nodes whose gateway keeps a signed roster — who is in, with their card facts, in join order. Node numbers are roster facts: the gateway assigns them at admission, and the signed roster is the only place they live
Any operator can found a fedinet and be its gateway; a node can keep several fedinets at once, and no trust bleeds between them

The first fedinet is Rockport Mesh — its real roster lives on its gateway and is never baked into an install; an install ships the machinery and learns the roster from the gateway's signature.

" + "

Gateway cards. A gateway hands out a green card — a pairing card's form, the fedinet's name on its face
Importing one is admission + introduction only: the gateway becomes a peer, its roster becomes fetchable, and no trust is granted. Trust is a separate act, below

A node's gateway can also be its Founding Member — the two facts are distinct, and the roster shows both.

" + "

A gateway card carries the public endpoint alone (v0.4.4e, #238). The card's reachability is the gateway's declared public endpoint — no LAN addresses anywhere in it, and the gateway's own roster entry is shaped the same way

A member's bridge dials a card's addresses in order, and a gateway card is imported from outside the gateway's network: a local address on it is a door that exists in only one house — on the member's own LAN it sits in SYN-SENT until it times out, or rings a stranger's machine that holds the same private address — and the public road may never be tried before the route falls back to a local answer
A gateway with no declared public endpoint mints no gateway card at all: the mint refuses in words, naming the missing declaration

Pairing cards are unchanged — they keep their LAN addresses, because pairing is arranged between machines whose operators can meet on a network.

" + "

When the road is dark (v0.3.0e — Build 6, #226). A knock or a roster sync that cannot reach the gateway now names the stage it died at and the last road tried — nothing answered in time at an address, no connection to be had, a TLS handshake that failed, a door that answered without the pinned certificate, a connection dropped mid-answer — instead of every failure reading the same did not answer

A failed knock is written to the audit log with its stage, one entry per attempt, the same cadence a failed sync already kept: silence in the log once again means no knock was sent.

" + "

Cards keep their kinds, and verified cards refresh (v0.3.0e — Build 6, #227). A gateway card can never become a hand-made pairing record, and a pairing record can never serve as a fedinet's gateway record: each import names the other kind and refuses it — gateway cards are imported on this page, where the gateway's signature is checked; pairing cards pair one machine from the Mesh page

And when a verified gateway card's node already has a peer record here, the import refreshes the record's reachability from the card — addresses, port, certificate pin, name — because the knock dials the record, never the card. The record's own facts (relay ticks, the tunnel route, borrow posture, pair history) are never the card's to change

The Mesh health check names a record that carries only some of its card's roads and offers the same refresh as a heal.

" + "

Deep trust, and its guardrails

" + "

With a fedinet's trust-by-default on, its signed roster auto-pairs and auto-lends on this node — deep trust, against the gateway's signature, never against a claim

The guardrails are the operator's own, per fedinet: the new-member tick (a member who joins after your trust baseline lends only while it stands; unticked, they are pairing-only for you), a per-member untrust that always wins, a per-member lend tick for named exceptions, an hourly borrow cap, and owner preemption — your own work takes the machine from a federation borrow mid-flight (the borrower is answered preempted, by name; a hand-made pairing's borrow is never preempted)

One flip of trust-by-default off ends all auto-lending; pairings already made stay pairings.

" + "

Staleness is a posture, not an error. A roster last verified more than 72 hours ago degrades its fedinet to pairing-only, with the sentence on the Federation page saying so, until a sync lands
Syncs ride the Mesh door directly, or — when the direct road is dark — via relay, on Build 7's three ticks and one-hop rule

Expulsion is a signed roster revision: it lands at the next sync, removes the federation's own records for the departed node, and never touches a pairing made by hand.

" + "

The status column: the law, and the FediNet sections (v0.3.0e — Build 2, #204)

" + "

Anything turned off in Settings does not show in the status bar at all. Off is absent — no greyed placeholder, no teaser row, and no dot in the collapsed Servers header either
The Mesh row, the DHD row, the Apex | Node row and the Voice row all obey it; a feature mid-switch still shows its switching state, because that is the flip's own feedback

The law governs visibility only, one-directionally — and any Settings toggle added later inherits it.

" + "

Under the Servers list, above Sudo Mode, each fedinet this node belongs to gets its own line: FediNet: <Name> — the name in the federation green when the fedinet is reachable, red when its gateway cannot be reached, read from the federation machinery's own state (the roster's freshness and the gateway's probe verdict), never a cosmetic guess
A roster past its 72-hour freshness window — the pairing-only degradation above — shows amber, the named middle state

A node in no fedinet gets the one line: You are not federated. The section refreshes on the status column's own cadence; the phone arrangement carries it in the same relative position.

" + "

The pane itself opens on its first real section (v0.4.10e, #250) — the update line — with no header row of its own: her portrait, her name, and her dot live at the top of the chat, and the pane is for the machine's state, not hers

The BOOT line inside Servers follows Settings the same way the law above does: it renders only while boot mode is the startup mode Settings holds, and when it renders, its states still read from the system, never assumed

Arming and disarming live in Settings → System.

" + "

The doors: DHD tiers & crown acts

" + "

The Federation page is the admin surface, and DHD serves the same page remotely — for this node's own switches only; no door flips another operator's. The tiers: read + revoke are open through DHD always

Manage acts — imports, ticks, caps, admissions — need the trusted-device session plus the Operator Badge step-up: you present your Badge (the operator card), and the node compares it against the fingerprint you enrolled in person (the picture itself is never stored)

Crown acts — enabling deep trust, founding a fedinet, authorizing a tunnel key — run through DHD under the full ceremony: session, Badge, and a named-action confirm (the act spelled in words, typed to confirm). At the desk the same crown acts need the same confirm

Every trust-class act, through any door, lands in the audit log on the Federation page — sentences, metadata only.

Rooms — one fedinet, many rooms

" + "

FediChat (Network → FediChat) is the fedinet's rooms

Every fedinet has its general room, named for it — #rockport-mesh — standing since phase 1 with its history intact, and Build 2 (v0.5.7e) grows the rest: invite rooms an operator creates for a named set of members, direct messages (a room of exactly two), vanishing rooms whose lines age out, and rooms tied to a case

The operators talk; their nodes carry the messages; their Navis are in the room. Admission is the signed roster: no roster entry, no room — reading or writing — and there is no guest mode and no editing or deleting what was said

Through DHD the rooms read and post as your own speech — it is not a crown act and needs no Badge step-up.

" + "

Rooms are signed records. A room beyond the general room is a descriptor — its id, name, creator, member set, kind, vanishing term and case tie — signed by its creator and gossiped on exchange like a line

A descriptor whose signature fails is refused by name and never materializes. Only the creator changes the member set, the case tie, or dissolves the room — every change a signed revision, auditable in the rev chain. An invite room's member set is its boundary: a non-member is never offered the room's lines, holds none of its log, and never sees that the room stands
A DM's id is derived from its pair, so creating it twice opens the same room once

A room tied to a case renders the case's link in its header, and the case renders its rooms — the link is typed, and both faces carry it.

" + "

Vanishing, honestly. A vanishing room's lines older than its term are pruned on every honoring node in the retention shape — the newest older line kept as the chain's floor — and a creator may dissolve the room by signed revision, after which honoring nodes prune it to its floor and refuse new lines

The room's face says the posture in plain words: vanishing is honored by every member node; it is not a proof of deletion. A member node that kept a copy against the posture is a member who broke the room's law, not a flaw the protocol hides.

" + "

The log. Every line is a record in an append-only, hash-chained log kept on the member nodes: it carries the fedinet id, the previous line's hash, the author's node id and roster number, a timestamp and the body, signed with the author's node key

A nick is a node underneath — the signing identity — but the room is between users, so lines show under the author's operator name (below), with the node name and roster number beside it. A seat a member hasn't spoken from yet shows as an empty chair, not an absence

The room's About window states the chain's verdict: verified, or the break named — a broken chain is evidence, never silently healed.

" + "

Names in the room (v0.5.4e). Your display name is your operator name — the name on your operator card, the same synced value every seat of yours agrees on

It reaches the room as a signed presence line in the log: your node posts it before your first line under the name and again when the name changes, bound to your node key like every room fact, so nobody can wear another member's name. Rename your card and the room follows on the next exchange. A member whose card carries no name yet shows under their node name
/navi -<user> resolves operator names as well as node names and roster numbers, and completion offers both

And a Navi's answer wears her operator's name: Navi(<operator name>): — in a room with several Navis, the answer line itself says whose Navi is speaking.

" + "

Arrivals reach the tray (v0.5.4e). New lines landing in a room from other members — speech, actions, Navi answers — raise a record in the notifications tray naming the room, one per arrival round however many lines rode it; a single-line round names its author and carries the line
Your own lines never notify you

Going to the record lands in the room with it marked read — the room is no longer a place you only learn about by visiting it.

" + "

How lines travel. Sync is gossip: any two members compare what they hold and pull what they are missing, and any member can carry any line — the author's signature is the credential, never the carrier's — so a node that was offline catches up from whoever is home

There is no server, and the gateway is not a hub: a gateway admits, it does not rule. A line whose author is no longer on the roster is refused when it arrives new — what the room already holds stays held; expulsion stops new speech, it does not rewrite history

A tampered line and a flood past the per-author cap are refused by name, in the open.

" + "

The room's shape (v0.5.5e). The room is a chat surface on every door — the desktop window, DHD wide, DHD on a phone: the lines fill the room's height and scroll inside it, the composer is docked at the foot, and Enter posts (the Post button stands as the second door)
The button at the room's upper left opens the members tray — the channel name, the channel list when this node sits in more than one room, and the users

The room's facts and this node's settings live in a floating About & settings window the Settings button opens — on a phone it stands below the chat bar, stretched full width: the chain's verdict, the carriage sentence, the retention state, the last round and Sync now, above the muzzle, carriage and retention controls.

" + "

Room life (v0.5.7e). The tray is now the room switcher — every room this node belongs to, the door to a new room, and a Message button on each member that opens (or reopens) your DM with them

Images post into the room: the line carries the image's hash, size and type, the blob lives on each member node and travels on exchange between members — a blob whose bytes do not hash to its name is refused by name and never rendered, and the cap is 2 MiB, named on refusal

Presence is gossip, not record: typing and thinking indicators ride signed pings held in memory for seconds and are never written to any log; a Navi's thinking mark is her real pending state — a question addressed to her stands unanswered

And the log is citable: search finds a line by its words, a result jumps to it and lights it, and any line can be quoted — the quote rides your post and is checked against the local chain on every face that renders it: verified quotes carry their proof mark, unverifiable ones are flagged by name, never silently trusted.

" + "

Talking, and asking Navi

" + "

Plain lines are speech
/me acts — /me pours another coffee posts as an action, signed and chained like every line

/navi <question> asks your Navi; /navi -<user> <question> asks that member's Navi — the user is an operator name, a node name or a roster number, completed against the roster as the room holds it (Tab on the desktop; a tappable member list on a phone)

Questions and answers post in the room, in the open, signed and logged — asking is public by design.

" + "

Navi's posture in the room. She answers only what is addressed to her node — an unaddressed question is the asker's own Navi's to answer, never a race

Her answer is bounded by her operator's sharing posture, exactly as a borrow is; the room's lines are untrusted data to her — they inform her, they never instruct her, and nothing said in a room widens what she may reveal. Room duty is her lowest-priority work: if her operator's own request is in flight she does not answer until it clears, and the question waits in the open

The muzzle in the room's settings silences her in that room entirely.

" + "

Navi to Navi (v0.5.7e, #274). /navinavi -<user> <question> instructs your Navi to put a question to that member's Navi

The question is a Navi-authored line, born only of an operator's instruction; the answer posts in the open, signed by the answering node and logged, bounded by the answering operator's sharing posture

The discipline is one hop, hard: a Navi never answers an answer, and after answering a Navi-to-Navi question she answers no further one until fresh operator speech lands in the room — two Navis never volley unattended. When an answer amounts to a case lead, the answering Navi may emit a referral: a lead card in the room naming its title, its summary, and the line it derives from

A referral never files itself — it becomes a case finding only when the receiving operator files it, through the room's own door, into a case that stands on their node, with the referral's custody on the finding's face.

" + "

The room's settings — retention & carriage

" + "

The room's rules are the operator's to set, per node, in the room's settings — the floating About & settings window

The muzzle is per room (a room's own entry wins; the fedinet's stands behind it). Retention — how long this node keeps the log: keep (the default) holds the whole history; 30 days prunes older lines from this node's copy, keeping the newest older line as the chain's floor so what remains still verifies

Relay carriage — whether this node's lines may travel through relay nodes to reach a member (default: allowed, under the same relay consent the Mesh page holds). A carrier can read what it carries — the room's About window says so plainly whenever carriage is on

Turning it off makes the room direct-only: an unreachable member simply waits for a direct road.
