The watch floor

" + "

Seraph (SIEM \u2192 Seraph) is Apex's SIEM suite \u2014 the watch floor (#153), named for the seraphim: the burning, watching order

She is a configuration of Apex, not a fork: any seat can take the sensor role, the console role, or both, set on the Seraph page itself, so the whole suite is manageable from DHD. A sensor watches one network segment \u2014 the one it is plugged into \u2014 and the dashboard states that vantage honestly, naming what this seat cannot see as gaps. More ground is more sensors

PIA, the Row's first physical sensor, registers here as the first remote sensor when she ships; the suite works whole without her.

" + "

What a sensor sees. Collection is passive: the segment's living inventory from ARP and DHCP leases, the seat's connection table (who talks to whom, when, how much \u2014 metadata, never payloads), its listening services, and its own auth logs

The one active act \u2014 a sweep \u2014 is not Seraph's to fire; it crosses the LOWC line in the open, like every active act in Apex.

" + "

What she detects. Watchlist matches (matched on the sensor \u2014 the list never leaves the machine; matches travel, it doesn't), a new face on the network, beaconing (calls landing on a metronome) and impossible hours (a sign-in inside the network's sleep window, yours to set), failed sign-in bursts, scan patterns seen from the receiving end, and a known host growing a new listening service
Every detection lands on the sensor's dashboard and in your tray in Navi's voice \u2014 she sends the alerts, not the system

From a detection you can file a case (the detection becomes the case's founding exhibit, hashed by the bridge at filing time) or dismiss it.

" + "

How sensors report. A remote sensor reports home over the Mesh, signed like every Mesh road; when the road is dark it spools its reports and drains them when the road lights \u2014 a sensor on a bad link loses nothing

The console's registry is the second lock on the door: a report files only from a registered, active sensor bound to the node that signed it. A client sensor is a limited citizen: its picture files under its own record and nothing else \u2014 admission is introduction, never transitive sight, and one client's evidence never surfaces in another's anything

Revoking a sensor is a tombstone: the record stays, marked, and a late report from it is refused by name.

" + "

The sensor's page carries its whole picture \u2014 timeline of detections, inventory, listeners, top talkers, the named gaps \u2014 with an SSH tab beside it: your own key, your own session, opened by hand each time; there is no standing session and the tab never rides the bridge's own door

Retention is yours to set (30 days on-box by default); open and filed detections never age out silently.

" }, { id: "dossier", title: "The Dossier — the people-finding app", related: ["case-files", "vault", "threat-intelligence"], html: "

One dossier, many doors

" + "

The Dossier (Casework → The Dossier) is Apex's people-finding app (#260) — since v0.5.15e (#290), the full kit: ten tabs across the top — Person, Username, Email, Phone, Photo, Courts, Business, License, Archive, Address — are keys into the same dossier: run any key and its findings land on the open dossier, rendered as markdown, and when two doors surface the same person, merge them — the merge is yours to make, and keys, sources and custody are kept
Every key, source, merge and case inclusion is stored on the dossier as a typed link

A key the kit has seen before opens the dossier that holds it, from any door — one dossier, many doors, and the civil spine accretes on one record instead of scattering.

" + "

The runs. Every run is bridge-side, public, passive and keyless, and every result is cited to its source: the handle swept across public platforms by polite profile checks; an email's posture from its MX, SPF and DMARC records, plus breach presence only — credential content never enters the kit; a phone's facts from the number's own structure and public sources, with cited search pointers in its common formats; a held domain's facts from RDAP, DNS, certificate transparency and its TLS certificate

Absence is named plainly — no public record found — never dressed up, and a hit is a lead, never a conclusion.

" + "

The registry check is the Person tab's anchor: it stands at the registries' own doors — the national NSOPW search and the state registry — and cites them; it does not mirror them, and a same-name hit is an unverified lead to disambiguate
When a record exists, its own identifiers — its listed aliases, a held domain — are what enrichment fans out from, so a name-collision guess never inherits a stranger's record

The Photo tab reads an image's EXIF metadata fully locally — nothing is uploaded anywhere, and no face recognition is performed, ever.

" + "

Cases, both ways. Open an OSINT case from a dossier — the dossier stands as its subject — and file a dossier, or a single run's findings, into any case, with provenance on the face; case files hold case substance only

Navi is the second door: dossier: person <name>, sweep the handle <name>, look up <email>, look up the number <phone> — her runs land in the same history, and while a dossier is open she holds it as context.

" + "

The full kit — courts, business, licenses, archives, the spine (v0.5.15e, #290)

" + "

Courts. Federal dockets and published opinions are read keyless through CourtListener (the RECAP archive) — each hit cited to its record, the caption's other side carried as an associated name, a lead with its source

PACER is credentialed and per-page, so it stands as a named pointer (RECAP, the same record, is checked first); govinfo's API is keyed; the state portals are session-driven forms — all named as pointers, never scraped around

Business. SEC EDGAR — filer match, company facts, recent filings, full-text — plus OpenCorporates registrations (their officers of record ride as associated names), ProPublica's nonprofit 990 filings, and USAspending federal awards; the FEC waits on your API-key choice and USPTO's TESS has no API door that fits, so both stand as pointers, as does Pennsylvania's form-driven entity search

License. What has a keyless machine shape is read directly — amateur callsigns from the FCC's ULS mirror, aircraft N-numbers from the FAA registry; professional licenses are kept by name behind the boards' session forms, so PA PALS, the ULS name search and the airmen inquiry stand as pointers and the run says so
Archive. A URL reads the Wayback Machine's snapshot index; a name reads scholarship — OpenAlex author records, Crossref works

Address — the civil spine. The gazetteer's read of the address (county, state), the county's own property door named, and the voter note for the state: a pointer where the state publishes a status check, an honest absence where the file is restricted by law.

" + "

The Person tab grew anchors. Beside the registry check stands the sanctions check: the OFAC lists (SDN + consolidated) read from the Treasury's own publication — a match is a lead to disambiguate by the record's own anchors, a miss is stated as a miss on the lists as read

Obituaries stand as a pointer to published postings. The Email tab adds OpenPGP keyserver presence; the Username sweep's corpus widened to 44 platforms.

" + "

Composition, in the open. Compose a run shows the shelves a starting key fans out to — each shelf named with its doors and its cost in requests — before anything fires; the confirm is the fire
Hits propose pivots: associated names and un-run shelves, one hop, proposed on the dossier and in Navi's context — the press is the go, and nothing ever auto-runs

Every shelf has its chat route, as every tool in this kit must: dossier: courts <name>, court records for <name>, look up the business <name>, license check <key>, wayback <url>, property records for <address>, dossier plan for person <name>, run the dossier plan for person <name>.

" + "

The built dossier, and deleting an element (v0.5.9e, #280)

" + "

The open dossier reads as one document made of its elements — one element per run — grouped by kind (person, username, email, phone, photo), each carrying its provenance on its face: the key it ran on, the door it came through, its sources with their verdicts, and the time it landed
An element that has been filed into cases names them, by name — the typed links, readable

The whole document renders through the product's one markdown renderer, exactly as Case Files and the Vault render: a rendered document, and any HTML a source filed stays inert text.

" + "

An element can be deleted — and deletion is global. Every element carries a Delete button; the confirm names the blast radius first (this dossier, the cases it stands in by name, the Vault formations), and a reason — irrelevant / repeat / incorrect — is optional, never required
Confirm, and the element leaves every home at once: the dossier, every case it was filed into, and the Vault's formed documents

The same delete stands at three doors — the dossier, the case (any finding's Delete; an element finding routes to the global delete), and the Vault (a formed case document lists its elements with their deletes) — and in chat: tell Navi “delete the dossier element <key>” and she acts on it, receipted from what the bridge actually did

She never deletes unbidden.

" + "

What remains is the custody line. When a case loses an element — from any door — the case keeps one line in its custody record (custody.md, in the case folder): the element's identity, when it left, where it was deleted from (the dossier / this case / another case / the Vault), and the reason if one was given

The formed case document carries no residue of the element at all. A case finding that is not a dossier element deletes from its case alone, the same custody line kept. A filing that carries several elements (a whole dossier filed at once) is a filing, not an element: deleting it from a case removes the filing there, and the elements stay in their dossier, each deletable on its own
Repeats are handled by deletion only — there is no merge for elements

Deletion crosses Sync as a fact about the element, so a stale copy on another seat cannot re-file what was deleted: the re-filing is refused, by name.

" }, { id: "docker", title: "Apex in Docker — the container node", related: ["dhd", "mesh", "settings"], html: "

The container node

" + "

Apex ships as a Docker image: a headless node in a container — the same bridge, the same Mesh door, the same DHD door, no desktop window

It is the easiest way to stand up a second (or a first) Mesh node: a homelab box, a NAS, a spare machine, a VPS. The image is free and AGPL, like the rest of Apex; there is no subscription anything. No identity is ever baked into the image — the node's Mesh keypair, its certificate, and its pairing card are minted on the machine that runs it, at first boot, inside the data volume

A shipped keypair would make every copy the same node, and one leak would be everyone's leak.

" + "

The model binary is not baked in either. On first run the container downloads navi.llamafile once — the installer's own pattern — and keeps it in the data volume, so the image stays small and the model persists across container replacements

One binary serves both architectures: the image is built for amd64 and arm64.

" + "

Up in one breath — DHD first

" + "

docker compose up, then read the first-boot output (the container's logs): a boxed banner prints your node's DHD access code, once, next to the node's name and Mesh fingerprint

Then browse to https://<this computer's address> — the DHD door, published on port 443 by the shipped compose file — type the code, name your device, and you are in: the first device at the door trusts itself with the code, and every device after it waits for an approval from one that is already trusted, exactly as on bare metal
Write the code down or take a photo of the banner. It is the only key to the DHD door; it is printed in the logs that one time only

The same banner is kept in a file named FIRST-BOOT.txt in the data volume, for the operator who missed the scroll.

" + "

The LAN-trust sentence, plainly: in the container, DHD is on from the first boot — the door answers on your local network from the moment the node starts
That is the container's posture, chosen because a container has no desk to sit at; a bare-metal install keeps DHD off until its operator turns it on

On-by-default never means open: anyone on the network still needs the code to knock, and the trusted-device list in Settings — System — Door is the roster of who got in, each with its own token you can revoke.

" + "

If you lose the code, it is a designed path, not a lockout — you need access to the computer the container runs on
Re-print the current code: docker exec <container> python3 /opt/navi-apex/bridge.py --dhd-code

Or mint a new one (the old code stops knocking at once; devices already trusted keep their own tokens): docker exec <container> python3 /opt/navi-apex/bridge.py --dhd-code-reset.

" + "

Ports, volumes, and the card warning

" + "

The shipped compose file publishes the Mesh door — 8765, 8443, 2475 (one door, one certificate, every number) and the DHD door — 443, plus 80 for its certificate machinery
The bridge itself keeps its standing loopback binding inside the container; the DHD proxy fronts it on the container's network face — the same architecture as bare metal, composed

Publish the Mesh ports onward (router forwards) only if the node should be reachable from beyond your network, and know that the Mesh door minds its knocks either way.

" + "

Everything that makes the node itself lives in one named volume, apex-data, mounted at /opt/navi-apex: the identity, the config, the chats and Case Files, the chips and knowledge packs, the model binary
Replacing the container never costs the node who it is — the installer's preservation law, in container form

Updates ride Apex's own updater, exactly as on bare metal.

" + "

The Docker card warning: inside a container there is no physical LAN interface to harvest addresses from — the card generator reads plumbing, not truth (the same reason it refuses a bare-metal card when every interface is a dead end)

So the declared public endpoint is the honest address for a container node: set it before minting cards for anyone — as the compose file's APEX_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT (for example mesh.example.org:8443), or later on the Mesh page, knowing a changed endpoint means re-sharing the card

An endpoint can name any of the door's numbers — 8443 is the face that travels best through other people's networks.

" + "

What the container does not do

" + "

No desktop window and no voice engines in this image — it is a node, run headless and driven through DHD

GitHub sign-in, Sync, chips, Guardian, The Wire, and the Mesh (pairing, borrowing, lending, the backup route, and relay) work as they do on bare metal, because it is the same bridge throughout.

" }, { id: "guardian", title: "Guardian — protecting Navi's headroom", related: ["mesh", "settings", "troubleshooting"], html: "

What the Guardian is

" + "

The Guardian is Apex's system monitor: a quiet engine in the bridge that watches this machine's memory and Navi's own footprint, and protects the headroom she needs to answer well

A machine can have free RAM on paper and still starve her — another program balloons, a browser eats the reserve, a generation slows to a crawl — and the Guardian is the part of Apex that notices, keeps score, and acts before her replies pay for someone else's appetite.

" + "

It lives with the bridge: always on while the bridge runs, even headless — a server install with no dashboard open is still guarded

Its face is the Guardian page in Utilities: the summary (pressure, free RAM against the reserve, Navi's footprint, whether she is generating now), the live watch of the machine's heaviest processes, what it has learned, its settings, and its action log

The page polls the bridge every few seconds while it is open and stops the moment you leave it.

" + "

The ladder — watch, warn, throttle, kill

" + "

The Guardian escalates one rung at a time, and only while the crowding lasts:

    " + "
  1. Watch. It samples the machine — free memory against the reserve you set, Navi's footprint, how long her generations are taking, and the heaviest processes — and keeps the watch table current

Watching costs nothing and accuses no one." + "
  • Warn. When a foreign process keeps crowding Navi past the warn delay, the Guardian says so — in its log, with the process named. A warning is a receipt, not a punishment.
    • " + "
  • Throttle. If the crowding continues, the offending process is capped to the CPU ceiling you set, so Navi gets her cores back while the offender keeps running, slower

Throttling is reversible and is lifted when the pressure passes." + "
  • Kill. The last rung, and the narrowest: only with killing enabled, only after the grace period following a final warning, and only ever a process on the expendable list — see below.
    • " + "

    Pressure is reported in plain words on the Guardian page — OK, Tight, Critical — with the free RAM and the reserve beside it, so you can see the same arithmetic the Guardian is acting on.

    " + "

    The expendable list — killing is impossible until you name a name

    " + "

    The expendable list is the Guardian's entire kill authority, and it ships empty on purpose
Until you type a process name into it on the Guardian page, the Guardian cannot kill anything at all — the top rung of the ladder simply does not exist

Even with the list filled, killing needs its own switch (Killing enabled) on top of the Guardian's main switch, and a named process still gets its warning and its grace period first.

" + "

Killing never happens to anything not on that list: not Navi, not Apex, not a system process, not a stranger the Guardian merely dislikes
If a process is worth protecting absolutely, the protection is structural — keep it off the list

Names are process names, one per line, exactly as the watch table shows them.

" + "

What it learns — collisions, counted

" + "

The Guardian learns this machine by counting collisions, not by modeling anything: every time a process crowds Navi — while she is generating, while memory is tight — that process's score grows: how often it has been seen, how many collisions, how many warnings it earned, how many times it was throttled, and whether it was ever killed

The Learned offenders card on the Guardian page is that scoreboard. A process that collides once and never again fades into trivia; a repeat offender is met higher on the ladder, sooner, because it has a record

There is no model, no cloud, and no profile leaving the machine — just arithmetic over what actually happened here.

" + "

The log is the receipts

" + "

Everything the Guardian does lands in its action log: warnings, throttles, kills, and the pressure changes that caused them, newest first on the Guardian page, each with its time, its kind, and the process it concerned
The Guardian never acts silently — if it touched a process on your machine, the receipt is there to read, and the offenders' scoreboard agrees with it

If you ever wonder why a program was slowed or closed, the log is the first and only place to look.

" + "

Its own footprint, and the Mesh note

" + "

A monitor that eats the headroom it guards would be a poor joke: the Guardian samples on a timer with the standard library, keeps only its counters and a short log in memory, and its own cost is measured and small — Navi's footprint on the summary card is the llamafile's real resident memory, read from the same process table the watch uses, so the numbers it judges by are the numbers you see.

" + "

Mesh-aware, like everything else in Apex now: when Apex | Mesh is on, the summary says borrowing is available and from how many paired machines — a Guardian that can lean on the Mesh leans there before it ever leans on a local process
When Mesh is off, the Guardian says so plainly and works locally only, with this machine's own memory

Either way it degrades gracefully: no Mesh is a posture, not an error.

" }, { id: "settings", title: "Settings & persona", related: ["installing", "voice", "github"], html: "

Her persona — Soul and Memory

" + "

Navi's personality is two documents in config/: soul.md (who she is) and memory.md (what she carries)

The bridge builds her system prompt from them on every chat. Both are editable in Settings, along with what she calls you. Nothing overwrites them once they exist: updates, reinstalls, and even a --fresh install stash and restore them, along with her installed chips and the llamafile

Only a first install creates them fresh.

" + "

Memory from chat — she writes things down herself

" + "

Navi pulls memories out of the conversation itself, two ways. The trigger: tell her remember this, remember: …, or save this to your memory — or tap Save to memory under any of your messages in Chat — and she writes the fact down
On her own: when you say something durable — a fact about you, a preference, a decision, a commitment, a correction — she saves it in the same reply she was already giving, with no extra round-trip

Small talk, command output, and questions are never saved.

" + "

Nothing is saved silently. Every save leaves a receipt in the chat showing exactly what she wrote, word for word, with a one-tap Undo. A save that corrects an existing entry replaces it — the receipt shows the old line struck through, and Undo restores it

Secrets are never saved, on any path: ask her to remember a password, a key, or a card number and she refuses, says why, and the receipt shows no payload.

" + "

Settings → Persona holds the leash: She saves on her own (the default), Ask first (each autonomous save waits as a proposal — in the chat receipt and under Settings → Persona — until you approve or dismiss it), or Only when I say (trigger only)

The entries live in two files, split by who authored them: Settings → Operator holds yours — added by hand, or saved because you asked — under About you — memories for Navi; Persona holds hers, under Her file — what she keeps

Every entry says how it got there.

" + "

Memory, the updater, and Settings

" + "

The status column is a tabbed pane: Status first — her presence, the update line, the servers, and the rest of the column as it has always been — and Chats second, the chat manager: the known chats (switch, new, delete) and the uploaded files

On a phone the whole pane is the dock, and it opens on Status. On a desktop the column starts hidden — its width belongs to the content until you open it: the pane button at the top right of her presence bar — the bar above every view — is its door, and on a phone the top bar's panel button is the other; hidden is the default at every launch, never a remembered choice

What she remembers from chat lives under Settings → Operator (your file) and Settings → Persona (her file and the leash). RAG holds her knowledge packs (the section above). The Vault holds the shared desk of notes — hers and yours. The Updater — folded into Settings → System, with the current version's notes as that menu's final block — watches the release channel

Settings is organized into topic tabs, and every setting lives under exactly one:

    " + "
  • Operator — what she calls you, your picture and your Operator Badge, and your file: the memories you handed her about you

Your picture rides beside your messages; upload one in the tab (it is trimmed to a square here, kept with your profile, and carried in the settings backup) or let the picture generated from your name stand in. The Operator Badge is your self-portrait in the cartridge format — a card with your chosen face and your name (and this node's name) carried inside the picture

It is not a credential: nothing reads a badge to prove identity, and a badge whose payload is damaged simply reads as no badge." + "
  • Persona — the Soul and Memory editors, her file of what she keeps from chat, the save-mode leash, and anything waiting on your word.
    • " + "
  • Appearance — the layout picker and the theme picker (two independent axes), Potato mode for low-power machines, and the UI scale.
    • " + "
  • Voice — her voice settings.
    • " + "
  • GitHub & Backup — sign-in and the backup/import block.
    • " + "
  • System — the hardware profile (the detected profile, its override, and re-detect), plus installed commands.
    • " + "

    There is no backend switch: the app always talks Live to the real bridge and llamafile, and the llamafile's Running state in the status column is the live signal.

    " + "

    Themes. Settings' Appearance tab holds the theme picker: twelve palettes over the same colors the whole app is built from, so every screen — dropdowns and typing boxes included — changes together:

      " + "
    • Nordic dark: the Nord family — Polar Night backgrounds in steps, pale Snow Storm words, and Frost-blue highlights with muted Aurora colors

In Nordic, each menu icon gets its own color from that palette — Chat is Frost blue, Voice Aurora purple, Chips Aurora yellow, and so on — the same color everywhere it appears, even in the collapsed rail, and her written answers dress the same way: Snow Storm words, Frost headings and links, and code sitting on the deepest Polar Night step." + "
  • Dark Liquid Glass comes second: frosted dark glass — deep near-black blue panels you can half see through, with a cheap blur on the big surfaces only (the side menu, the status column, the bar you type in), so it stays smooth on modest graphics; where blur or see-through panels are unavailable it falls back gracefully to the same colors, solid.
    • " + "
  • Terminal is green on black, the classic console.
    • " + "
  • Signature dark is her original console, cyan on near-black.
    • " + "
  • Light is the same console on pale slate.
    • " + "
  • High contrast is pure black with white words and bright signals.
    • " + "
  • Nocturne Row is the default: a rain-slick Rockport night — blue-black streets with neon cyan and magenta signs.
    • " + "
  • Abyss is the deep sea off her app icon — near-black and quiet, with one bioluminescent cyan, the anglerfish lure, as the only loud color.
    • " + "
  • Case File is a light theme — warm paper, ink-black words, evidence-red string accents, and terminal blocks set like a typewriter.
    • " + "
  • Blood Moon is crimson over black with gold thread for highlights.
    • " + "
  • Phosphor Amber is amber on black, Terminal's warmer sibling.
    • " + "
  • LCARS (v0.6.4e, #324) is the starship console — the one theme that changes the shapes as well as the colors: a black field, pill-ended bars and buttons with black text on the color, elbow-curved cards, uppercase condensed labels, in the classic accent family (orange, peach, lilac, periwinkle, brick) with the modern 2.0 cooler blues and teals woven through

It is a skin over the same screens — the rail's groups still collapse to their header pills, every switch still answers to the same state — and the lettering is your system's own condensed face; nothing is fetched." + "

Layout. Beside the theme picker, Appearance holds a second, independent choice (v0.6.5e, #325): the layout. Standard is the shipped geometry

LCARS Mode re-geometries the same screens — elbow-swept cards, the rail as numbered pill stacks, sweep-tab headings, pill-ended controls, condensed uppercase labels on the furniture — while the colors still come from whichever theme is picked: all twelve palettes work in both layouts, and the LCARS palette inside LCARS Mode is the flagship pairing

The two choices are separate facts in your config; flip either and the other holds. Flipping layouts translates, it never resets: the flip is a re-render of the surface you are standing on — same screen, same place in the thread, same open case or document and its edits, same half-typed line, same switches, same rail groups open or closed — in either direction, on the desktop and on the phone's interface alike
And the picker itself lives in Appearance under both layouts, in its accustomed place, so the way back is always where you left it

The choice persists in your config like the theme and rides the settings backup beside it.

" + "

Pick one and it stays picked — the choice is saved in your config like the other settings, and a choice you already saved is always honored over the default.

" + "

Motion. The whole app moves in one language — menus unfold, panes swap, and views arrive on the same curves

On a low-power machine, Appearance's Potato mode turns the decorative motion off across Apex: state changes become instant, and the glass theme's backdrop blur is suspended as well, since on weak graphics the blur costs more than the motion does

Your operating system's reduced-motion setting always wins over the switch, either way.

" + "

Interface size. Appearance's UI scale — 100%, 110%, 125%, 150% — scales the whole interface, words and layout together, like a display scale: one knob, deliberately, because a separate text size would multiply against it and squeeze the fixed rows at the big end

It applies the moment you pick it and persists beside the theme.

" + "

Hardware profile. Settings' System tab shows the profile the installer made of your machine: what it detected (the CPU and its core count, how much memory, the graphics chip — separate or built in, and its memory), and the settings it chose from that — threads, context size, batch size, and graphics layers

Her settings are picked from your machine at install, never copied from the developer's: a modest laptop gets the proven gentle numbers, a strong machine gets more room. Type your own numbers to override them, or press Re-detect to profile the machine again and return to the automatic choice

The installer writes what it found and why it chose it to hardware-profile.log in the install folder.

" + "

Apex | Node — Apex on your phone or tablet

" + "

The DHD page holds the Apex | Node [local] controls, under the DHD options — Settings' System tab keeps only a pointer to them

Apex | Node is off by default: off, Apex answers only this machine. Turn it on and she also serves her page to your home network — the same Apex, in a phone or tablet browser. The choice is saved in config/navi.config.json with your other settings and kept across updates

Flipping the switch is the whole job: Apex restarts her own bridge so the choice takes effect — the row says Restarting the bridge… while it happens, then confirms the live state read from the bridge that actually answers: On your network, or This machine only. Turning it off is the same one flip in reverse

No relaunching the app yourself, no hunting for a process.

" + "

If a restart ever fails, the row says so in plain words: it names the step that failed (the old bridge would not stop, the new bridge did not answer, or the answering bridge's bind does not match your choice), states the state that is actually live — the old bridge keeps serving its old setting, untouched, until a new one is confirmed — and offers the fallbacks: press Restart bridge to try again, or quit Apex fully and relaunch

A restart never leaves a half-state behind.

" + "

While the toggle is on, the row shows two things only someone sitting at this machine should see: the address to open on your phone — http://<your machine's network address>:8675, as a button that copies it — and your access code

A phone that visits knocks with the code and a name for itself: the first phone approves itself, and every phone after that waits in the Door list (Settings → System → Door, and the DHD page) until a trusted session approves it; an approved phone holds its own 30-day session, renewed while it stays in use. The code never applies on this machine itself

Press Regenerate for a new code: new knocks need the new code at once, while phones already approved keep their own sessions — the Door list revokes those one by one.

" + "

The honest warning, in full: anyone on the network who has the access code can knock, and an approved device can use Apex in full — chat, the command line, and settings included
The code plus your approvals are the lock on that door — and the first device at a fresh door approves itself, so guard the code like the key it is

Share it like a house key, and turn the toggle off when you no longer want the door there.

" }, { id: "github", title: "GitHub — the pulse, issues & backups", related: ["settings", "installing"], html: "

The pulse — a peek into the project

" + "

The GitHub item in the side menu is her window into the project itself: AlexKollar/Apex, the repo this rebuild lives in (the original Navi she grew from stays at SaintsSec/Navi as the legacy archive)

The section has four tabs:

    " + "
  • Overview is the pulse: the repo's description, its stars, forks, and watchers, the latest release, the most recent commits, the open-issue count, and when it last moved — read live from GitHub through the bridge, with a Refresh button, and honest about it when a read fails.
    • " + "
  • Issues is the repo's current open-issues list — number, title, labels, author, when it last changed — also live, also refreshable.
    • " + "
  • Roadmap is Alex's project board for Apex.
    • " + "
  • Discussions are the project's open forum.
" + "

In her desktop window, Roadmap and Discussions each open as a webview in its own window — GitHub will not be framed inside a web page, so where no webview exists the tab says so and links out to GitHub instead of showing a blank frame

At the bottom of the Issues, Roadmap, and Discussions tabs sits one quiet link to the matching place on GitHub — file an issue, open the board, start a discussion. Looking needs no account at all, in any tab

Clicking an issue opens its log in a window of its own — in her desktop window, a native window of the app like the Roadmap and Discussions windows; in a plain browser, a new tab — never framed inside her window. Filing an issue happens on GitHub's own pages too: when you write one, GitHub asks you to sign in there, with your own account. That is GitHub's door, not Navi's — she never stands between you and it

Account things — sign-in, backup, import — live in Settings → GitHub & Backup; this section is for looking at the project.

" + "

Signing in — only for GitHub things, never for Navi

" + "

Navi never needs you to sign in. She starts, chats, runs commands, uses her chips and knowledge packs, and works with no internet at all — signed out, forever, if you like

Signing in exists for one reason: a few actions write to GitHub (backups and imports, below), and GitHub only lets an account write to its own things.

" + "

What signing in turns on:

    " + "
  • Publish to GitHub for your RAG packs and chips (Navi does the whole chain — repo, topic, files, tag, and the published release, picture attached).
    • " + "
  • Automatic backups to a repo under your own account.
    • " + "
  • Taking part in the GitHub section's live issues, roadmap, and discussions — looking never needed an account; joining in does.
" + "

None of it is required: Export for GitHub is always available, signed in or not — sign-in only adds the upload route; it never gates exporting or publishing by hand.

" + "

Sign-in uses GitHub's Device Flow — the way made for apps like hers

Press Sign in with GitHub and you get a short code. Open github.com/login/device in your browser, type the code, and say yes. GitHub tells Navi you're in. Your password is never typed into Navi, and there is no secret key hidden inside the app. The token GitHub hands back is kept in one file on your own machine (config/github-auth.json, readable only by you)

It is never written into a backup and never logged.

" + "

One thing has to exist before sign-in can work: a client ID — a short public label for the app, not a secret. Since Build 6, Apex ships with the project's registered client ID in config/github-signin.json, so sign-in works out of the box: no OAuth App to register, no token to create and paste

(Running a fork? Put your own OAuth App's client ID in that file — it needs Device Flow enabled.) And since Build 6 the sign-in is the only GitHub credential Apex holds: the app's own reads — the Updater, the NUR, this section's pulse and issues — ride it too
The separate Apex Runtime token earlier builds asked you to paste is retired; if an old config/github-runtime.json is still on disk, it is simply ignored

Signed out, the reads go unauthenticated and their failures say so in words; everything local works regardless.

" + "

Backups — the ready-to-fly essentials

" + "

A backup is a copy of Navi, kept in a repository (a project's folder on GitHub) under your own account — the name is yours to pick; navi-backup is the starter suggestion

It is made private unless you choose otherwise, and the page warns you plainly if you pick public: a public backup puts her Soul and Memory on the open internet.

" + "

The backup carries only the essentials — the things a fresh Navi needs to be fully herself

Fresh install + import = ready to fly:

    " + "
  • Her Soul document — who she is.
    • " + "
  • Her Memory document — what she carries.
    • " + "
  • Settings & config — what she calls you, her theme, her installed commands, and her voice choice and voice settings.
    • " + "
  • Her installed chips — the whole chips, so they come back working, not just named.
    • " + "
  • Her RAG packs — their documents, their built indexes, and which ones are switched on.
    • " + "
  • Her workflows — the saved chains of chips.
    • " + "
  • Your chats — the threads themselves, which live on the server now

A restore converges them rather than overwriting: newest wins per thread, and a thread both machines moved on survives whole, as a dated sibling." + "
  • The Vault — the shared desk of notes, cases included.
    • " + "
  • Her Mesh pairing cards — the pictures themselves: her own card, minted fresh as the backup runs, and a re-drawn picture for every machine she is paired with, so a restored Navi can re-pair without meeting everyone from nothing

Her node keypair is never among them — a restored machine still mints its own identity." + "

Some things are never backed up, on purpose: your call logs (those are history, not identity), caches and log files, her hardware profile (a new machine gets profiled fresh at its own install — an old machine's numbers must never be forced onto it), and her voice model files (big downloads that reinstall themselves; her voice settings are backed up).

" + "

The essentials checklist in Settings → GitHub & Backup starts with every essential ticked
Soul, Memory, and Settings & config are ticked automatically and stay ticked — they are what makes an imported Navi her, so every backup carries them

Installed chips, RAG packs, workflows, the Vault, and Mesh pairing cards are yours to choose; untick one of those and it tells you what it means: an import from that backup will no longer be fully ready-to-fly, because the unticked part stays behind.

" + "

When backups happen, and bringing her back

" + "

You pick how often: every day, every 3 days, every 5 days, or every 7 days

Navi checks the clock herself — when she starts, and while she is running — and when a backup is due and she is signed in, she runs it. That is the honest limit: backups happen while Navi is running. If the machine is off when one comes due, it simply runs at her next start

Settings → GitHub & Backup shows the last backup's time and what it wrote, and the same for the last import — and the status column carries a Backup section with the last backup's time and result at a glance (or says plainly that no backup has run yet).

" + "

Import (in Settings → GitHub & Backup) is how a backup becomes a Navi again — on a fresh install, or any time you want to roll back to the backed-up her
Press Preview what would change first: it lists, essential by essential, what the backup holds and what restoring it would replace. Nothing is overwritten until you press Confirm import

What was never backed up — call logs, the old machine's hardware numbers, voice models — starts fresh, which is exactly what a new home should do.

" + "

Account sync — the Operator Badge pulls

" + "

Import has a second door, made for the ordinary case: you worked on one machine and want this machine caught up

In Settings → GitHub & Backup, the Account sync card slots your Operator Badge. The badge is a pointer, never a key — it says whose backup to pull; the GitHub sign-in remains the only thing that can unlock it, and signed out, the sync stops at its first step and fetches nothing

Slotting it pulls the latest backup and builds the same per-item preview Import builds, laid on a live operation card in Chat: Navi speaks before it and after it, nothing is generated while it runs, and nothing is applied until you confirm on the card. Her node keypair and Mesh certificate never ride a backup, so they can never ride a sync

Since Build 6 the badge itself also travels as its own plain file — cards/operator-badge.png in the backup repo, exactly the card's bytes, no archive — so the card can be listed and fetched on its own, one card at a time, on the phone over DHD, without opening the whole backup; a restore takes the card from that file, byte for byte
The Mesh node keypair is never in any file a backup writes — the card is the operator's picture and profile, nothing of the node's keys

As of Build 13 the badge also slots from a file — on the Account sync card itself, and in Settings → Operator beside the minting controls — because a badge minted on one machine reaches another as a picture file; both slots feed the one badge state, and a file that is not an operator badge is refused in plain words

Pressing the sync button takes you to Chat at once, where the card runs, and a pull that has not answered in 45 seconds says so in plain words rather than leaving Settings spinning.

" + "

Sync — One Navi. All the screens. (The Sync Update, v0.3.0e Build 1)

" + "

The badge round above is the deliberate ceremony; Sync is the everyday gesture it grew into

Sync sits in the menu's Utilities group. It opens no page: one tap pops a small card and runs the whole round — pull, converge, push — so a conversation started at the desk is waiting on the phone over DHD, and the other way around

The card says only the essentials: the state (Syncing…, Synced, Can't reach — held, Needs your eyes), what moved, the route actually used — the Mesh whenever a paired machine's road is lit (named on the card, Mesh — <that machine>), the backup repo otherwise — and at most one action, Retry

A success lingers five seconds and dismisses itself; a held or Needs your eyes card stays until you deal with it. Pulls also happen on their own: at app start, when a DHD session starts, when a window opens (the seat notes itself to the bridge, which refreshes the room for it — the desk was the one seat that never announced itself before this build), and on Mesh contact

Publishing was the button's act alone until v0.5.1e (#257) taught writes to push themselves — see Fluid sync below. There is still no polling daemon.

" + "

Sync shows itself (v0.4.10e, #254)

The head of the status pane is the sync bar: at rest it reads System Synced; while any round runs — from the button, at app start, at a DHD session's start, on Mesh contact — it becomes a progress bar naming the phase the bridge is in (fetch, merge, write), with counts only where the bridge can measure them, and an honest indeterminate pulse where it can't

A round that stalls names its stall and the leg it is stuck on; a round that fails names its failure. When a round lands, the receipt hangs off the bar in plain terms — messages merged into the main thread, ghost threads folded, case/chat pairs made whole or the gaps named, deletions honored — or simply nothing changed. The durable copy is the sync record itself; the bar is its face

And when a round materially changed things — a fold, a pairing repaired, another machine's deletion honored — Navi announces it in the main chat herself, from that same record; a routine round stays quiet.

" + "

What rides is the whole living her, anchored to your GitHub account — the set's manifest names the account, and a set from a different account is refused by name at the door, on both transports, before anything is applied: different accounts are different people's work

The set: the chat store; Case Files whole; the ChipDeck as one unit — chips with their install record, RAG packs with theirs, and the cards that tie machines together (your own pairing card and one per paired peer, re-drawn fresh each round, and a gateway card for every fedinet you keep; a gateway card landing on a machine that doesn't keep that fedinet yet admits it — admission and introduction only, never trust); your operator picture and badge; her memory entries; and her Soul and her memory book
The Operator Badge keeps its crown jobs — recovery root, the acts that need the ceremony — but it is not the sync key anymore; the account is

Settings stay with the badge backup, as ever.

" + "

Convergence is the badge round's, widened: per chat, the newest copy wins; a pair that genuinely diverged parks both copies — the later one as a dated sibling — and only then does the card say Needs your eyes, naming the chat or case

Her two documents converge per document and are never silently overwritten: a side untouched since the last sync takes the other side's text; both changed, the newer text wins and the losing text is parked beside the document as a named .from-sync- conflict copy for your eyes

Memory entries union by fact — each fact keeps the origin it was born with (by hand, from chat at your ask, her own call, a correction), and a correction replaces its fact's text rather than piling up beside it. Forgetting is a tombstone too (v0.5.1e, #256): forget an entry on any seat and the forget itself syncs — the entry leaves every seat and a stale copy cannot resurrect it

Your name, picture and badge are single values: the latest change wins. Deletions travel as tombstones: delete a chat, a case, or a note on one machine and the deletion itself syncs — and since v0.4.10e (#253) a chat's tombstone is a fact at any timestamp: the thread is gone from every seat and stays gone, however new a late-syncing copy claims to be; a deleted conversation does not come back

(Cases and notes keep the older courtesy: work genuinely newer than their deletion survives.) A case's chat deletes through its case — deleting the case takes its chat with it, and the Chats tab offers no bare delete for a case chat

The main thread is one thread on every machine (v0.4.10e, #251): a main arriving from another seat merges into yours by message — each line once, in order — instead of landing beside it as another thread, and ghost mains left by older rounds fold into it once, receipted in the sync record. New threads are born only two ways: you start one, or a case does

And a case and its chat travel together (v0.4.10e, #252): a case chat whose case cannot land does not list as a case chat at all — it folds away, and the gap is named in the sync record. One exception is absolute: the main chat cannot be deleted — not from the Chats tab, not through sync; /clear or /cls empties it

The one law that does not bend: backups already taken are snapshots and are never reached into — a tombstone governs live machines, not history. Failures are named in the usual discipline: offline is held and retried at the next trigger, a spent rate limit is named with its wait, a refused credential is named as auth, a foreign account is named as the account it belongs to.

The operator class converges (v0.5.1e, #256). What she knows about you — your name, your picture, your badge, and her memory entries about you — is one class of its own, and since this build it actually crosses

The bridge's seat record is the truth: a window's list is a cache of it, written through on every change and replaced by the converged answer, so a fact added at the server is simply there at the laptop — no seat keeps a private list the sync merges underneath
The status pane's MEMORY line reports the class's true state — the entry count and the sync clock, in the sync bar's own terms — and the (local) it used to confess to is retired

On the backup road the same discipline names its keys: an import applies a deliberate list — your name, threat level, sudo mode, installed commands, updater channel — and nothing else in the config crosses; a machine keeps its own hardware profile, its Mesh identity, and its install facts, always.

" + "

Fluid sync — push-on-write (v0.5.1e, #257)

The occasions above still fire, but a change no longer waits for one: a write on any seat — a chat message, a memory entry added or forgotten, a case change, a deletion — asks for a round of its own, promptly, and the receiving seat converges inside ten seconds while both seats are up and in Mesh contact

The Mesh is the primary road; the repo push is the writing seat's fallback act, and a seat off both roads converges at its next occasion, as before. The standard is the account's, not one operator's: it holds for anyone with an account, on their own seats

Every landing receipt on the sync bar names the road the round took and the time it measured — landed in 3s via Mesh — so the standard is checkable at a glance, and a push that cannot land names its stall on the bar rather than silently aging

No daemon was added: the push rides the bridge's own resident life, and a burst of writes coalesces into one round.

" + "

Substance, not shells (v0.5.13e, #262). A round used to converge whatever arrived and call it synced — and once, a case chat's existence crossed to the phone while its transcript stayed behind, and a theme never crossed at all
Now the set's manifest declares the substance: every chat's message count and a digest of its messages, and a digest of the seat (your settings and theme) and of the Pulse store

The receiving side verifies arrivals against the declaration — a chat whose count or digest falls short is named incomplete on the sync bar and in the record; a seat or Pulse payload whose bytes fail their digest is refused rather than merged over good local substance; and where this seat already holds more of a conversation, a short copy never replaces it

A shell is not a dead end: the next round's full arrival heals it in place, and the name clears. Sets from older builds declare nothing and are taken as they come, as before.

" + "

The override — Send or Receive (v0.6.2e, #303). Sometimes you do not want the cadence's timing; you want it now, in one direction

A setting — Settings → GitHub & Backup → The Sync button, on by default — makes the Sync control offer a choice when pressed: Send a sync publishes this seat's set and pulls nothing down; Receive a sync pulls the converged set and publishes nothing

Each is the standing machinery standing alone by direction, over the same roads, and each lands with its own receipt naming what actually moved — files published, what came down — or saying plainly that there was nothing to move. Turn the setting off and a press runs the whole round at once, as it always did. The automatic rounds never consult the setting.

" + "

The override overrides (v0.6.3e, #317)

A chosen direction does not queue behind a round already in flight: the running round stops at its next phase boundary — its partial work stands, since convergence is idempotent — and your Send or Receive runs immediately after. Both receipts tell the truth: the stopped round's record names the supersession and the phase it stopped at, and its card face reads Overridden — your call runs now, never held

Choose again mid-flight and the newest choice is the one that runs. Machine triggers — push-on-write, the occasions — still hold behind a running round, as they should: preemption is the operator's privilege, exercised through the choice.

" + "

A cleared main chat stays cleared (v0.6.3e, #318)
Emptying the main thread with /clear or /cls is a synced act: the thread carries a clear marker — the moment it was emptied, and the seat that emptied it — and convergence honors it on every seat

Content stamped at or before the clear yields to the emptied state however new the copy carrying it claims to be; lines written after the clear are untouched, and the ghost-fold can never resurrect what a clear retired

And the verdict is honest about it: after every round the main thread's count and digest are checked against the converged set, and on a disagreement the round is renamed — Mostly synced — the main thread disagrees, with both counts named — on the receipt and on the Sync card

A clean converged is only ever printed over a main thread that actually agrees.

" + "

One sign-in, and failures with names (Build 2, completed in Build 6)

" + "

Who Apex speaks as. Build 2 taught Apex to keep its GitHub identities apart — your sign-in for backup and import, a separate pasted token for the app's own reads — and Build 6 finished the thought by collapsing them to one: your GitHub account sign-in, and nothing else

There is no token to create, paste, or rotate; the Updater's checks, the NUR's catalog searches, downloads, sync's repo transport, backup and import all ride the one sign-in, which lives in config/github-auth.json (readable only by you, never backed up, deleted by signing out)
Release Automation still holds no credential in Apex at all, by design: releases are published from your signed-in browser session and the local git remote

And failures keep their names everywhere GitHub is read: auth (the credential itself is refused), rate (a bucket is spent — the sentence carries its reset), abuse (GitHub's secondary safeguard — the sentence carries the wait it asked for, and Apex stops rather than retrying)

No surface shows a bare “HTTP 403”.

Apex without the window

" + "

A server does not need a window
./start.sh --headless starts exactly the services — the llamafile (check-first, as always: an answering server is left alone) and the bridge, supervised — and opens no window

It is safe over SSH, safe to run twice (a service already answering is adopted, never doubled), and it writes the same start.log the desktop launch writes, so a headless start explains itself after the fact the same way

Run it after a reboot and Apex — with DHD, if DHD was left on — is simply back.

" + "

The desktop launch adopts, too: open the app on a machine whose services are already running (from boot, or from a headless start) and it uses them as they are instead of starting second copies.

" + "

At boot, honestly

" + "

Choose At system boot in the installer and it registers two systemd user services — navi-llamafile.service and navi-bridge.service (the bridge unit runs start.sh --headless) — and tries to enable lingering for your user, which is what lets user services start at boot rather than at login

If the installer cannot enable lingering itself, it prints the exact command — sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER — rather than assuming: a boot-armed Apex you only believe in is worse than one that tells you the step it could not take

The status column's Servers group carries a Boot row that reads the armed state from the system every time — both units and the linger state — so what it shows is what the machine says, never what an installer once hoped.

The app can now change it

Arm at boot and Disarm in the status column's Servers \u2192 Boot row \u2014 and the same control in Settings \u2192 System \u2014 register and enable both units from the templates the package ships, and try to enable linger. If linger cannot be enabled from the app, the row shows the exact command \u2014 sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER \u2014 instead of pretending

After any action the row re-reads the system, and a half-done arm shows as half-done. Disarm disables the units \u2014 what is running keeps running; it just won't come up at boot \u2014 and leaves linger as it is

Arming is a local action \u2014 it is not offered through the DHD door.

Headless auto-start

" + "

Apex's headless mode starts the bridge on boot, with no app window and nobody logged in — so a machine can power on and simply be on duty: answering locally, over DHD, and lending to the Mesh

This page covers the one-time setup, the one environment trap that can silently defeat it (a Wi-Fi profile with no stored secret), and the boot test that proves the whole chain. Everything below is a one-liner where a command is needed.

" + "

1. One-time setup

" + "

Boot-arming lives in the app
In the status column's Servers group, the Boot row carries an Arm at boot button \u2014 the same control sits in Settings \u2192 System, on the Startup \u2014 at boot card

Press it and the app:

    " + "
  • registers and enables two systemd user services \u2014 navi-llamafile.service and navi-bridge.service (the bridge unit runs start.sh --headless) \u2014 from the templates the package ships, and
    • " + "
  • tries to enable lingering for your user, which is what lets user services start at boot rather than at login

If linger cannot be enabled from the app, the row shows the exact command instead of pretending:" + "
sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER
" + "

After any action the row re-reads the system, so what it shows is what the machine reports now \u2014 and a half-done arm shows as half-done

Disarm \u2014 don't start at boot disables the units (what is running keeps running; it just won't come up at boot) and leaves linger as it is. Arming is a local action \u2014 it is not offered through the DHD door

The installer remains the alternative path: run it and choose At system boot, and it registers the same units and tries linger the same way, as the initial state.

" + "

You can also start the services headlessly at any time by hand — safe over SSH, and safe to run twice (a service already answering is adopted, never doubled):

" + "
./start.sh --headless
" + "

Check the armed state in the app, no terminal needed: the status column's Servers group carries a Boot row that reads the state from the system every time it shows — Armed — Apex comes up headless at boot, or Not armed — Apex starts when you open it — with a detail line naming both units and the linger state (on/off), read live, never assumed.

" + "

Reaching the machine from your own network: if you want other devices (a phone, a second laptop) to reach this machine without DHD, turn the Local server toggle on in Settings → System

Off (the default), the bridge listens only on the machine itself (127.0.0.1:8675); on, it answers on the LAN on port 8675, and anything that isn't the machine itself must present your Apex access code first.

" + "

Verify the boot machinery from a terminal:

" + "
systemctl --user is-enabled navi-bridge.service navi-llamafile.service\nloginctl show-user \"$(id -un)\" --property=Linger --value
" + "

You want enabled twice and yes

If the linger query gives you trouble, the ground truth is the directory — your username listed means linger is on:

" + "
ls /var/lib/systemd/linger/
" + "

If the Boot row says Not armed, press Arm at boot on the row (or in Settings \u2192 System) \u2014 re-running the installer and choosing At system boot is the fallback if the units cannot be registered from the app

If it is armed but linger is off, run the enable-linger command the row shows, once.

" + "

2. The trap: a Wi-Fi profile with no stored secret

" + "

Headless Apex can only answer on a network that exists
On Pop!_OS / Ubuntu (the netplan-backed NetworkManager stack), a Wi-Fi connection created without a system-stored password keeps its secret in the desktop session

At boot, NetworkManager asks for the secret, no session agent exists yet, and activation fails with:

" + "
<warn> no secrets: No agents were available for this request\n<info> Activation: failed for connection '<SSID>'
" + "

NetworkManager then backs off and retries much later — so after a reboot the machine is dark to SSH, DHD, and the Mesh until a human logs into the desktop, at which point everything \"mysteriously\" comes back at once

This is an environment defect, not an Apex defect: the bridge started fine; the network underneath it never arrived.

" + "

Check whether your profile stores its secret:

" + "
sudo grep -c password /etc/netplan/90-NM-*.yaml
" + "
  • 1 or more — the password is stored in the system profile

You're clean." + "
  • 0 — the profile is secretless. Apply the fix below.
    • " + "

    (The netplan source file is named 90-NM-<connection-uuid>.yaml

Wired connections don't have this problem; it is Wi-Fi-specific.)

" + "

The fix. Type this yourself, at the machine, with your real Wi-Fi password — never send the password through a chat, a ticket, or a screenshot:

" + "
sudo nmcli connection modify \"<SSID>\" wifi-sec.psk \"<your-wifi-password>\"
" + "

On the netplan-backed stack this writes through to the netplan source file, so the generated boot profile carries the secret and NetworkManager can activate Wi-Fi with nobody logged in

Expect the connection to bounce once when you apply it (an SSH session may drop; reconnect).

" + "

Verify the write landed — again without printing the secret: run the grep -c check above again. You want 1 or more now.

" + "

3

The verdict test (local — no DHD required)" + "

This proves auto-start on one machine using only a phone:

    " + "
  1. Reboot the machine.
    2. " + "
  2. Do not log in. Leave the login screen completely untouched — hands off is the whole test

If you log in, you've proven nothing." + "
  • Wait about two minutes.
    • " + "
  • On your phone, on the same Wi-Fi, open http://<machine-LAN-IP>:8675 and enter your Apex access code. (Requires the Local server toggle from §1.)
    • " + "
  • Pass: Navi answers while the login screen still sits untouched

The node auto-fired: service up, network up, no human involved." + "

Wrinkle: some networks (many workplace and guest Wi-Fi setups) isolate clients from each other, so the phone can't see the machine

Then put the machine on your phone's hotspot instead and browse to it there — same test, your own network.

" + "

The remote variant. Once the local test passes, the same proof works from anywhere, through whichever doors you've set up — from another machine, try your SSH door and/or your DHD address after a no-login reboot:

" + "
ssh -p <your-ssh-port> <user>@<your-host>
" + "

If either answers with the login screen untouched, headless auto-start is proven end to end on that machine.

" + "

4

If it fails" + "

Log into the desktop — everything recovers; that recovery is itself a clue (it means the services were waiting on something the login provided)

Then read the boot record before changing anything:

" + "
journalctl -b -u NetworkManager --no-pager | grep -i -E \"no secrets|activation.*fail\"\nsystemctl --user status navi-bridge --no-pager

    • " + "
  • The bridge unit is failed or missing → the problem is in the Apex layer; the unit's own journal lines say why.
    • " + "
  • Neither → note the exact boot time and what did answer, and file it with those two outputs attached

Guessing wastes more time than the journal takes to read." + "

    • " + "

    • " + "

    • " + "

    • " + "

Installing Navi, and keeping her up to date

" + "

Navi lives on your own computer — the app, her model, her memory, and her voice are all on your machine.

" + "

Right now Navi installs on Linux. That is the one installer in the package: install.sh

How you run it depends on where your copy came from — from the release zip, run ./install.sh (its scripts arrive executable, so that just works); from a git clone or GitHub's source zip, run bash install.sh instead (the paragraph below explains why, in plain words)

Windows and macOS installers are planned for later — they are not in this package yet, so there is nothing to run on those systems today.

    " + "

" + "
