The health check learns to heal what it finds, the backup route becomes a walked path, Quick Sync learns to ride the road it syncs over, GitHub sign-in becomes the product's only key — and the Operator card learns to travel as itself.
### Build 6

- **The health check heals in place (#143).** When a peer's record carries only dead-end addresses — loopback in any spelling, the unspecified address, a link-local, or the default Docker bridge gateway (172.17.0.1) — the peer's health card names the record as junk in a sentence (*the record points nowhere, so this pair has never actually been asked*) and offers the heal on the same card: **Import a fresh card** (which replaces the record's addresses in place, through the one pairing path) or **Clear the dead addresses** (the junk is stripped from the stored record now; the pairing, its pin, its tunnel route, and its history are kept)

A record holding at least one plausible address is never "repaired" — that is an edit, and edits arrive as fresh cards. - **The backup route is a walked path (#143, #178).** Three presses: flip the switch to arm the route, fill whichever field is still blank, Save route

The SSH host arrives prefilled from the public endpoint the peer declared on its card, when it declared one; Build 5's arm-instead-of-snap-back behavior is untouched. The route card also says, in plain words, the one step no button can take: the peer must authorize this machine's tunnel key on its own dashboard, in person — authorization is never given from over the wire

- **First-run certificate warning (#143).** The first time an operator pairs, the Mesh page says the quiet part before any trust is pinned: the door's certificate is self-signed, no authority vouches for it, and the card you were handed *is* the trust — importing it pins that machine's fingerprint here, and a door presenting a different certificate is named, never quietly trusted
The notice rides with the first pairing and is not shown again on that machine

- **Quick Sync rides the Mesh (#176 phase 2).** When a paired peer's road is lit, a sync round rides the Mesh itself: one whole signed Mesh request carries this machine's sync set to the peer, the peer converges it and answers with its own set in the same exchange — one answered door settles both machines, and the card names the route (*Mesh — <that machine>*)

Trigger pulls (app start, DHD session start) take the same road first. When no Mesh route answers, the round falls back to the backup-repo transport, unchanged. The set, the triggers, and the convergence are untouched — newest wins, diverged threads kept whole as siblings, and deletion tombstones are honored over **both** transports

Two guards ride the new road: the set is size-capped (past the cap the repo carries the round), and when both machines know their operator's GitHub login and the logins differ, nothing crosses — different people's work never merges on a pairing. - **One GitHub credential (#173 phase 3).** The separate **Apex Runtime** PAT is retired

The app's reads — the Updater's checks, the NUR's searches and repo reads, downloads, the GitHub section's pulse and issues — now ride the operator's own device-flow sign-in, the only GitHub credential Apex holds; a leftover `config/github-runtime.json` is ignored, never read

Sign-in itself needs nothing set up: the OAuth App is registered with Device Flow enabled, and Apex ships its client ID — a public identifier, no secret exists or is needed — in `config/github-signin.json`, so **Sign in with GitHub** works out of the box, on the desktop page and over DHD on a phone alike

Signed out, the reads degrade exactly as before (unauthenticated, failures naming the allowance) and every local feature is unaffected. The Identities panel now shows the truth: Operator and Release Automation, and no third token pretending to exist

- **Operator cards travel as themselves (#180).** When a backup runs, the Operator card also lands in the backup repo as its own plain file — `cards/operator-badge.png`, exactly the card's bytes, no archive — listable and fetchable one card at a time, on the phone over DHD, without opening the whole backup

A restore takes the card from that file and reproduces it byte-for-byte (the `dashboard.json` copy stays for older restores; the file is canonical). The bright line holds and is bench-proven: no Mesh node key material appears in any file a backup writes — the card is the operator's picture and profile, never the node's keys.

**Build 7** — the relay build, and the awareness build. The Mesh gains its third road: when every direct road between two paired machines is dark, a third paired machine both can reach carries the ask — three consents, one hop, metadata only. Apex also ships as a Docker image for the first time: a headless node in a container, DHD-first, its identity minted at first boot and never baked in

And the Threat Intelligence Center becomes the awareness home: a Dashboard glance over four families, each on its own tab — the news wire (#188), the Center's CVEs, the CTF board (#189), and the bounty board — with Navi carrying the same picture in chat, where asking *what's the sitch* returns the briefing with her take labeled as hers.
### Build 7
- **Relay — the third road (#154).** When the direct addresses, the declared public endpoint, and the managed backup tunnel all fail, a paired machine that can see both ends may **carry** the borrow

The inner request is today's signed Mesh request, byte-identical, wrapped in a second signed envelope addressed to the carrier; the carrier verifies consent, signature, and size, forwards it verbatim to the lender's door, and returns the sealed answer the same way. It sees envelope metadata only — who asks, who is asked, how many bytes, what stage it ended at — and its ledger records exactly that

Consent is **three ticks, one on each machine**, each set on that machine's own dashboard on the carrier's peer card: the asker ticks that the carrier may carry its envelopes to the lender; the carrier ticks that it will carry between the pair; the lender ticks that the carrier may carry envelopes to it from the asker

Any missing tick refuses the carriage **by name** — the refusal says which machine has not consented — and unticking any one stops the next carriage, because every machine re-reads its consent on every request. Consent is given **in person**, like lending: through the DHD door a tick can be unticked from anywhere, but never ticked on

The road is **one hop, hard**: a relayed envelope is never re-relayed, and an envelope whose inner ask does not name this carrier is refused as already-carried. Direct is always tried first; only chat answers (`generate` class) ride the relay

When an answer comes back carried, the reply's pill names the machine that **answered** and a line under it names the road — *via relay <machine>*; when the relay road fails, the local fallback keeps the stage's name (*no-consent*, *relay-dark*, *dest-dark*, *dest-refused*, *dest-unknown*, *hop-limit*) in the same sentence style as every other failure

The Mesh health check gains a **relay verdict** for every consented road: a signed, content-free probe asks the carrier whether its own tick is in place and whether the destination is paired there at all, and the verdict is honest about the one end no probe can read — the destination's acceptance is proven when it answers a carriage. A dark relay costs one short probe, never a timeout spiral

- **Apex in Docker — the container node.** The tree now ships a `Dockerfile`, a `docker-compose.yml`, and the first-boot machinery (`docker/entrypoint.sh`, `docker/first_boot.py`): a headless Apex node in a container — the same bridge, the same Mesh door (8765, 8443, 2475 published), the same DHD door

**No identity is ever baked into the image**: the node's Mesh keypair, certificate, and pairing card are minted on the machine that runs it, at first boot, inside the data volume, and the build context structurally excludes every identity directory

The model binary is not baked in either — the container downloads `navi.llamafile` once on first run (the installer's pattern) and keeps it in the volume; one binary serves both architectures, and the image is multi-arch (amd64 + arm64) by construction
One named volume over the whole app directory carries the --fresh preservation law into container form: identity, config, chats, and chips persist across container replacement

The out-of-box is **DHD-first**: DHD is enabled by default at first boot in the container only (bare-metal defaults are untouched), and the first boot **mints a fresh access code** — never a shared or shipped default — and prints it exactly once, in an unmissable boxed banner in the first-boot output, beside the node's name and Mesh fingerprint; the same banner is kept in `FIRST-BOOT.txt` in the data volume

Later boots never re-print it. Losing it is a designed path, not a lockout: `docker exec <container> python3 /opt/navi-apex/bridge.py --dhd-code` re-prints it, and `--dhd-code-reset` mints a new one (already-trusted devices keep their own tokens). While no device has ever been approved, a container node's door page carries one hint sentence pointing at the first-boot output

The Docker warning rides the docs: inside a container there is no physical LAN interface to harvest, so the **declared public endpoint is the honest address** — set it (the compose file wires `APEX_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT`) before minting cards for others

- **The awareness home — Dashboard, News, CVEs, CTFs, Bounties (#188, #189).** The Threat Intelligence Center's page becomes the awareness home: it opens on a **Dashboard** — one glance card per family (top news, newest CVEs, next CTFs, bounty programs), each with its freshness stamp, each opening its full view — and every family gets its own dedicated tab carrying as much data as its source gives; the Center itself keeps a tab, whole

**News** is the wire: a bridge-side fetcher over BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Krebs on Security, Dark Reading, SecurityWeek, The Record, and CISA advisories, plus the CVE sources (NVD recent, CISA KEV additions), into a local store with headline, source, date, link, and a summary-depth excerpt
Stories dedupe by link; a story whose text changes updates in place and is marked **developing**; retention defaults to 7 days and is the operator's setting

**CTFs** is the CTFtime board: running-now and upcoming sections, cards carrying format, online or on-site location, weight, restrictions, organizers, logo, description, prizes, and the listing link, times rendered in the operator's own timezone; the menu's **CTF Board** item lands on the tab

**Bounties** lists public programs from ProjectDiscovery's Chaos index (verified live at bake time: the index now lives on the data host, `chaos-data.projectdiscovery.io`) — name, platform, program link, bounty-paying flag, and scope size; the index states no safe-harbor terms, so the cards say so, and disclosed reports ship as a **named empty section** (HackerOne's hacktivity proved to have no keyless feed) rather than invented rows
All four families share one posture: outbound-only, no accounts, no keys, local stores, named staleness, a dead source is a sentence and last-good data stays up

**Navi is aware of all of it in chat**: the three stores ride her context as one bounded briefing, and asking *what's the sitch* returns the situation — top news, new CVEs, developing stories, the boards — facts cited by source and date, then her assessment under **“My take,”** labeled as opinion and never dressed as reporting

**Articles open in the app**: tapping a headline tries an in-app reader (the bridge fetches that one article, on demand, only for links the wire is carrying, and extracts a readable view with the source, the date, and an Open-original button always present); when extraction cannot honestly produce the article — paywall, script shell, non-article — the failure is named and the fallback is the original: a new tab on desktop, the article proper on mobile.
**Build 8** — the federation build (#154)

The Mesh stops being a set of pairs and becomes what it was designed to be: named **fedinets** of nodes, each with a gateway keeping a **signed roster**, **deep trust** ruled by the founder (a fedinet's roster auto-pairs and auto-lends when its operator's toggle is on), a **Federation page** of its own, and doors tiered for it — read and revoke open through DHD, manage acts behind the **Operator Badge step-up**, and the **crown acts** (enable deep trust, found a fedinet, authorize tunnel keys) running through DHD under the full ceremony: trusted-device session, Badge, a named-action confirm, and an audit entry
The Mesh status headline graduates from a census to the state: **Mesh Online**.
### Build 8

- **Fedinets + signed rosters (#154).** A fedinet is a named set of nodes; its **gateway** maintains and **signs** the roster — member node ids, card fingerprints, and join order (**Node numbers are roster facts**, assigned at admission)

Roster sync rides the Mesh door, direct first and then **via relay** (Build 8 admits the roster class to Build 7's sealed carriage — same three ticks, same one-hop rule, the destination's own consent check at its roster door). Versions only move forward; a forged, unsigned, or rolled-back roster is **refused by name** and the stored roster stands

A roster last verified more than **72 hours** ago degrades its fedinet to **pairing-only**, with the sentence on the Federation page saying so. **Expulsion** is a signed roster revision, effective at the next sync; pairings made by hand outside the fedinet are never touched — a hand pairing that was later admitted is unmarked, not deleted, and a federation-made record for a departed member is removed

- **Gateway cards.** A pairing card's form, rendered **green**, the fedinet's name on its face, the payload riding a `navi-gateway-card` chunk and signed by the gateway. Import is **admission + introduction only**: the gateway becomes a peer and its roster becomes fetchable; no trust is granted by the import itself

A gateway that founded its fedinet is representable as both facts at once — **gateway AND Founding Member** (Node 1) — and the roster shows both. - **Deep trust, with its guardrails (#154; ruled 2026-11-13).** Trust is **deep** by the founder's ruling: with a fedinet's **trust-by-default** toggle on, the signed roster **auto-pairs and auto-lends** on this node — against the gateway's signature, never against a claim

Refining it, per operator, per fedinet: the **lend-to-new-members tick** (default on; unticked, a member who joins after your trust baseline is pairing-only for you until ticked), a **per-member untrust** that always wins, a **per-member lend tick** for named exceptions, an hourly **borrow cap** as local policy, and **owner preemption** — your own work takes the machine from a federation borrow mid-flight, the borrower answered *preempted* by name; a hand-made pairing's borrow is never preempted

One flip of trust-by-default off ends all auto-lending; pairings already made stay pairings, and lending is re-judged fresh on every ask, so an untick, an untrust, or an expulsion stops the next borrow, not a later one. - **Founding.** Any operator can mint a fedinet, become its gateway, and sign roster v1 with themselves as **Founding Member**; a node keeps several fedinets at once, with zero trust bleed across them

**Rockport Mesh** ships as the default fedinet *definition* only — the product carries the machinery and the invitation story, never a hardcoded roster: the real roster lives on its gateway. First runs meet Rockport through its gateway card; a container image built to join carries that card as its **preload invitation** (below)

- **The Federation page.** Its own page (desktop canvas + a dedicated phone arrangement), not a Mesh tab: the fedinets and their rosters with each member's posture in a sentence, gateway cards to import, display, download, and re-share, the trust toggles and ticks, founding controls, borrow caps, pending knocks with admit/deny, and the **trust audit log** — every trust-class act on this node, through any door, in sentences, metadata only

Every switch on the page is benched to the switch gate: flip, stored state, and reload read one truth because the page renders only what the bridge answers, and a refusal lands as a sentence on the same card

- **DHD tiers + crown acts (ruled 2026-11-13 20:56 EST).** DHD is the remote admin surface for **the operator's own nodes only** — each node enforces its own operator auth, and no door flips another operator's switches. **Read + revoke** are open via DHD always. **Manage** acts (imports, ticks, caps, admissions) need a trusted-device session plus the **step-up**

**Crown acts** — enabling deep trust, founding a fedinet, authorizing tunnel keys — run through DHD under the full ceremony: trusted-device session + **Operator Badge** presentation + a **named-action confirm** (the act spelled in words, typed to confirm) + an audit entry; at the desk, the same acts need the same confirm + audit

The Badge factor: the node stores only the Badge's **SHA-256 fingerprint**, enrolled **in person** (enrollment itself never rides DHD); the picture is presented, hashed, compared, and never stored. A node with no Badge enrolled refuses DHD crown/manage acts **by name** — the ceremony cannot run, and says so

Build 4's in-person-only tunnel-key rule is amended accordingly: authorize is a crown act now; **revoke stays open through every door**. - **"Mesh Online."** While a node keeps any fedinet, the Mesh status headline is the state — **Mesh Online** — not a census of pairs. Warnings still outrank it; with no fedinet kept, every surface speaks as before

- **Docker preload (Build 7's image, wired).** A container image built to join a fedinet carries the gateway's card at `docker/gateway-card.png`; the first boot places it as the node's waiting invitation (`config/federation/invitation.png`) and the bridge imports it at start — **admission-only**, and under the container's ruled Rockport default the imported fedinet's trust-by-default starts ON (it engages only when a signed roster syncs; the import itself lends nothing)

Node keypairs still mint at first boot and are never baked; the gateway's identity never leaves the gateway — the card is minted there, in the field. The tree's `docker/sample-gateway-card.png` is a clearly-labeled **sample** of the shape, with sample facts, never wired as an invitation.

**Build 10** — the installer rebuild (#193), the Federation page's render guard (#195), and an app brush-up (#196), baked the night the first federation was founded in the field

That night is also the rebuild's evidence: three installer incidents in one evening on one machine — an install that died mid-copy on files a remedy had left root-owned, an install run under sudo that stranded its service registration, and a half-promoted install whose new face ran over an old bridge until the Federation page strobed against a route the bridge had never heard of
Build 10 is the rebuild those incidents specified.
### Build 10
- **The installer is rebuilt (#193).** Three pieces, one law each

**The payload is a contract:** MANIFEST.txt now declares every file the package carries with a class (payload / seed-config / generated / package-only) and a sha256; the installer copies and verifies *from the manifest* — the hand-written per-file copy blocks that desynced in #192 are deleted, and a payload file missing from the package, or whose bytes are not the declared bytes, fails the install *by name before the bridge is stopped*

**Placement is one act:** the new tree is assembled in a staging directory beside the live one — from the live tree itself, so operator state rides wholesale — and promoted by rename; a kill or failure at any point leaves the previous version *entirely* live or the new version entirely live, never a mixture, and the two-file `.pending` flip ceremony is gone

**Provisioning is not placement:** a first install provisions an operator-owned root once and placement never needs sudo again; an install invoked *through* sudo refuses up front, by name, before anything is touched (under sudo, `systemctl --user` cannot reach the operator's bus and files land root-owned), and a tree the operator cannot write refuses the same way, with the one repair command named; payload files a past sudo repair left root-owned inside a writable tree no longer block placement at all — the swap never writes into the old tree's files, so they are left behind in the previous tree, which the installer names if the operator cannot delete it

After the swap, **the product verifies itself** — `bridge.py --self-check` proves the stamps agree, every manifest payload digest verifies against the live tree, and every runtime engine imports from the installed directory — and the install stands or *rolls back whole* on that verdict, never on a version proxy

What an install preserves is unchanged: the llamafile, chips and packs, the Vault, DHD certificates, the Mesh identity, chats, config, the voice venv, Soul and Memory. Docker's whole-tree image build is untouched

- **The Federation page cannot strobe (#195).** The page fetched its state from inside its own render — and re-rendered on every answer — so any answer that set no state (the field case: a pre-federation bridge answering `{"error": "not found"}`) repainted the page forever

No silent retry loop remains on any door

**Build 11** — the homecoming build (#198) and token renewal everywhere (#197). Build 10's rebuilt installer met its first unattended pull and died honestly: stage-and-swap assembles the new tree *beside* the live one, and beside /opt/navi-apex is /opt — root-owned on any stock system — so the promotion the design promises can never run there

The operator's ruling was not a patch but a move: Apex's home was the problem, so Apex comes home. The same week's second field report — a GitHub sign-in that demanded re-signing every morning on every authenticated surface — turned out to be one missing wire, repeated everywhere: renewal existed, and exactly one consumer used it.
### Build 11

- **The homecoming (#198).** Apex's default install home is now **~/.local/share/navi-apex** — the operator's XDG data home, resolved from the installing operator's $HOME (the passwd entry is the fallback when a detached context arrives with no HOME at all). There is no other default and no /opt continuation path

When the new installer runs against a legacy tree at /opt/navi-apex — including invoked detached by the legacy Updater's apply helper, which passes its own root as --dir — it **migrates on that run**: the new build installs into the new home through the same manifest/stage-and-swap path, then every piece of operator state is carried from the legacy tree — chips and RAG packs with their indexes, the Vault, DHD certificates, the Operator card, chats with their sync state and tombstones, Case Files, config including the GitHub sign-in, Soul/Memory, the model, the voice venv — and above all **the Mesh identity: node keypair, door certificate, pairing records, federation state, tunnel keypair, byte-for-byte**, so a gateway's fingerprint (and every pin held against it across a federation) survives the move untouched

Boot units pointing at the legacy tree are retired before the carry and services are re-registered against the new home; the post-install relaunch — the installer's own, and the apply helper's after it adopts the migration marker the installer leaves — starts the **new home's** start.sh

The legacy tree is **parked, never deleted**: left in place with a `MIGRATED.txt` marker naming the new home, the date, and the removal one-liner (`sudo rm -rf /opt/navi-apex` — sudo because deleting the directory takes its parent, which is the honest reason an unprivileged installer cannot do it for you), and the same sentence is printed in the install output

Migration runs **at most once** (the new home records it); a second run is a plain same-home upgrade. If both homes somehow hold state, the new home is canonical — nothing is carried over it, and the output says so in a sentence instead of merging silently

- **The permissions doctrine (#198).** The second defect in the stranded pull — a preflight that checked the install dir and never its staging parent — and the manual-install death the same morning (an assembly copy dying on an unreadable root-owned `config/github-auth.json` and a root-owned `.pyc`, discovered one file at a time) become one doctrine

**Before anything is stopped**, the installer proves it can create its staging and park locations under the new parent, refusing by name with the remedy when it cannot; and it audits the source tree in **one exhaustive pass** for files the operator cannot read, handling each offender **by class**: **regenerable** bytecode (`__pycache__`, `*.pyc`) is never carried and never blocks — the carry reads exclude it, so it cannot kill a copy again; **re-issuable credentials** (`config/github-auth.json` and its retired sibling) are left behind when unreadable, and the completion output and the install record name the casualty and its remedy in one sentence — *"GitHub sign-in was not carried — sign in again from Identities"*; **irreplaceable state** unreadable (Mesh identity and certs, cards, chats, Case Files, Soul/Memory, all other config) refuses the install up front, naming **every** offending file plus the exact `sudo chown` one-liner that repairs them all — never whack-a-mole

After the swap, the product's **self-check grows an ownership verdict** over the new tree — every file operator-owned and operator-readable, offenders named in `config/install-self-check.json` and the install record — so the tree can never quietly rot root-owned again without the product saying so itself

The boundary is stated plainly: an unprivileged installer cannot chown root's files; the fix is that it never needs to — except for irreplaceable state, and there the stop comes first, complete, with its remedy attached

- **Token renewal everywhere (#197).** The GitHub sign-in's refresh machinery existed since the sign-in build — and its only callers were the chip-publish loop's private wrappers, so the Updater, the NUR, the GitHub section, the backup and Quick Sync transports each discovered the access token's ~8-hour death as a fresh 401 and demanded a re-sign, every morning, forever
Now there is **one shared authenticated-call wrapper**: every `github_api` / `github_api_raw` consumer rides it, as do the runtime read path (`_github_read`: Updater checks, NUR reads) and downloads

Riding the stored token, a call **renews pre-emptively** when the token's recorded expiry — persisted as an absolute `expires_at` at save time since this build, instead of a lifetime nothing read — says it is dead or inside the margin; a 401 that still arrives earns **exactly one renewal and one retry**. The publish loop's own renewal is retired into the wrapper

Failure honesty is unchanged: a 401 surviving renewal (or with no refresh token stored) surfaces the existing named auth sentence exactly once, and rate/abuse classification and wording are untouched. - **The reader, widened and un-clipped (#196 rider).** Two field notes on The Wire's article reader, answered together
The desktop panel was a 680px newspaper column; it is now `min(1120px, calc(100vw - 48px))` — the page, not a column of it (the phone sheet is unchanged in shape)

And the reader's top bar could clip the headline: the bar was a `position:sticky` first child *inside* the scrolling panel, so its painted place at open rode on the engine's sticky-vs-padding origin and the panel's initial scroll origin — the field screenshot shows the headline's first line half-clipped at the sheet's top edge, above the source/Close bar, on the phone and the desktop alike

The structure is what changed: the panel is now a flex column that never scrolls, the bar is a fixed first child, and the article scrolls in its own box below it — at open the headline stands fully below the bar, and at no scroll position can the bar overlap or clip a content line, on either door, by construction.
**Build 12** — the #201 fix build

v0.2.0e — Build 11's first unattended pull died within two seconds on both field machines (incident 21): the apply helper descends from the bridge, so it lives inside the bridge's systemd unit, and the installer's homecoming retired the legacy boot units with `systemctl --user disable --now` — stopping the unit signalled every process in it: the bridge, the helper, and the installer itself

The helper's trace recorded the SIGTERM and the failure; the install log ended at the homecoming heading; the migration never ran, and both legacy trees stood intact. This build is that one defect, answered in both halves of the apply, under one stated invariant — and nothing else.
### Build 12

- **The no-ancestry-signalling invariant (#201).** Stated in the code, in the in-app Docs, and here: an apply may end exactly one process by signal — the bridge it replaces, by its proven pid, through the installer's stop machinery

It may never use a group-shaped signal — a systemd unit stop, a process-group kill, a cgroup kill — because those mechanisms cannot tell the bridge apart from the apply's own ancestry: the helper descends from the bridge, and the installer descends from the helper. A new session is not an escape from a cgroup; Build 11's helper had one, and died anyway

- **The helper escape (#201).** The bridge now spawns the apply helper **outside its own systemd unit**: via `systemd-run --user --scope`, in a transient scope of its own (probed first; the recorded helper pid is the scope's waiting parent, whose lifetime tracks the helper's, so the panel and the watchdog keep their meaning)
No stop of the bridge's unit — this installer's, a future installer's, an operator's — can reach it

Where no scope can be had (systemd-run absent, or no user manager answers — the container shape), the spawn falls back to the plain own-session spawn and **says so**: the step log's first line and the apply record both name the mode the run actually has, and on such a machine the installer's ordering below is the protection

- **The installer's ordering (#201).** Defense in depth, in the homecoming leg and the pre-/opt migration leg alike: the legacy bridge, model server and window are stopped **by pid first**, through the proven stop machinery (the model server gains a pid-stop of its own, matched on its directory and command line the way the bridge's has always been); only then are the legacy units' files retired — `disable` + remove + daemon-reload, **stopping nothing** — and a final stop proof after the retirement closes the resurrection window, with no unit definition left to resurrect anything

A whole-script audit found no other unit stop or broad signal: the only remaining `--now` in the installer *starts* the new home's services after the swap, and every other kill in the script was already a proven single pid

- **The interrupted-home guard (#201).** A migration is complete only when a marker proves it — the new home's own `config/migration.json`, or the legacy tree's `.apex-migration.json` naming this home

A live-looking tree at the new home with **no** marker is an **interrupted home** — the remains of a migration that died between the swap and the park — and is never canonical and never converged onto: the migration runs again, state is carried from the legacy tree whole, and the interrupted tree is renamed aside by the swap like any previous tree, with the situation named in the output

The both-homes rule survives exactly where it belongs: when a marker proves the earlier migration completed, the new home is canonical and the legacy tree stays parked. - **The bench that convicts (unitapply12).** The regression that let incident 21 through was a bench that ran every apply from a shell no unit owned

The new fixture runs full applies with the helper standing inside a real cgroup standing in for the bridge's unit, against a `systemctl` whose unit stop performs systemd's actual control-group kill: the Build 11 package fails it with the field's own signature (SIGTERM in the helper's trace, the record failed at the installing step, the install log ending at the homecoming heading), and v0.2.0e — Build 12 passes it three ways — under the old bridge on the installer's ordering alone, under its own bridge with the plain fallback, and under its own bridge with the helper genuinely relocated into a transient scope while a Build 11 installer fires its unit stop anyway.

Release tag: v0.1.9. The casework release. Case Files grew from a folder of notes into the room investigations live in — every case with a chat of its own, its evidence shown as evidence, and Navi filing findings in her own name — while the Threat Intelligence Center opened beside it, the Guardian took up its watch over Navi's headroom, and Apex learned to arm itself at boot and come up headless from a cold start

All of it was built in the open on the Edge channel as 0.1.9e, Builds 1–15, and checked in the field build by build. This full release is that line with its identity flipped: the bare number, the stable status, Latest. The code is the Edge line's final build, plus one mark the field caught missing after that build shipped — the Threat Intelligence Center's radar (#168).
### What graduated

- **Case Files is where an investigation lives (#137, #161, #162, #163).** Opening a case ensures a chat tied to that case — one canonical thread on the server-side store, a CASE tag on the Chats tab, a chip on the case chat that jumps back to the case — and while a case is open Navi files her own findings into it, under her own name, never silently and never in the background

Exports embed image evidence as images inside the single report file, and a case can be deleted completely — the case, every Vault file it owns, and its tied chat — behind one confirmation that names all of it, backups stated plainly as out of reach

- **The Threat Intelligence Center, v1 (#165).** A local intel store (`intel.py`, stdlib only) fed by keyless public sources only — the NVD API 2.0 keyless tier, the CISA KEV catalog, EPSS, CISA advisories RSS, and curated RSS — merged on the CVE ID with each source owning its fields, fetched under ETag/Last-Modified discipline, and stamped so staleness is labeled everywhere (fresh <12h · aging <48h · stale beyond)

Navi carries a bounded standing brief of it in chat, answers deliberate lookups straight from the store, and matches records locally against the watchlist, the Mesh roster, and the words of open cases; the digest rides the Mesh door, so one node collects and the rest import and match locally. From a record, File into the open case lands it as a finding with its citation

- **The Guardian, the profile, and the boot arm (#156, #157, #159).** The Guardian (`guardian.py`, stdlib only) samples the machine against a headroom model of what Navi needs and works a watch → warn → throttle → kill ladder whose kill rung may only ever touch the operator-approved expendable list — which ships empty on purpose — with every event provenance-tagged from day one

The optimization pass measured first and claimed no cosmetics: an automatic hardware profile for a config that never set one, and warm-up so the first ask carries no model-load dead air. Arm at boot registers both systemd user services from inside the app and shows the state as the system reports it — half-armed reads half-armed

- **Chats live on the server; the badge carries them (#139, #136, #150, #151).** Chats are stored by the bridge in `config/chats/` — local storage is a cache, never the record — and follow the Operator Badge between machines through the GitHub backup's convergence

The badge gained a true slot, in Settings → Operator and as the same shared intake on the sync card; sync starts in Chat, where its operation card carries the progress and the verdict under a 45-second plain-words timeout. The DHD door wears the Row's favicon, served on both doors

- **Headless, from a cold boot (#142).** The bridge and the DHD door come up with no login at all, the armed state read live in the status column's Servers → Boot row, and the full guide ships in both docs surfaces — including the Wi-Fi secret trap the field round found and proved was the environment, not the app: a profile with no stored secret fails at boot with "no secrets" until `nmcli` stores it, typed at the machine, never through chat

- **The quality-of-life line underneath (Builds 1–11).** The server names unified into the Apex product family and chip faces drawn, not rolled (#92); chips run like programs with `./<name>`, short names and prefix resolution (#97); knowledge packs ride pictures as cartridges (#93); ChipDeck, the binder for everything that rides a picture (#94); Publish runs the whole GitHub chain in one action; the live install-visibility defect fixed at its root (#95); and the Chip Studio's dedicated phone arrangement with focus mode as the app's one expand idiom (#146, #135)

- **Fifteen builds, verified one by one.** Everything above arrived on the Edge channel as Builds 1–15 of 0.1.9e (public Build 5 skipped by design), each staged byte-exact and gated on the extracted bytes, and the line closes the way graduations close: a full regression on the final package, not a delta. The full release keeps the Edge line's final stamps: build 2026-11-12.915, build sequence 15.

Release tag: v0.1.9e — **Build 15**, the fifteenth build of this version and its thirteenth publication (the first was Build 1; the Build 15 notes sit directly below in their own section, and everything under "Build 14" and below further down is those builds' notes, unchanged). Build 1 bundled the whole 0.1.9 QOL line into one build, directed 2026-11-10. Its features:

- **The server names unify into the Apex product family** (issue #92, in-app pass). The status column's Servers group now reads, in order: **Navi** (the engine row — its detail line keeps the technical truth, "llamafile · port 8080"), **Apex Node**, **Apex Mesh**, **Apex DHD**; the menu and pages wear the same names
Names are display only — config keys, routes, ports, the model id, and every protocol string are untouched. - **Chip faces are drawn, not rolled** (issue #92)

A new forge wears the family shell — black body, coral notched bands — with one chunky pixel glyph that means the chip's function, named in the chip's metadata (the `glyph` field in navi-chip.json); a keyword read picks one when none is named, and the old name-seeded pattern survives only as the fallback. Installed and published pictures are never redrawn
- **The live install-visibility defect is fixed at its root** (issue #95)

A NUR install answered success and the catalog card flipped to INSTALLED, but Local Chips kept showing 0 and no pill appeared: the bridge was innocent — install wrote the cartridge, recorded it, and verified it against the same folder scan Local Chips reads — but the dashboard's install/update/delete completion invalidated only the catalog cache, never the workflows payload (`wfData`) that Local Chips, its tab count, and the pill row all render from, and that payload is fetched once and cached for the session

The completion now invalidates both, so an install shows in Local Chips in the same session, no restart. **Uninstall grew reachability in the same round**: an installed chip's catalog card and its ChipDeck sleeve both carry Uninstall now, alongside Local Chips' Delete; cartridge and record go together, and a chip with local edits asks first

The audit also caught a quieter lie — a chip dropped into chips/ by hand has no install record, so its Delete removed nothing while saying "Deleted"; a local/ delete now takes the picture with it. - **Chips run like programs** (issue #97)

`./<name> <args>` in chat runs a chip, args passing through as they always have; bare `./` answers with the shelf; short names resolve (`./cryptex` finds navi-cryptex), a unique prefix runs, an ambiguous one answers with its candidates, and an unknown one answers with the shelf instead of a dead end. `/chip` keeps working as the long-form alias. Under the CLI latch, `./` belongs to the shell again — the latch decides

The composer's chip pill shelf is retired: running lives at the keyboard, and the chips' browsable home is ChipDeck. Attribution pills under replies are untouched. - **Knowledge packs ride pictures** (issue #93)

A pack exports as a **knowledge cartridge** — one PNG carrying its manifest and every document's text, compressed — and installs from the picture alone (RAG tab or a ChipDeck drop), its index built locally at install from the carried texts; a cartridge never carries an index, and retrieval never reads the picture. Past the 8 MB ceiling the export refuses in plain words and points at the ZIP; nothing truncates

- **ChipDeck** (issue #94). A new top-level surface — the binder, under a binder-rings mark: sleeves holding the actual pictures of everything that rides one (installed chips, Mesh pairing cards, knowledge cartridges), each with its state and its actions gathered — run, download the picture, Studio, uninstall; pair and unpair; activate, deactivate, remove
Drop a picture anywhere on the Deck and it slots in by the payload inside it. Soul, Memory, config, the Vault, and keys never ride cartridges; they stay in backups, where they belong.
- **Publish does everything** (the fully automated chain). Publishing a chip or a pack used to stop at the upload — the release was the operator's manual step on GitHub

**Publish to GitHub** now runs the whole chain in one action: create the repo if it is missing, upload the file set, set the topic (navi-chips / navi-rag), create the tag from the manifest version, and **publish** the release (never a draft) with the cartridge picture attached — the chip PNG for chips, the knowledge cartridge for packs (which also lands at the pack repo's root). Release notes come from the README

A version that is already released is refused before anything uploads — bump the version in the manifest; a release is never overwritten silently. The unsigned route is unchanged: Export-for-GitHub ZIP, everything by hand.
### Build 15

- **Every case gets its chat, and Navi files her own findings** (issue #161). Opening a case now ensures **a chat tied to that case** — created on first open, returned to ever after, one canonical thread per case, riding the server-side chat store (#139) like every other thread and marked with a CASE tag on the Chats tab. **Open the case chat** on the case page walks straight into it

While a case is open, **Navi can file her own findings** into it: conclusions she reaches, in her own words, under her own name — the finding's frontmatter carries `author: navi`, the case page marks it FILED BY NAVI, and a line lands in the case's timeline

Filing is never silent and never background: it happens in the thread where she reached the conclusion, and the receipt — the finding's title and its path — hangs on her message there (the same judgment-marker discipline as her memory saves, at most two per reply; a stray marker with no case open is stripped and dropped)

The **open case is visible**: the status column carries it in its stats, and the case chat wears a chip naming it that jumps back to the case; closing the case clears both. - **Case exports show image evidence as images** (issue #162)

The report's evidence section now **embeds** PNG/JPG/GIF/WebP evidence into `report.md` as base64 data URIs — the evidence travels inside the single file, so the #138 single-file promise holds for the downloaded copy too, not just in the app's own preview. An image over ~8 MB stays listed by name with the reason stated; non-image evidence keeps the name-and-size listing; the internal-withholding rules are untouched

- **A case can be deleted — completely** (issue #163). The case page gains a delete control with **one confirmation that names what will be removed**: the case, every file it owns in the Vault (findings, evidence, timeline, manifest, exported report), and — since this build ties chats to cases — **its tied chat**, the whole conversation

Deleting purges the case folder from the Vault entirely, removes the bound chat from the store (so no machine's write-through can resurrect it), and clears the open-case pointer when the deleted case was the open one. The confirmation states the backup truth plainly: backups are snapshots and are **not** reached into — a case inside an existing backup stays in that backup
- **The Threat Intelligence Center, v1** (issue #165)

A new Apps surface and a new engine (`intel.py`, stdlib only) beside the bridge: a **local intel store** (`config/intel.db`) fed by **keyless public sources only** — the NVD API 2.0 (keyless tier, incremental lastMod windows, politely paced), the CISA KEV JSON catalog, EPSS (daily, batched over the store), CISA advisories RSS, and curated RSS (Krebs, BleepingComputer)

A record's identity is its CVE ID, and each source owns its fields — KEV the exploited status and due dates, NVD the CVSS/CPE/description, EPSS the likelihood — merged by UPSERT, fetched with ETag/Last-Modified discipline, and stamped per source so **staleness is labeled everywhere** (fresh <12h · aging <48h · stale beyond; last-good is served, never a silent old picture)

**Navi is contextually aware**: the digest enters her chat context as a bounded standing brief (~700 tokens, freshness stamps included), a deliberate lookup (`intel: <query>`, “what do we know about CVE-…”) answers straight from the store without a model round-trip, and naming a CVE or a watched product in ordinary chat pulls that record into the reply (in a case chat, the case's matched records ride too)

**Matching is local and declared**: the operator's watchlist, the Mesh roster, and words from open cases — CPE-grade matches labeled exact, text hits labeled keyword; the inventory never leaves the machine

**The Mesh carries the weight**: one node collects, the digest object (`navi-intel-digest/1`, ~300 ranked records, collector and per-source stamps in its header) travels the Mesh door to thin clients that import it and match locally; a receiver with the fallback off never polls the feeds, and the fallback is a setting, never a surprise

From a record, **File into the open case** lands it as a finding with its citation (CVE ID + digest stamp) written into the note, so case exports carry it. The page is desktop-first — freshness strip, triage queue, the record, and the brief rail — with a dedicated phone arrangement (one column, brief first) in the same round.
### Build 14
- **The Guardian — a system monitor that protects Navi's headroom** (issue #156)

A new engine (`guardian.py`, stdlib only) lives in the system-integration layer beside the bridge, awake independent of the UI: it samples processes from `/proc`, keeps a headroom model of what Navi needs (a memory reserve that tightens while Navi is generating), and learns per-process collision statistics in a small persistent store (`config/guardian-stats.json`) — how often a process has collided, warned, been throttled, or been killed

Its action ladder is watch → warn → throttle → kill: throttle is a reversible duty-cycle (SIGSTOP/SIGCONT slices to a CPU cap) plus a best-effort renice, and kill (SIGTERM, grace, SIGKILL) may only ever touch processes on the operator-approved expendable list, which **ships empty on purpose**. Its own processes, the bridge, and the llamafile are protected by PID, name, and uid

Every action lands in a bounded in-memory log and an append-only `config/guardian-log.jsonl`; every event carries provenance from day one — `origin` (which device and door it came from) and `foreground` (what the operator is doing there, `unknown` until a later pass teaches it to see) — so the future mobile-whisper and foreground-posture concepts need no schema migration

The face is a new **Utilities → Guardian** page: a summary card with a plain-words pressure chip and a Mesh line (borrowing/peers when the Mesh is present, working locally only when it is not — the Guardian is mesh-aware and degrades gracefully), a live watch table, the learned-offenders table, the full ladder settings (persisted in config, restored on restart), and the action log
On a phone (≤800px) the page is a dedicated interface, not a squeezed desktop: cards stack full-width, the PID column drops, and every row, input, and the Save button meets the 44px floor

Navi can answer questions about the Guardian in chat: the bridge appends the Guardian's current state as a short structured block (≤110 words) to the chat system prompt, and `GET /api/guardian/state` / `POST /api/guardian/settings` expose the same state to the page

The Guardian's own footprint was measured in this build's audit (issue #157): about 0.20% of one core for its sampler loop and no measurable resident memory beyond the module import. - **The optimization pass** (issue #157)

Measured first, on the bench, against the Build 13 tree as baseline with an identical stub harness: bridge spawn → status 412.4 ms, chat round-trip median 1,261.9 ms, of which the bridge pipeline itself is only ~6.2 ms — there was no fat worth cutting, and **no cosmetic optimization is claimed**

What the numbers did justify shipped: an **automatic hardware profile** — a config with no `hardware_profile` now profiles the machine once on startup (detect + derive), persists it, and fills derived runtime defaults only where the operator has not set them, so modest machines get sane context, threads, and batch without a setup step; the profile view now names its tier plainly (**potato** / **standard** / **beast**) and where the profile came from (`profileSource`)

**Warm-up** removes the model-load dead air before the first ask: after a bridge-initiated llamafile start reports healthy, one one-token warm-up completion fires (gated by `runtime.warmup` — explicit setting wins; unset, it is on for potato/standard tiers and off for beast), and `runtime.warm_at` ("HH:MM") schedules a daily warm through the same start path

The derivation table itself is unchanged — its 6–12 GiB row's ctx 4096 is the size already proven fluid on the 9.4 GiB Framework baseline, and doubling it would eat the Guardian's reserve on exactly the machines the Guardian protects. The full before/after table is posted on issue #157. - **Arm at boot, from inside the app** (issue #159)

The status column's **Servers → Boot** row — which has read the armed state live since Build 12 — gains the hand to go with the eyes, and **Settings → System** carries the same control: **Arm at boot** registers and enables both systemd user services (`navi-llamafile.service`, `navi-bridge.service`) from the unit templates the package ships, with this install folder substituted, exactly as the installer's boot choice does, and records the startup choice in config

Linger is attempted the one way the app honestly can — a plain `loginctl enable-linger`, no sudo, nothing borrowed from the parked sudo toggle — and when the system refuses it, the surface shows the exact `sudo loginctl enable-linger $USER` command instead of pretending, and the arm shows as **half-armed** (services enabled, starting at login rather than boot)

After every action the state is re-read from the system and shown as found; partial success shows as partial. **Disarm** disables both units — what is running keeps running, it simply will not come up at boot — and leaves linger as it is. Both directions are idempotent, starting an already-running service is adoption, never doubling, and arming is a local action only: the bridge refuses it through the DHD door

- **The rail takes its settled order** (issue #160). ### Build 10

- **The update that needed a reboot.** Field report: after updating to the build that added the PNG pairing cards, the new UI never appeared — not after the update, not after relaunching — until the whole computer was rebooted. The files on disk were the new build the whole time; what survived was the old *process*

The installer's stop step fired one polite signal and one second of patience, deleted the pid file either way, and replaced the files — so a bridge that did not die on cue (stopped, stuck, mid-something-it-could-not-put-down) kept the port and kept serving the new pages with its old code, now unfindable: the pid file that named it was gone. The replacement bridge could never bind

The Updater honestly reported the restart failed, and the remedy it offered — relaunch, re-run — could not work against a process nothing would name. Only a reboot, which kills everything without asking, cleared it. That is the one thing an update on Linux must never need

- **The stop is now a proof, not a gesture.** Before a single file is replaced, the installer finds the running bridge three ways — the pid file, the process holding the port, and every bridge process working out of the install folder (the way a launcher-started bridge is found at all: its command line never names the folder) — asks it to stop, and *waits*, up to fifteen seconds, for the process to be gone and the port to be free

A bridge that will not go politely is ended by force and the wait repeated. If the port still cannot be cleared, the installer stops the install instead: no files are replaced, the pid file is left exactly where it was, and the output names the process holding the port and the exact command that ends it — 'kill -9 <pid>' — so the next step is a decision, not a mystery

The apply helper runs the same check before it relaunches and escalates the same way, and its failure text names the holding process the same way; "launch the app again" is never offered while the port is wedged. A bridge that starts against an incumbent which accepts no requests names that process's pid in its startup message too, even when no pid file survives to consult

- **A manual install finishes the job it starts.** The installer used to stop the old bridge, lay down new files, and end — the update live on disk, nothing running, until the operator thought to launch the app

Now, when a bridge was running as the install began, the installer relaunches Apex itself at the end and verifies the bridge that answers reports the new build before it says "Done." An install over a stopped app still just installs (launch her when you are ready), and '--no-relaunch' says the quiet part out loud instead: Apex is not running

- **An open dashboard heals itself.** A dashboard left open across an update is the old build's page talking to the new build's bridge — every response no-store, and still the page itself was the stale half, with no way to know it

The dashboard now compares the build the bridge reports against its own on its regular status check, and when the bridge is the newer one it says so at the top of the status column, with a Reload button: one click lands on the new build's page

(The reverse mismatch — a new page over an old bridge — keeps its BRIDGE OUT OF DATE warning, unchanged.) Behind the DHD door, a forwarded response now carries a single no-store header instead of the pair it used to.

### Build 7

- **Paired machines sat at "not checked yet" forever.** Field report from the first real pair, photographed on both machines: pairing worked, lending was armed, the consent toggles held — and both rosters still said the other machine was "not checked yet", so no borrowed answer could ever start. The check itself was sound; nothing ever ran it

The only thing that ever probed a peer was a chat message attempting a borrow, and the status display read a cache that forgot every result after sixty seconds — so a machine that only lends, or a pair nobody had chatted across yet, showed "not checked yet" as its resting state, and a failed check quietly decayed back to it, taking the reason with it

- **The fix: the bridge watches its peers itself.** A background health check now probes every paired peer about every thirty seconds while Mesh is on — and immediately when a peer is paired and when Mesh is turned on — so a pair reaches "checked" on its own, with no chat sent

A probe result no longer decays: the roster and the status column keep the last word — *unreachable — unauthorized (last checked 42s ago)* — until a newer check replaces it, and "not checked yet" now means only that no check has ever run. The bridge log notes a peer going dark or coming back, with the reason, and stays quiet otherwise

- **A trap behind the first trap, removed.** Inbound requests were authorized against the lender's own "can borrow" flag for the requester — one flag doing two opposite jobs — so on a pair where that flag was off, the first real check or borrow would have been refused as unauthorized, with the reason shown nowhere

Pairing is the consent now: a paired machine's validly signed request is accepted, and the flag means one thing only, on the borrowing side — this machine will not borrow from a peer whose "can borrow" is off

- **Cards and first knocks, hardened.** A card now carries every non-loopback address the machine has — the LAN address first — instead of freezing the one address the default route happened to pick, and a certificate fingerprint mismatch at one address no longer aborts the attempt: the borrower notes it and tries the next address on the card, refusing only when no address both answers and matches

And a machine whose Mesh name was never set no longer sits "Unnamed": turning Mesh on with the name blank keeps the machine's hostname as its name. - **The lending caps are yours to set.** The share of each hour a lender gives up, the borrowed generations it takes an hour, and the per-machine share of those were fixed numbers — 25%, 20, 10 — written for a modest laptop and never meant as a server's ceiling
They are settings now, on the lending machine's own Mesh page, in the Lending section beside the Caps line: share of each hour (1–100%), generations per hour, and per machine per hour (1–10,000 each)

They save into the machine's config and govern the very next admission and the very next card it shows — no restart — and because the card advertises the caps you set, a paired machine sees the real offer ("lends at most 50% of each hour, 60 generations an hour") instead of the defaults it shipped with

The defaults themselves are unchanged: a fresh install still lends at most 25% of each hour, 20 generations an hour, 10 per machine, until you say otherwise. - **Idle-only lending has an override.** A lender used to serve only after sixty seconds of quiet — right for a laptop, wrong for a server that has taken concurrent work before and can again

The Lending section gains a **Lend only when idle** switch, on as shipped: turn it off and the machine lends without waiting to be idle, borrowed generations running alongside your own work (your own replies may slow down — the switch's own line says so). The caps still bind, and one borrowed generation at a time still holds: a request that arrives mid-generation waits for the next slot, as it always has

The card and the status line state the posture truthfully either way — *lends when idle*, or *lends even while busy*. - **A re-enabled lender is believed at once.** A borrow decided "not lending" from a status the health check had cached moments earlier — so after "Stop lending now" and a quick re-enable, borrows kept refusing with the stale answer and were never even attempted
A not-lending verdict now earns one fresh check before the borrow gives up: a lender that is lending again serves the request, and only a lender still off on the fresh check answers "not lending"

- **Pairing travels as a picture now.** "Show my Mesh card" gains **Download PNG card**: a real .png whose face is the card a person reads — the machine's name, its node identity, and the offer in words (its capabilities, the lending limits it is configured with, whether it lends when idle or even while busy) — with the whole card riding inside the picture in the same data-in-picture format the chips use, so Apex keeps one cartridge language

On the other machine, drop the picture onto the Mesh page's Paired machines area, or use **Upload a PNG card** there: the peer is added exactly as a pasted text card adds it — same validation, same record — and text cards from every earlier build still pair

The picture has to travel as a file: chat apps like Discord recompress uploaded pictures and strip the data out, so the docs say to send it inside a .zip, and the Mesh page says the same when it meets a picture whose payload is gone — no readable Mesh card data, probably recompressed by a chat app, resend the original inside a .zip
A damaged or cut-short payload, a chip cartridge dropped in by mistake, and a file that is not a PNG at all are each refused with their own specific words — never a silent no-op

- **A borrow refused for not being idle no longer falls back in silence.** Serving a borrow restarts the lender's idle clock, so the very next chat — anything sent inside the lender's idle minute — was refused at the door as not idle yet and answered locally instead, with nothing to show a borrow had ever been attempted; a borrow refused that way never even registers on the lender
The borrower now waits out the lender's remaining idle window inside the same borrow grace it already gives a busy lender: it checks until the lender itself reports idle, then asks once more

The wait is deliberately bounded by that grace and no longer — a lender that goes idle only after the grace is spent serves the next request, exactly as a busy one does — and admission on the lender is untouched: it still refuses until it has been quiet. Only the borrower's handling of that one refusal changed

- **A recorded drop is not erased by the next failed check.** Once a lender had died mid-answer, the drop it left on the roster was being cleared by the borrow meant to find it: the borrow read a recently cached failed check, forced one more check, found the peer still dark, and threw the drop record away — so the status row fell back to a plain "unreachable" and the warning the drop earned never showed

A failed check — cached or fresh — now never clears a recorded drop: the drop is the freshest thing this machine knows about the peer, and it stands until a check actually succeeds, a borrow is served, or five minutes pass.

### Build 5

- **The update helper died in silence, and the install was left with no bridge.** Caught by Build 4's own round-trip gate — a genuine Build 3 install applying a package through its own Updater, the new closure bar doing exactly its job

The staged installer ran through to "Done.", and then nothing: the detached helper that runs the installer, relaunches Apex, and finishes the apply record left apply.log at 0 bytes, never created its relaunch log, and left the record frozen at working/installing — no bridge relaunched, the install left bridge-less

The helper's code was identical in Build 3 and Build 4; the machinery was older than both, and it was built traceless: it printed nothing by design, kept no log of its own, wrote the record only at step boundaries, and carried no guard and no signal handlers — so any death between two writes was indistinguishable from any other, and from a hang

- **The diagnosis, ranked.** First and best-fitting: an external signal kill at the installer's end — the helper sits in its own session but in the same process tree and user-service world as everything the installer stops and restarts at exactly that moment, and a SIGTERM or SIGKILL leaves no trace in the victim; crucially, it is the only mechanism consistent with all the evidence at once, since a Python-level exception would have left a traceback in apply.log and the log was empty

Second: an uncaught exception in the helper's unguarded post-installer segment (its record writes run against a config tree the installer has just replaced) — a real path, now closed, though it predicts a traceback this incident did not leave. Third: a block inside the installer wait — the old design could not tell a block from a death at all, which is part of the indictment

- **The fix: the helper keeps a diary, and the record can no longer freeze.** From its first instruction the helper writes a step log — updates/<tag>/apply-trace.log, its path carried on the apply record — timestamping every step boundary, the installer's exit, the relaunch spawn, and the confirmation's found-vs-expected values, with a heartbeat every 30 seconds while it works (a log still beating at one step is a block; a log whose beats stop is a kill — the field can finally convict the mechanism)

A top-level guard turns any exception into a failed record naming the step and the reason in words, and mirrors the traceback into apply.log; handlers do the same for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP before the helper exits

A relaunch that cannot even start now fails loudly at the restart step, and a relaunched bridge that never answers fails at restarting with what was expected and what was found — never a frozen working/installing

And for the one death no in-process guard survives (SIGKILL, the kernel's OOM killer, power loss), the bridge's **apply watchdog** closes a record whose helper is gone and whose last write has gone stale — failed, at the last step the helper provably completed, quoting its step log's final line

Build 4's three locks stand exactly as they were — the leftover size check, the package build-identity verification, and done-requires-target-build (the relaunched bridge reports the target build AND the bridge on disk carries it) — along with the apply checklist, state preservation, channel logic, and the build-named labels.
### Build 4

- **A refresh that installed the previous build and called it done.** Field report from a live install: the Build 2 → Build 3 refresh downloaded, installed, and passed its checklist — then the install still identified as Build 2, so every new check offered Build 3 again. The root cause sat in the apply's own download step

An update stages its package under a folder named by the release tag, in a file named by the release asset — and both names are the same for every publication of one version. The Build 2 apply had left its downloaded package at that exact path, and the Build 3 apply's download step read a package already beside the app back instead of fetching the offered one — so it staged and installed Build 2's bytes a second time

Nothing downstream could catch it: the apply's confirmation compared only the VERSION number, which is deliberately identical on both sides of a refresh, and the "Updated v0.1.8e Build 2 → Build 3" label was composed from the release feed, never read back from what had actually landed

The installer's copy set, its state preservation, and the relaunch were all innocent — the relaunched bridge really was a new process, faithfully running the old build's files. - **The fix: the apply proves the build, three times.** A package already beside the app is now reused only when its byte size equals the size the feed names for the offered asset; anything else is fetched fresh, overwriting the leftover

Verification then reads the build sequence baked into the package's own bridge.py and requires it to be the build on offer — a stale leftover that slips past the size check is discarded and the offered package fetched fresh once, while a fresh download that itself names the wrong build fails at the verifying step, in words, with nothing staged

And the confirmation at the end observes the build itself: the status answer now reports the running bridge's build sequence beside its stamp, and the apply helper confirms "Updated" only when the relaunched bridge reports the target build AND the bridge.py on disk carries it — otherwise the record fails at the restart step, naming the build it found instead of the one it expected

The rule is general — it holds for any same-version refresh, Build N → Build N+1 — and graduations and new-version updates, whose tags (and therefore staging paths) always differ, are untouched. What Build 3 built is preserved exactly: the build-named refresh labels, the apply checklist, state preservation, and channel resolution.
