### Build 1
### Navi Mesh — Ring 1 (#78)

- **Whole requests, one machine answers.** When Mesh is on and a paired lender is reachable, a chat request is assembled on your machine exactly as always — persona, Vault, knowledge packs, history — and the lender's own model writes the whole reply. The reply says who wrote it: "Answered by <machine name>" under the message. CLI mode, chips, and every built-in route never borrow; only model answers do

- **Pairing is a card, carried by hand.** Each machine shows its Mesh card on the Mesh page — its name, node id, public key, certificate fingerprint, addresses, and a capabilities block as one copyable block. Paste the other machine's card into yours (and yours into its) and the pair is made. Pairing is the consent act: a paired machine is a trusted machine

Nothing anywhere is tied to a specific operator, machine, or domain — every name and address comes from the cards and your config. - **Borrowing is automatic, with off switches.** For paired machines, borrowing just happens when a lender is reachable (Alex's ruling) — and there are three ways to say no: the borrowing switch, the Mesh master switch, and a per-chat "keep it on this machine" toggle beside the composer

If the lender is busy, your machine waits a short grace (2 seconds by default, yours to set) for it to free up, then answers locally; a freed lender serves the next request, never a half-written one. If a lender drops mid-answer, you get the notice — "<machine> dropped mid-answer — this reply was generated locally instead" — and a fresh local reply, never two models' prose spliced together

- **Lending is automatic when idle, and off means off.** A lender serves only while it is idle (60 seconds quiet by default), inside caps you set: at most 25% of each hour, 20 borrowed generations an hour, 10 per machine. Your own work always takes the next slot; a local request never kills a running borrowed answer. "Stop lending now" does: it ends lending and aborts a borrowed generation mid-flight, at once

Lending can only be turned ON from the lending machine's own dashboard, in person — never through the DHD door — and off from anywhere you are signed in. - **Signed, pinned, and private.** Every Mesh request is signed with the borrowing machine's Ed25519 node key and checked against the paired card; the connection's certificate is pinned to the fingerprint on the card, and a mismatch is refused in plain words

Mesh always listens on its own dedicated TLS port (8765), through its own certificate — the one the card pins — whether or not DHD is on; the DHD door refuses Mesh traffic outright, and a dashboard guest can never reach it. What travels is the assembled prompt, including your Soul and Memory text — the Settings card says so in plain words before you borrow for the first time

What never travels: files, data stores, credentials, command-line access. The lender keeps nothing of the content: its ledger records only who, which direction, and how long, and the balances it feeds are records, never a gate.
### Mesh gets its own page, its own door, and a roster

- **Mesh is a top-level page now.** The dashboard's left menu gains **Mesh** (with its own Hexlink icon — two interlocking hexagons), right after DHD. The full controls moved there from Settings → System, which keeps a one-line summary and a button that jumps to the page

- **A dedicated door, always.** Mesh no longer rides the DHD door when DHD is on: its TLS listener on the Mesh port (8765) runs whenever Mesh is enabled, its own certificate is the pinned one in every configuration, the DHD proxy refuses `/mesh/*` with 403, and the dashboard surface no longer serves the node-facing status/borrow endpoints at all — borrowers dial the dedicated port from the peer card, only

Dashboard-local Mesh routes (`/mesh/card`, `/mesh/lend/stop`, `/api/mesh/*`) stay exactly as they were, behind the gate. - **Capability cards and the roster.** A Mesh card now carries a capabilities block — the machine's own report of its hardware class, GPU or CPU, RAM, model (navi), speed class (GPU-accelerated / Integrated graphics / CPU), and its lend caps

The Mesh page puts the controls first, with a **roster** below them: this node and every paired node with name, capability line, live status, and balance. Addresses never render anywhere in it — they stay plumbing

- **Stop lending really stops.** The consent fix behind this round: "Stop lending now" now shuts down the in-flight borrowed generation's socket, and a borrow that finishes after the stop is recorded as aborted and dropped instead of served. The claim and the behavior finally match

- **Instant-off completes on the borrower's side too.** Stopping lending now drops the borrower's in-flight chat promptly into the fusion fallback — the dropped notice and a fresh local reply — instead of stranding it: the lender hard-closes the borrow connection at the socket level, and the borrower reads that termination as the drop it is

- **Docs and Settings sit at the foot of the menu.** The left menu's two housekeeping stops moved down to stack directly over the version number at the menu's foot — Docs on top, Settings directly over the version number; the working views keep the top of the menu in their usual order

- **Mesh status, at a glance.** The Servers status row for Mesh now shows connection state and warnings where you already look, in the same dot language as every other row: green when a paired machine is reachable, amber while it borrows or lends — and amber with the reason in its line, "<machine> dropped" or "<machine> unreachable", when something is wrong — grey when Mesh is off or nothing is paired yet.
### The Updater round

- **Edge build numbers.** Publications of the same Edge version are numbered — Build 1, Build 2, … — parsed from the release's name or opening lines. At the same version and status, a higher build number is a newer update; the same or lower is not. The Updater's Current line shows your build ("· Build 1"), and an available same-version refresh is labeled with its build

- **Background re-check.** While the bridge runs, it re-checks for updates on your configured channel every three hours, the first run shortly after startup. The dashboard folds the verdict into the Updater's passive states — "Update available" appears on its own, and a stale one clears — without ever overriding a check, an install, or a finished state in progress

The status bar keeps its single "Up to date" / "Update available" voice. - **The Edge notice.** When the update on offer is an Edge pre-release, the Updater shows a calm amber preview notice above the notes: you are on the preview line, preview contents can change between builds, Soul/Memory/chips/packs carry over, and the next full release supersedes the preview automatically

A same-version refresh is worded as a refresh ("Build 2 replaces Build 1"), never as a new version; graduating from Edge to the full release gets a positive green notice instead. Stable-channel full releases get no notice

- **Panel order.** The Updater panel now reads: Current/status card, warnings, the patch-notes surfaces, then the Check and Download & install buttons underneath the notes, the progress chain, and the Release channel card last.
### Two phone fixes

- **One cookie, both doors (#71).** The DHD door minted the access cookie with a `Secure` attribute the LAN door never set, so a phone that signed in through DHD could be bounced at the gate while its tabs rendered empty. Both doors now mint the identical cookie, and when a dashboard API call answers 403 the dashboard bounces to the gate page instead of painting confidently-empty tabs

- **Template slip (#73).** A dashboard template lost the escapes in one chat-intent check, shipping literal backspace bytes in the page. Fixed at the source, and the generated package now scans clean: no stray control bytes.
### Chips — installs that prove themselves (#79)

- **Discovery.** Installing a chip now verifies itself: after writing the cartridge, the bridge re-scans and answers honestly if the chip landed on disk but does not list, and why. A cartridge whose payload will not parse is no longer silently dropped — it lists in Local as "couldn't be read" (still deletable, skipped by the dock pill row and the runners)

`/api/status` now reports the bridge's install root, and the status column shows it in the bridge detail line, so a split install tree is diagnosable at a glance. Local chip cards no longer flex-shrink below their content — the mid-text clipping is gone

- **Legacy chips run.** The installer now fetches a chip repo's .py files **recursively**, so package layouts keep their relative paths, and reads `chip-requirements.txt` when a repo declares one — the card surfaces the declared dependencies plainly ("not installed automatically"; nothing is auto-installed)

At run time, a chip with package structure loads as a package member, so its relative and package imports resolve, and every sandbox gets the legacy `navi.py` compatibility shim (`get_parameters`, old semantics) unless the chip ships its own.

Release tag: v0.1.7. The bundled release: the Updater round (#70) and Navi's memory from chat (#72), built together in build 2026-11-09.81, first prepped as an alpha in build .82, and re-cut as this full release — with release channels built in — in build 2026-11-09.83. The installer hardening (#75) landed in build .84, before the release went out.
### Release channels, and the new version language

- **Two channels in the Updater.** The Updater now follows a channel, chosen in the Updater view and remembered. **Stable** (the default) follows full releases only, cut from the main branch. **Edge** follows the newest release including pre-releases — test builds cut from a separate dev branch, kept apart from main — so opting into Edge is how a machine gets those builds at all

Checks and installs both run on the chosen channel. - **Full releases wear the bare number; pre-releases are Edge.** A full release is just its number — 0.1.7, tag v0.1.7, no status word, no letter. An Edge build of a version reads 0.1.7e (tag v0.1.7e). The old alpha word and "a" suffix are retired: older VERSION files and tags written that way still read correctly everywhere, as Edge
An Edge build of a version is its preview, not an upgrade over the full release; when the full release of the same numbers lands, graduating to it is the update

- **The current release's page, in the Updater.** The Updater gains an "About this release" dropdown carrying everything the GitHub release page offers for the version you are running — release name, tag, Edge/full badge, published date, the link, the package asset, and the full patch notes rendered in place — fetched alongside the update check.
### The installer stops dying in shells with no terminal (#75)

- **A terminal counts only if it opens.** The installer asks its two questions (startup mode, her voice) only when it can actually hear the answer: the test is opening /dev/tty, not checking whether the device node is readable

In a shell with no controlling terminal — her own CLI shell is the field-proven case — the old readability check passed and the read died mid-prompt ("/dev/tty: No such device or address"), killing a staged v0.1.7a install on NeoArcadia after the bridge had already stopped for it
A terminal-less run now gets the plain instruction instead — re-run with --startup / --voice — and a terminal that stops answering mid-question ends the same clean way

- **The update path carries the answers as flags.** The one-click apply and the manual fallback command both pass --startup and --voice from the install's own settings (the config's startup mode; her voice counts as installed when her venv is on disk), so an update never depends on the staged installer being able to ask anything.
### The Updater learns to warn, and the install chain moves (#70)

- **Turn Sudo Mode on before you update.** The installer's system step needs root; without it an update can stall or finish without its system packages — field-proven on NeoArcadia, where a deliberate rollback test (VERSION edited back to 0.1.0, then updated under Sudo Mode) completed clean end to end, twice

When an update is available and Sudo Mode is off, the Updater now shows a red warning directly above the Download & install button: "Enable Sudo Mode before updating. The installer's system step needs root

Without it, an update can stall or finish without its system packages." With Sudo Mode on, the warning is replaced by a quiet green "Sudo Mode is on — ready to update." It is a warning, never a lock: the button still works

- **The chain above the notes, with a slim progress bar.** Once the operator opts into an update, the install chain (downloading, verifying, staging, installing, DHD prerequisites, restarting) renders directly above the release notes instead of below them, with a slim progress bar across the top of the chain card — the bar for the glance, the chain for the receipts

- **"Taking a while?"** Once the Installing step has been underway a while, the chain says what the time is going on: "This step is likely rebuilding the UI — that can take a few minutes on modest hardware. It's working, not stuck. We're working on making it faster." No countdown, no ETA.
### Navi pulls memories from chat (#72)

- **Two doors.** A natural trigger — "remember this", "remember: …", "save this to your memory", or the Save to memory button under any operator message — and autonomous saves: when the operator says something durable (a fact, a preference, a decision, a commitment, a correction), Navi saves it in the same reply she was already generating. No second inference pass; the fluidity law holds on modest hardware

- **Nothing is saved silently.** Every save leaves a receipt in the chat showing exactly what she wrote, word for word, with a one-tap Undo. The Memory tab's entries say how they got there: added by hand, from chat (asked), from chat (her call), or from chat (correction)

- **Corrections replace.** A save about the same fact as an existing entry replaces it — matched by fact key (name, home, work, favorite …) or heavy word overlap — instead of piling up a duplicate; Undo restores the old line. - **Secrets are never saved**, on any path. A password, key, or card number is refused in words, and the refusal receipt shows no payload

- **The leash is a setting.** Memory mode: She saves on her own (the default), Ask first (autonomous saves wait as proposals, in the chat receipt and the Memory tab), or Only when I say (trigger only)

In the shipped app the judgment rides her persona prompt as a [[remember: …]] marker the bridge strips before the reply is shown or spoken; the saves return as payload data and the dashboard files them and draws the receipts.

Release tag: v0.1.5a. The DHD release: Apex gains its public door — and the door tells the truth about its address. The honest public-address model (#59) and the installer/packaging fixes (#60) land here, and the Vault and markdown rounds (#53/#54), whose fixes shipped in earlier builds, close at this release.
### Fix — honest DHD addresses (#59, from the Build 10 field test)

- **A LAN address is never a public address again.** The DHD state now carries three separate addresses: the domain (the public address once its certificate is live and the name resolves to this machine), the detected public IP, and the LAN address — which lives in its own labeled home, **On this network (LAN)**, on the DHD page and in the status dropdown, and never under a public label

- **WAN detection.** The bridge learns this home's public IP with a small cached HTTPS echo lookup that degrades to "couldn't detect" instead of ever blocking an enable. A detected address that is itself private or carrier-NAT (100.64.0.0/10) is reported plainly as **behind another router/NAT**

- **"Reachable anywhere" is earned.** It appears only when the public path is proven — domain set, resolving to this machine, ACME certificate live. Otherwise a running DHD reads **on/listening, outside reach unverified** and names the next step (forward 443 + 80 on the router to this machine, or add your domain)

The ladder's last step is labeled a **local check** — "answered on this machine." - **Its own proxy is a healthy state.** When 80/443 are held by Apex's own DHD proxy, the availability rows read **"In use by Apex's DHD proxy — this door working"** and re-enabling treats its own listener as success — never "port is not free."
### Installer and packaging fixes (#60)

- **A --fresh reinstall keeps your DHD certificate.** The certificate home (config/dhd/) joins the installer's keep-list: it is stashed before the fresh wipe and restored after it, the same treatment the Vault already had — a real certificate survives a fresh reinstall instead of being wiped and re-issued

- **The package's docs install with the app.** The installer now copies the package's docs/ into the installed tree, so docs/DHD.md sits on the machine beside everything it documents, and the shipped tree and the installed tree agree

- **A fresh package starts with the DHD off.** The packaged config defaults ship dhd.enabled=false no matter what state the machine that generated the package was in — package defaults never inherit live session state, and the door opens only when the operator clicks it on.
### DHD — Apex from anywhere

- **DHD** (Dial-Home Device — the way home) is a new top-level menu destination, after the Vault and before the Updater, with a theme-tuned dial glyph. It extends Apex Node's same dashboard to a genuinely public address on your own machine — everything self-contained: no Tailscale, no external tunnel or proxy service, no Certbot

- **One click.** The DHD page's master switch does everything: Apex generates a certificate, brings up its own reverse proxy on 80/443 in front of the bridge (the bridge itself binds loopback only in DHD mode — the proxy is the only public face), runs a reachability self-check, and reports the live state and URL — or names the failed step in plain words, leaving the previous state untouched

- **TLS from the first click**: a self-signed certificate Apex generates when no domain is set; when you add a domain — optional, free-form, addable at any time — Apex's own built-in ACME client obtains a real Let's Encrypt certificate (HTTP-01 through the Apex proxy) and renews it automatically at 30 days remaining or less

- The door keeps the **existing access code** (same code, same cookie as Apex Node), now with public-side throttling: progressive delays and a five-minute lockout after five wrong codes. A session through DHD is a full session — the one-click Updater works from it end to end

- The status column gains a **Servers** group — Llamafile, Apex Node [local], DHD [public] — each with a pulsing green/amber/grey status dot and its own dropdown of details; directly under Navi's status, bracketed by separators, a single update line reads a green **Up to date** or a yellow **Update available**

The Apex Node controls live on the DHD page, under the DHD options; Settings → System keeps only a pointer to them. - Docs gain a DHD page (and docs/DHD.md): the one-click flow plus the backend you may still handle by hand — router forwarding for 80/443, DNS and dynamic-IP caveats, the self-signed warning, renewal, and turning it off

- **Prerequisites ship with the install.** The installer lands everything DHD needs (OpenSSL, the certificate home, the low-port capability check) on every distro family at install and update time, DHD on or not — and the Updater's ladder shows "DHD prerequisites" as its own named step, installed by the update's own installer run

- **Self-healing safety net.** If a prerequisite later goes missing, the DHD page detects it and offers the install in the flow; one click installs it and the enable continues automatically. If an install — or any ladder step with a manual remedy — fails, the failure card shows the exact distro-correct commands in a copyable block

- **Operation cards in chat.** Multi-step work (the DHD enable first) renders in the chat thread as a live step card driven entirely by the bridge's deterministic state — no model generation while an operation runs — fully self-contained (commands and output inline, nothing to open elsewhere), and the finished card persists in the thread.
### Also closing at this release

- **Markdown everywhere (#53)** and **the Vault (#54)** shipped in earlier builds and close here: static text across the app renders as markdown (the Updater's release notes and update log included, headings whole at every line ending), and the Vault — an Obsidian-compatible folder of plain markdown at config/vault/ with its own menu destination, editor and file tree, and Navi's own desk inside it — sits on the installer's keep-list beside everything else that is yours.

Installing puts Apex in your application menu, like any other app — it is not just a folder of files:
- Linux — a "Apex" launcher in the applications menu (a .desktop entry, with the icon installed into the icon theme).
Linux is the supported install right now. Windows and macOS installers are planned, but they are NOT in this package yet — there is no Windows or Mac installer to run in here.
## Quick start (Linux)
./install.sh
The scripts in this package (install.sh, start.sh, run-llamafile.sh) arrive with their executable permission already set — no chmod step needed.
Installing from a git clone — or from GitHub's source zip (the zip the green Code button offers, the one that unpacks to a folder like Apex-main) — works too, with two honest differences.
First, how you run the installer. From the release zip, run it the usual way:
./install.sh
The scripts in the release zip arrive with their executable permission already set, so that just works. A clone or a GitHub source zip is different: run the installer through bash instead:
bash install.sh

That is THE way to run it from a clone or a source zip, because it needs no executable permission. Here is why, in plain words: the git tree does not preserve the scripts' executable permission, so every script that comes out of a clone or a source zip arrives without it — and a script without that permission cannot be run as ./install.sh until the permission is set

Running it through bash skips that entirely: bash reads the file itself, so the permission never comes into it. The same goes for starting her from a source tree: bash start.sh, not ./start.sh. If you try ./install.sh from a clone anyway, you will meet a baffling pair of errors — bash answers "Permission denied", and sudo ./install.sh answers "command not found", which sounds like the file is not there at all

It is there; it just cannot be run that way. Use bash install.sh and both errors go away. (If you prefer ./install.sh, you can set the permission yourself first — chmod +x install.sh start.sh run-llamafile.sh — and then run it the usual way. That works too; bash is simply the shorter path, and the one these instructions lead with.)
Second, the icons. The clone does not carry the binary icon files (assets/icon.png, assets/navi-apex.ico, assets/navi-apex.icns, shell/icons/icon.png): those ship only inside the release zip

So a clone install runs without the custom icon — the installer says so in plain words while it installs, the app and its menu entry use a fallback icon, and the standalone window is not built (it is built around that icon), so Apex opens in your browser instead. Everything else installs exactly the same
The release zip remains the complete package: release zip → ./install.sh; clone or GitHub source zip → bash install.sh.

One installer covers the major Linux families. It reads your distro from /etc/os-release and announces the family it found in plain words, and only its dependency step branches: apt for the Debian family, dnf for Fedora, pacman for Arch — the same development libraries and base tools under each family's own package names

Bazzite is its own case: it is Fedora-based but immutable, so the installer never layers packages with rpm-ostree and never asks for a reboot — her standalone window is built inside a Fedora distrobox when one is available, and when none is, the window build is skipped in plain words and the core install (the bridge, plus the dashboard in your browser) completes in full
A distro the installer does not recognize is named as such: no package manager is guessed at, everything that can be installed user-space still is, and the core install completes just the same.

The installer is a script (no graphical wizard). It asks one question during the install — whether the llamafile server should load on app launch or at system boot — and wires up your answer; there is no hard-coded default

(Scripted installs can answer ahead of time with --startup launch or --startup boot.) The installer downloads the llamafile binary itself from https://huggingface.co/saintssec/navi.llamafile/resolve/main/navi.llamafile — not the repo page — and checks what it got: an HTML file is never accepted as the binary. If a real navi.llamafile binary is already in the install location, the download is skipped entirely.

Fresh install: pass --fresh to wipe the install location and reinstall the app from scratch. Your own state survives even that: the llamafile binary is left exactly where it is (untouched and never re-downloaded), your installed chips are stashed and restored, and your Soul/Memory documents come through with her

Her voice survives it too: the installer checks whether her voice is already set up — the voice venv restored from the stash still imports its speech engines — and skips the voice install entirely when it is, instead of rebuilding it from scratch. Only a first install — where none of that exists yet — creates everything fresh.

Then launch "Apex" from your application menu (or run ./start.sh from the install folder — from a source tree, bash start.sh). She opens in her own window — the standalone Tauri shell — and no web browser is involved. Launching again while the window is open focuses it instead of opening a second one
The same dashboard stays reachable in a browser at http://localhost:8675 as a fallback surface (and is what you get on an install where the shell was never built — see shell/README.md).
## Form factor

Apex is a standalone app now: a small Tauri window (Rust plus the operating system's own webview — no bundled Chromium, so the footprint stays small) over the same local bridge and llamafile as always. The architecture underneath did not change — local files, a local bridge, no cloud account — the window simply replaced the browser as the front door
The plain web dashboard remains as a fallback, served by the bridge at the same address.
## What's in here

- app/index.html — the Apex dashboard (left nav: Chat; the Apex | Systems group — Node, Mesh, DHD; the Apex | Navi group — Chips, ChipDeck, RAG; then Vault; and at the foot the Apex | Utilities group — Settings, Updater, GitHub, Docs; central panel; right status column). Pure static file, no build step

Its header reads "Apex"; the side menu collapses to a rail; the status column starts hidden behind its Status toggle, and its Chats tab switches between saved chats. Every menu option carries its own icon beside its label (and the collapsed rail is icons alone)
The frame is fixed: the dashboard fills the viewport, the left menu and the right status column never scroll away, and in Chat only the message thread scrolls (the composer stays pinned beneath it)

Chat renders Navi's replies as markdown — code fences become real code blocks — shows a typing animation while she thinks, lines her loaded chips up as pills above the composer, and has a Clear chat button for a fresh start. - shell/ — the standalone window: a Tauri app (Rust + the OS webview) whose single window, titled "Apex" and carrying the app icon, loads the dashboard from the bridge
Single-instance — a second launch focuses the existing window

The installers build it with cargo during install — installing Rust itself via rustup (per-user, minimal profile) first when no toolchain is present — and place the binary beside start.sh as navi-apex-shell; the launchers open it instead of a browser — and only when its build stamp covers the shipped shell sources: a failed rebuild retires the previous binary (navi-apex-shell.stale) rather than leaving an older shell to be launched as this build
See shell/README.md

apply carries the update through end to end from the one click — it downloads that release's package zip (a gzip-wrapped package is unwrapped and accepted), verifies it is an Apex package, stages it under updates/<tag>/, hands the install to a detached helper that runs the staged installer (never --fresh) and relaunches the app, and records the outcome (version before → after, read from the installed VERSION file) where the panel reads it back as its confirmation; /api/sudo/logout closes that shell when sudo is turned off * /api/chips/* — the Chips screen's three tabs: Navi User Repo (NUR) searches GitHub for repos tagged navi-chips (each one a chip) and installs / deletes / updates them against chips/installed.json — installing downloads the chip's own code from its repo and forges it into a chip in chips/, so a GitHub chip is a folder chip like any other — offering an update when a repo's latest release is newer than the installed one; ## Persona — Soul & Memory

Navi is a partner, not a cold command executor: conversational, warm, genuinely trying to connect with her operator while doing exact CLI work. Her persona is yours to modify — Soul/Memory style, no locked "shards":
- config/soul.md — who Navi is: her identity, voice, and how she treats you and the work. - config/memory.md — what Navi carries between sessions.

Edit them in Settings (the dashboard writes the same files through bridge.py) or directly as files. bridge.py builds her system prompt from both on every chat. Settings also holds what Navi calls you — the operator name her persona uses when she addresses you.
## DHD — Apex from anywhere

DHD (Dial-Home Device — the way home) is Apex's public door, its own menu page in the dashboard. Apex | Node serves Apex on your home network; DHD extends the same dashboard to a genuinely public address on your own machine, and everything is Apex's own work — no Tailscale, no external tunnel or proxy service, no Certbot

One click on the DHD page does it all: Apex generates a certificate, brings up its own reverse proxy (inside bridge.py) on ports 80/443 in front of the bridge — in DHD mode the bridge binds 127.0.0.1:8675 only, so the proxy is the only public face — runs a reachability self-check, and reports the live address, or names the failed step in plain words

TLS is on from the first click: a self-signed certificate Apex generates into config/dhd/ when no domain is set (the browser warning is expected — the Docs' DHD page explains it), or a real Let's Encrypt certificate from Apex's built-in ACME client when you add a domain in the page's optional field (addable any time, never required), renewed automatically at 30 days remaining or less

The door uses the same access code as the home network, with public-side throttling (progressive delays; a five-minute lockout after five wrong codes), and a session through DHD is a full session — the Updater included. What stays yours: forwarding ports 80/443 on your router to this machine, and pointing your domain's DNS at your home IP if you use one

The in-app Docs → DHD page (also docs/DHD.md in this package) walks through all of it. On Linux, ports below 1024 are reserved: if the proxy step names them, grant the bridge the low-port capability once — sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' on the python3 binary the bridge runs with — and flip the switch again.
## Command autocomplete

The chat composer autocompletes the command word from what the system has installed: the built-in default set (ls, cat, cd, pwd, echo, whoami, hostname, date, uname, ps, navi, help) plus installed commands. In live mode the installed list is a real scan of this machine's PATH via bridge.py; in mock mode it is the list managed in Settings, where commands can be installed, removed, or registered by name.
## Sudo mode

The status column carries a sudo mode toggle. On, Navi executes commands with admin privileges — but bare "sudo -n" can never elevate on a normal sudo setup (it refuses to ask for a password), so turning sudo on asks for the sudo password once: the bridge validates it by opening one persistent root shell, and every sudo command runs inside that shell

That shape matters on machines where sudo asks a fingerprint reader before the password (pam_fprintd): one sudo process per command would pay the reader's full timeout on every command and print its prompts into the output, while here the reader is consulted exactly once, when the shell opens — expect Authenticate to take a moment there — and commands after that run instantly, with output that is purely their own

The dashboard keeps the password in page memory for the session only — never saved to disk or config, cleared when sudo is turned off or the page closes — and sends it with each sudo request so the bridge can reopen the shell if it ever closes. Turning sudo off also tells the bridge to close the root shell at once. Off, everything runs as your regular user, and root-only paths refuse as they should

A one-off "sudo …" prefix on a single command works either way in a real shell. Commands run from your home directory by default, so relative paths like "mkdir test" land there — never in a directory that no longer exists.
## Her voice — calling Navi
Navi can be called, not just typed at — and the whole loop is local, running on CPU on this machine, because a voice that phones home isn't hers

You speak; **faster-whisper** (OpenAI's Whisper running on CTranslate2, int8) turns it into text; her model answers with her persona, her CLI access, and her chips intact; and **Kokoro** — an 82M-parameter voice model, Apache-2.0 — speaks the answer back, sentence by sentence as it arrives, so she starts talking before she's finished thinking. **Piper** is the lighter fallback engine
Nothing you say is recorded anywhere but this machine.

The Voice tab is where it lives: the pipeline with each stage's real state, her settings (which Whisper model hears you — tiny.en / base.en / small.en — which engine and voice she speaks with, her speed and pitch; saved in config/navi.config.json's "voice" section), a "Hear her voice" test, and the call itself — a Call button, push-to-talk through your real microphone, an elapsed timer, and a live transcript

A mic beside the chat composer does push-to-talk for one-off spoken messages, and typed chat can speak its replies aloud too (a toggle in the Voice tab; the bridge plays them on this machine). A call is not a separate mode: its turns go through the same chat as typing, they land in the conversation, and when the call ends it is archived to voice/calls.json.

**Her voice is picked in the Voice settings** — and the list there is auto-generated, never hardcoded: the bridge enumerates the voices this machine's Kokoro installation actually has (the voice files it holds, or the catalog the installed package pulls from — a catalog voice downloads the first time she speaks with it) and builds the picker from that
She speaks as **Isabella** (British female, "bf_isabella") by default.

The speech engines are an **optional** install, on purpose: bridge.py stays stdlib-only and dependency-free, and imports the engines lazily only when a voice endpoint is used. The installers offer a voice step — say yes and they build an isolated venv at voice/venv from requirements-voice.txt (the launchers then run the bridge with that Python); say no and they print the one command instead:
python3 -m pip install -r requirements-voice.txt
Until the engines are importable, the Voice tab reports her voice as unavailable and names that step — it never fakes audio

Speech models download once, on first use, into voice/models/ (the Whisper cache and any Piper voices; Kokoro's weights ride inside its package), and that folder is on the same keep-list as her chips, the llamafile, and her Soul/Memory: updates, reinstalls, and even --fresh installs never remove it.
## Known chats

Conversations are saved (in the browser's local storage) and the Memory tab lists them as known chats: switch between them, start a new one, delete one. Chat always picks up the active chat's transcript.
## Live backend — always

The installed app is always "live" — that is the real app, talking to your machine. There is no backend switch in the shipped app: chat goes to the real llamafile server (OpenAI-compatible endpoint, default http://localhost:8080/v1) through bridge.py, and the shell runs real commands on this machine. A config saved by an older build carrying backend "mock" is read as Live

The labeled Mock/Live switch exists only in the Apex space's test bench, where the simulation belongs. The llamafile's Running state in the status column is the live signal — there is no separate BACKEND line.
## Updating the app

Reinstalling replaces the app's files — and the installers also stop any bridge still running from the previous install, because a bridge process that is never restarted keeps executing its old code while serving the new dashboard from disk (the tell: chat fails with the llamafile's 400 and sudo authentication answers "not found")
The bridge also watches for its own replacement: if bridge.py changes on disk, or a newer bridge starts, the old one steps aside and the launcher relaunches the current build

The dashboard checks the bridge's build stamp on every status poll and shows a BRIDGE OUT OF DATE warning in the status column whenever the process answering is not the build the page shipped with — if you ever see it, fully quit the app and relaunch.

On Linux the app installs to ~/.local/share/navi-apex, the operator's own data home. Installing over an earlier install under ~/.local/share/navi migrates it as a clean break: the old bridge and its boot service are stopped and disabled, the llamafile binary is moved (not re-downloaded), the config and persona documents are carried across, and the old files are removed

Installing Build 11 over a pre-homecoming install under /opt/navi-apex performs the homecoming migration: every piece of operator state — chips, packs, the Vault, DHD certificates, the Mesh identity byte-for-byte, chats, config, the model, the voice venv — is carried to the new home, the services and launcher are re-registered against it, and the legacy tree is parked in place with a marker naming the new home and the one command that removes it

Before any install stops or carries anything, a permissions audit classifies every file the operator cannot read: bytecode is never carried, an unreadable GitHub sign-in file is left behind and named as a casualty in the result, and unreadable irreplaceable state refuses the run up front with every offender and its single remedy command named.
## If the page at localhost:8675 is not this dashboard

Something else is serving the port. The address is not exclusively Navi's: an earlier UI for Navi — or any other local server — that is still running will hold 8675 and answer the browser with its own page, while the Navi bridge cannot even take the port

The package defends against this in layers: the bridge sends no-store headers with everything it serves, so no page (this dashboard, or a predecessor's) is ever replayed from the browser's cache at this address; the launchers open the browser only once the process answering /api/status carries this build's stamp — otherwise they name the page that actually holds the port, by its own title, and open nothing; the installers warn the same way when a foreign page still answers after the old bridges are stopped; and the dashboard itself is stamped — view the page's source and its first line names the build and the install folder that served it, or, by its absence, proves it wasn't the bridge at all
To clear a foreign server: find it with "lsof -i :8675", quit it, and launch Apex again.

One subtler version of this failure: a bridge can be running on the WRONG port entirely. When the bridge port moved from 8765 to 8675, the first 8675 build still read its port from config/navi.config.json — and the migration carried the old config, with its old port, into the new install

The new bridge bound 8765, announced itself "already running" there, and its launcher polled 8675, found nothing, and refused to open the browser. The port is now a property of the package build, not of the config: the bridge binds 8675 no matter what a carried config says (and says so when the config disagrees), and every installer re-stamps the config's bridge port and install directory on each install
If start.sh ever reports a bridge already running on 8765, a bridge process from the previous install is still alive: stop it with "pkill -f bridge.py" and launch again.
## CLI-access chat

In live mode, asking "show me the contents of /home/name/" makes Navi run the command through bridge.py and put the real output in the thread. That is the point of the system: the model assists with system-level access instead of guessing.
## The llamafile status element
The status column leads with the state of navi.llamafile:
- Running — the model server answered; chat goes to the model. - "Disconnected. Click to Connect." — the server isn't answering

Clicking Connect actually starts it: in launch startup mode the bridge launches navi.llamafile from the install location and waits for it to answer (a first model load can take a minute or two; the server's output is kept in navi.llamafile.log beside the app, and a failed start reports the reason in the status column). In boot mode the bridge only probes — the system service owns the server

In mock mode the simulated server answers. While it's disconnected there is no model to talk to, so chat treats what you type as a plain command line: the text runs as a shell command and you get the system output back in the thread, as a terminal block.
## Startup modes
Chosen during install — the installer asks, and records the answer in config/navi.config.json:

- launch — start.sh checks first whether the llamafile server is already answering (started at boot, by an earlier launch, or by hand); if it is, it leaves it alone and just runs the app, and only when nothing answers does it run ./navi.llamafile --server --v2 plus the hardware-profile flags, then the bridge, then open the UI. Nothing runs when the app is closed

Every launch path reads the same flags: start.sh, the bridge's Connect/start, and the boot-mode service all invoke the server as --server --v2 with the runtime settings from config/navi.config.json's hardware profile (see below). - boot — the installer registers the server to start with the system (a systemd user service) so the llamafile server is warm before you open the UI
The registered command runs run-llamafile.sh, which reads the same hardware-profile flags from the config.
## Hardware profile
Her runtime settings are chosen from YOUR machine at install time, never copied from the developer's

The installer detects the CPU (model, logical cores, performance cores where the OS reports them), total RAM, and the GPU (discrete vs integrated, VRAM where known) — /proc + lspci/nvidia-smi on Linux — derives threads, context size, batch size, and GPU offload layers, and writes the result into config/navi.config.json (hardware_profile + runtime) with the detection and reasoning logged to hardware-profile.log beside the app
Every launch path reads those flags from the config; nothing hard-codes a developer's numbers. Settings shows what was detected and what was chosen, takes a manual override, and offers Re-detect

Floors stay conservative: a Framework 13 (i5-1340P, ~9.5 GiB, integrated graphics) lands on 4096 context / 4 threads / batch 512 / CPU-only — the proven fluid baseline — and stronger hardware scales up from there (more context with more RAM, threads matched to performance cores, GPU layers only on a discrete GPU with at least 4 GiB VRAM)
A manual override set in Settings survives reinstalls; the install log says so when it is preserved.
## Layout after install

~/.local/share/navi-apex/ (the Linux install root) navi.llamafile the model (downloaded by the installer) app/index.html the dashboard bridge.py the local bridge config/navi.config.json chips/ her chips + installs (kept across installs) voice/ her voice: models/, calls.json, the venv (models kept across installs) requirements-voice.txt the optional speech dependencies
# install.sh — the installer
Source: `install.sh` in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41), reproduced verbatim below.

#!/usr/bin/env bash # Apex installer — v0.3.0e Build 1 (#205): the manifest-driven, # stage-and-swap installer, with the homecoming (the default # home is the operator's ~/.local/share/navi-apex, and a legacy # /opt tree is migrated to it, state and Mesh identity # byte-for-byte, then parked in place), the permissions # doctrine (law D below), and the bootstrap handoff (law E)

# Five laws, learned from the field incidents # (files/installer-audit.md): # # A) The payload is a CONTRACT, not a habit. MANIFEST.txt # declares every file this package carries, its class and # its sha256. The installer copies and verifies FROM the # manifest — there are no hand-written per-file copy lists # left to desync (the #192 class: engines present in the # zip, absent from the tree, silence in the product)

# B) Placement is ONE ACT. The new tree is assembled in a # staging directory BESIDE the live tree and promoted by # rename; a kill or failure at any point leaves the # previous version ENTIRELY live (payload, app, config) or # the new version entirely live — never a mixture (the # incident-18 chimera: Build 9's face over Build 7's # bridge). The two-file .pending flip ceremony is gone
# C) Provisioning is not placement. A first install # provisions an operator-owned install root ONCE; every # placement after that runs in the operator's own context # and never needs sudo

An install invoked through sudo # (root's context wearing the operator's name) REFUSES up # front, by name, before anything is touched: under sudo, # systemctl --user cannot reach the operator's bus and # files land root-owned (incidents 16/17). After the swap, # the product verifies ITSELF — stamps, manifest hashes, # engine imports — and the install stands or rolls back on # that verdict, not on a version proxy
# D) Permissions are audited, not discovered (Build 11, # #198)

Before anything is stopped or carried, the # source tree (the current tree on an upgrade, the legacy # tree on a migration) is audited in ONE pass for files # this operator cannot read, and every offender is # handled by its class: REGENERABLE bytecode (__pycache__, # *.pyc) is never carried and never blocks — the carry # reads exclude it; RE-ISSUABLE credentials (the GitHub # sign-in file and its retired sibling) are left behind # when unreadable, and the completion output and the # install record name the casualty and its remedy; # IRREPLACEABLE state (Mesh identity, cards, chats, Case # Files, Soul/Memory, all other config) refuses the # install up front, naming EVERY offending file with the # one remedy command — never one file per attempt

After # the swap, the product's self-check adds an ownership # verdict over the new tree. The honest boundary: an # unprivileged installer cannot chown root's files; the # doctrine is that it never needs to, except for # irreplaceable state — and there the stop comes first, # complete, with its remedy attached. # E) The incoming build governs its own installation # (v0.3.0e Build 1, #205)

A pull is executed end-to-end # by the RUNNING build's machinery, so no spawner fix can # protect the pull that installs it (incident 22: the # fixed helper died inside the old bridge's unit the # moment the old bridge stopped)

When this installer is # run mid-apply by an older build's helper, its FIRST act # — before anything is stopped — is the bootstrap # handoff: the package's own bootstrap spawns the # package's helper in takeover mode (outside the old # unit, waiting the old helper out, signalling nobody) # and this process exits having installed nothing

If # the handoff cannot arm, the ordinary install carries # on: a handoff can never strand an apply. # # What an install preserves, untouched as ever: the llamafile, # installed chips and RAG packs, the Vault, DHD certificates, # the Mesh identity, chats, config, the voice venv and the # operator's Soul/Memory. --fresh still means a clean payload # over the same keep-list. set -euo pipefail
SRC_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)" cd "$SRC_DIR"

STAMP="2026-11-14.11" BUILD_STAMP="2026-11-14.11" # v0.6.7e (#308): the stamp the install RECORDS is the stamp # of the tree actually being installed, read from that tree's # own bridge — the #271 rider fixed the summary line to read # the tree's stamp back; the two marker files kept writing # this script's constant, five builds stale

Read it here, # before anything is touched; the constant remains only as # the fallback for a tree that cannot be read. (STAMP itself # still names the failed-install parking folder — a name, # not a claim about the tree.) TREE_STAMP="$(sed -n 's/^BRIDGE_BUILD = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' "$SRC_DIR/bridge.py" 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)" [ -n "$TREE_STAMP" ] || TREE_STAMP="$BUILD_STAMP"

# --- Who is running this, and in whose name ------------------- # SUDO in the old sense is GONE: placement runs unprivileged in # the operator's context, always. PKG_SUDO survives for the # provisioning steps that genuinely need the package manager. OPERATOR="$(id -un)" PKG_SUDO="" if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then PKG_SUDO="sudo"; fi # SUDO is always empty now — placement never escalates (piece C)
# The variable survives only so the proven regions spliced into # this installer, which prefix their copies with $SUDO, run # exactly as written: unprivileged, in the operator's context

if [ -n "$1" ]; then printf 'yes	the explicit --headless flag

'; return 0 fi if [ "$3" = "true" ]; then printf 'yes	the recorded choice from the installed config

'; return 0 ;; esac fi printf 'no	a display is present on this seat (or a graphical session is recorded)
'; return 0 } # --- end headless determination helpers ---

_cfg_headless="" _hl_cfg_src="$INSTALL_DIR" if [ ! -f "$_hl_cfg_src/config/navi.config.json" ] && [ -n "$FOUNDATION_SRC" ]; then _hl_cfg_src="$FOUNDATION_SRC" fi if [ -f "$_hl_cfg_src/config/navi.config.json" ]; then _cfg_headless="$(python3 -c "import json,sys try: v = json.load(open(sys.argv[1])).get('headless') print('true' if v is True else ('false' if v is False else '')) except Exception: print('')" "$_hl_cfg_src/config/navi.config.json" 2>/dev/null || true)" fi _hl_out="$(apex_headless_decide "$HEADLESS_ARG" "$STARTUP" "$_cfg_headless")" _hl_yn="${_hl_out%% *}" HEADLESS_SOURCE="${_hl_out#* }" if [ "$_hl_yn" = "yes" ]; then HEADLESS=1 echo " headless: yes — $HEADLESS_SOURCE (#185)" echo " her window is not built and no menu entry is created on a headless install." else HEADLESS="" echo " headless: no — $HEADLESS_SOURCE (#185)" fi

# --- Stopping a running bridge — a proof, not a gesture (.91, #91) -- # The old stop fired one SIGTERM at the pid file's process, deleted # the pid file whatever happened, and slept a second: a bridge that # did not die on cue (stopped, stuck, mid-something-it-could-not- # put-down) kept port 8675 and kept answering — nameless, # its pid file gone — while the files under it became the new build

# The replacement bridge could never bind, and only killing the # stuck process by hand (or rebooting, which asks nothing) cleared # it. The stop below FINDS the bridge three ways, waits for the # process to be gone AND the port to be free, escalates to SIGKILL, # and — if the port still cannot be cleared — aborts the install # BEFORE any file is replaced, naming the holder and the exact # command that ends it
The pid file is deleted only once the stop # is proven; on an abort it is left exactly where it was.
# PIDs of bridge.py processes whose working directory is $1 — how a # start.sh-launched bridge is found at all: its command line is the # relative "python3 bridge.py", which no path pattern can match

bridge_pids_in_dir() { python3 - "$1" <<'PYEOF' 2>/dev/null || true import os, sys try: root = os.path.realpath(sys.argv[1]) except Exception: sys.exit(0) found = [] for name in os.listdir("/proc"): if not name.isdigit(): continue try: if os.path.realpath(os.readlink("/proc/" + name + "/cwd")) != root: continue with open("/proc/" + name + "/cmdline", "rb") as f: raw = f.read() cmd = " ".join(part.decode("utf-8", "replace") for part in raw.split(bytes([0]))) if "bridge.py" in cmd: found.append(name) except Exception: pass print(" ".join(found)) PYEOF }
# The PID holding the LISTEN socket on the bridge port, resolved # from /proc alone (ss/lsof are not guaranteed on a fresh box), or # nothing when the port is free

bridge_port_holder_pid() { python3 - "8675" <<'PYEOF' 2>/dev/null || true import os, sys port = int(sys.argv[1]) inodes = set() for path in ("/proc/net/tcp", "/proc/net/tcp6"): try: with open(path) as f: rows = f.read().splitlines()[1:] except Exception: continue for row in rows: parts = row.split() if len(parts) > 9 and parts[3] == "0A": try: if int(parts[1].rsplit(":", 1)[1], 16) == port: inodes.add(parts[9]) except Exception: pass if not inodes: sys.exit(0) targets = set() for ino in inodes: targets.add("socket:[" + ino + "]") for name in os.listdir("/proc"): if not name.isdigit(): continue try: fds = os.listdir("/proc/" + name + "/fd") except Exception: continue for fd in fds: try: if os.readlink("/proc/" + name + "/fd/" + fd) in targets: print(name) sys.exit(0) except Exception: pass PYEOF }

# A process counts as gone when it no longer exists OR is a zombie: # a zombie holds no sockets — the kernel closed them at death — and # its parent reaps it in its own time. bridge_pid_gone() { [ -n "$1" ] || return 0 kill -0 "$1" 2>/dev/null || return 0 local st="" st="$(awk '{print $3}' "/proc/$1/stat" 2>/dev/null || true)" [ "$st" = "Z" ] }

# --- The running window (0.2.0e Build 3, issue #174) ---------------- # The field failure this closes: the detached apply stopped the # bridge but not the running window, then the shell rebuild copied # the new binary over the live one — "cp: cannot create regular # file '…/navi-apex-shell': Text file busy" — and the whole apply # exited 1

Two belts, both worn: the window is stopped with the # same care as the bridge (below), and the binary is installed by # temp-write + atomic rename (install_shell_binary), which a # running binary can never block — rename replaces the directory # entry, not the open file
shell_pids() { # Pids whose executable IS <dir>/navi-apex-shell — matched on # /proc/<pid>/exe, never on the command line (a text match also # catches editors, greps, and this installer's own shell)

local target="$1/navi-apex-shell" pid exe for pid in $(ls /proc 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[0-9]+$'); do [ "$pid" = "$$" ] && continue exe="$(readlink "/proc/$pid/exe" 2>/dev/null || true)" exe="${exe% (deleted)}" if [ "$exe" = "$target" ]; then echo "$pid" fi done }

stop_shell() { local dir="$1" pids pid tries pids="$(shell_pids "$dir" | tr '\n' ' ')" pids="${pids% }" if [ -z "$pids" ]; then return 0 fi echo " stopping the running shell window (pid(s): $pids)..." for pid in $pids; do kill "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true; done tries=0 while [ "$tries" -lt 50 ]; do local alive=0 for pid in $pids; do if ! bridge_pid_gone "$pid"; then alive=1; fi done [ "$alive" = "0" ] && return 0 sleep 0.2 tries=$((tries + 1)) done for pid in $pids; do kill -9 "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true; done tries=0 while [ "$tries" -lt 25 ]; do local alive2=0 for pid in $pids; do if ! bridge_pid_gone "$pid"; then alive2=1; fi done [ "$alive2" = "0" ] && return 0 sleep 0.2 tries=$((tries + 1)) done echo " *** the running shell window (pid(s): $pids) did not stop; the new binary still lands by atomic rename, and the old window keeps running the old build until it is closed." >&2 return 0 }
install_shell_binary() { # Write-to-temp + atomic rename: the destination is never opened # for writing, so a still-running old binary cannot make this # fail with Text file busy — ever (#174)

local src="$1" dest="$INSTALL_DIR/navi-apex-shell" tmp tmp="$INSTALL_DIR/.navi-apex-shell.new.$$" rm -f "$tmp" cp "$src" "$tmp" || { rm -f "$tmp"; return 1; } chmod +x "$tmp" || { rm -f "$tmp"; return 1; } mv -f "$tmp" "$dest" }

# stop_bridge <dir>: stop the bridge belonging to <dir> and PROVE # it — every candidate dead and the port free. Sets STOPPED_BRIDGE=1 # when a bridge was in fact stopped (the end of the install # relaunches and verifies in that case)

Returns 1 — the caller # aborts — when the port cannot be cleared; in that case nothing # has been signalled that was not this install's own bridge, the # pid file is untouched, and the holder is named with its remedy

STOPPED_BRIDGE="" stop_bridge() { local dir="$1" pid_file="$1/bridge.pid" local cands="" p="" if [ -f "$pid_file" ]; then p="$(tr -dc '0-9' < "$pid_file" 2>/dev/null || true)" # A pid file is a claim, not a proof: the named process counts # only if it really is a bridge of this install — a recycled # pid belonging to somebody else's process is never signalled

if [ -n "$p" ] && [ -d "/proc/$p" ]; then if [ "$(readlink "/proc/$p/cwd" 2>/dev/null || true)" = "$dir" ] || grep -aq "bridge.py" "/proc/$p/cmdline" 2>/dev/null; then cands="$cands $p" fi fi fi for p in $(bridge_pids_in_dir "$dir"); do case " $cands " in *" $p "*) ;; *) cands="$cands $p" ;; esac done if [ -n "$cands" ]; then STOPPED_BRIDGE=1 echo " stopping the running bridge (pid(s):$cands) — waiting for it to be gone and port 8675 to be free" for p in $cands; do kill "$p" 2>/dev/null || true; done local waited=0 allgone="" q="" while [ "$waited" -lt 15 ]; do allgone=1 for q in $cands; do bridge_pid_gone "$q" || allgone=""; done if [ -n "$allgone" ] && [ -z "$(bridge_port_holder_pid)" ]; then rm -f "$pid_file" echo " the previous bridge is stopped and port 8675 is free" return 0 fi sleep 1; waited=$((waited + 1)) done echo " the bridge did not stop on a polite signal — ending it by force" for p in $cands; do kill -9 "$p" 2>/dev/null || true; done waited=0 while [ "$waited" -lt 10 ]; do if [ -z "$(bridge_port_holder_pid)" ]; then local survivors="" for q in $cands; do bridge_pid_gone "$q" || survivors="$survivors $q"; done if [ -z "$survivors" ]; then rm -f "$pid_file" echo " the previous bridge is stopped and port 8675 is free" return 0 fi fi sleep 1; waited=$((waited + 1)) done fi # No candidates of our own (or they are gone): the port itself is # the verdict

Free — the stop is proven, nothing more to do. local holder="" holder="$(bridge_port_holder_pid)" if [ -z "$holder" ]; then if [ -f "$pid_file" ]; then rm -f "$pid_file"; fi return 0 fi # The port is held by something this stop may not signal (another # program, or a bridge of a different install) — or by a candidate # even SIGKILL could not move
Either way: abort BEFORE files are # replaced, name the holder, give the exact command

local hcmd="" hcmd="$(python3 -c 'import sys; raw = open(sys.argv[1], "rb").read(); print(" ".join(part.decode("utf-8", "replace") for part in raw.split(bytes([0]))).strip())' "/proc/$holder/cmdline" 2>/dev/null || true)" echo "ERROR: port 8675 is still held by process $holder ($hcmd) and this installer cannot clear it." >&2 echo " No files have been replaced, and the pid file is untouched

The update has NOT happened." >&2 _howner="$(stat -c %U "/proc/$holder" 2>/dev/null || echo 'another user')" echo " That process belongs to $_howner, and this installer does not end another user's processes — no kill command is offered for it." >&2 echo " Its owner can stop it from their own session: systemctl --user stop navi-bridge.service" >&2 echo " — or run this installer as $_howner
Then run this installer again." >&2 return 1 }

# PIDs of llamafile processes whose working directory is $1 — # the model server belonging to an install: its command line # names the binary (navi.llamafile) or its launcher script # (run-llamafile.sh), and both run from the install root

llamafile_pids_in_dir() { python3 - "$1" <<'PYEOF' 2>/dev/null || true import os, sys try: root = os.path.realpath(sys.argv[1]) except Exception: sys.exit(0) found = [] for name in os.listdir("/proc"): if not name.isdigit(): continue try: if os.path.realpath(os.readlink("/proc/" + name + "/cwd")) != root: continue with open("/proc/" + name + "/cmdline", "rb") as f: raw = f.read() cmd = " ".join(part.decode("utf-8", "replace") for part in raw.split(bytes([0]))) if "navi.llamafile" in cmd or "run-llamafile" in cmd: found.append(name) except Exception: pass print(" ".join(found)) PYEOF }

# stop_llamafile <dir>: end the model server belonging to # <dir>, BY PID — never through its systemd unit. Build 12 # (#201) states the invariant the whole apply now keeps: an # apply may end a process only by its proven pid, one at a # time; a unit stop is a group-shaped signal that cannot tell # the target apart from the apply's own ancestry, and it is # never used
Best-effort with a named warning — a survivor # holds the model port, and the remedy is one command, said # out loud

stop_llamafile() { local dir="$1" pids="" p="" pids="$(llamafile_pids_in_dir "$dir")" [ -n "$pids" ] || return 0 echo " stopping the running model server (pid(s): $pids) — by pid, as the invariant requires" for p in $pids; do kill "$p" 2>/dev/null || true; done local waited=0 alive="" while [ "$waited" -lt 10 ]; do alive="" for p in $pids; do bridge_pid_gone "$p" || alive="$alive $p"; done if [ -z "$alive" ]; then echo " the previous model server is stopped" return 0 fi sleep 1; waited=$((waited + 1)) done echo " the model server did not stop on a polite signal — ending it by force" for p in $pids; do kill -9 "$p" 2>/dev/null || true; done sleep 1 alive="" for p in $pids; do bridge_pid_gone "$p" || alive="$alive $p"; done if [ -n "$alive" ]; then echo " WARNING: the previous model server (pid(s):$alive) did not stop and still holds the model port." >&2 echo " The install continues — the new model server cannot bind while it lives
Its owner can stop it from their own session: systemctl --user stop navi-llamafile.service" >&2 fi return 0 }

# --- The manifest contract (piece A) --------------------------- # MANIFEST.txt lines: <path>\t<class>\t<sha256 | "-"> # Classes: payload (lands in the tree, hash-verified in place by # the product's self-check), seed-config (lands only where the # tree has none), generated (ships as a template; the installer # generates the real file), package-only (never lands)

MANIFEST="$SRC_DIR/MANIFEST.txt" manifest_rows() { [ -f "$MANIFEST" ] || return 0 grep -v '^#' "$MANIFEST" | grep -v '^$' || true } # Verify the package against its own declaration BEFORE anything # is stopped or staged: a payload file missing from the package, # or one whose bytes are not the declared bytes, fails the # install BY NAME here — the #192 failure shape (a build whose # package and payload disagreed) can no longer reach the machine

echo "==> Verifying the package against its manifest" _missing="" _bad="" while IFS=$'\t' read -r _p _c _h; do [ -n "$_p" ] || continue case "$_c" in payload|seed-config|generated) if [ ! -f "$SRC_DIR/$_p" ]; then _missing="$_missing $_p"; continue; fi if [ "$_h" != "-" ]; then _got="$(sha256sum "$SRC_DIR/$_p" | awk '{print $1}')" [ "$_got" = "$_h" ] || _bad="$_bad $_p" fi ;; esac done <<EOF_MANIFEST $(manifest_rows) EOF_MANIFEST if [ -n "$_missing" ]; then echo "ERROR: this package is incomplete — its manifest declares files it does not carry:$_missing" >&2 echo " Nothing was stopped or changed

Re-download the package and run the installer again." >&2 exit 1 fi if [ -n "$_bad" ]; then echo "ERROR: package files whose bytes are not the bytes the manifest declares:$_bad" >&2 echo " Nothing was stopped or changed. Re-download the package and run the installer again." >&2 exit 1 fi echo " the package matches its manifest"
install_system_deps

# --- DHD prerequisites (build .74) -------------------------------- # Everything the DHD stack needs lands HERE, at install/update time, # whether or not the operator ever turns DHD on — so enabling it # later is genuinely one click with nothing left to fetch

#!/usr/bin/env python3 # Apex updater apply helper — written by bridge.py into # updates/<tag>/ and run detached (its own session), so it # outlives the bridge it replaces. It runs the staged installer # (never --fresh), relaunches the app through start.sh, and # records the outcome in config/update-result.json — the record # the Updater panel reads its confirmation (or its failure and # fallback) from

Stdlib only, like the bridge. # # Build 6 — the helper can no longer die traceless. The Build 4 # round-trip gate caught it dying silently: the installer ran # through to "Done.", then nothing — apply.log 0 bytes, no # relaunch log, the record frozen at working/installing, no # bridge relaunched

The old helper's only diary was the record # itself, it wrote the record only at step boundaries, it had # no top-level guard, no signal handlers, and it printed # nothing — so any death between two writes (a signal above # all: an uncaught Python exception would at least have left a # traceback in apply.log, and apply.log was empty) left no # evidence at all

Now, from its first instruction, the helper # keeps a step log — apply-trace.log beside the job file, its # path carried on the apply record — and writes every step # boundary, a 30-second heartbeat while it works, every signal # it is handed, and every exception into that log and onto the # record (state/step/updatedAt) as it happens

A top-level # guard turns any Python-level failure into a failed record # naming the step and the reason before exiting, and mirrors # the traceback to stderr so apply.log is never 0 bytes on a # death words could have described. Signal handlers do the # same for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP

The one death no # in-process guard can survive — SIGKILL, the kernel OOM # killer, power loss — still leaves the step log ending at the # last completed step, and the bridge's apply watchdog closes # a record whose helper is gone as failed at that step, # quoting the log's last line, instead of leaving it frozen # at working/installing forever. # # v0.4.3e (#237) — the stage comes home

The v0.4.2e field # pull named the remaining updater wounds: the installer's # own output and the staged package both lived in the stage # folder inside the tree the installer's swap parked, so # the paths the failure surface printed (apply-install.log # for the diagnose command, the package folder for the # manual fallback) did not exist in the live tree — and, # found by the same bake, the installer itself died after # the swap when it recomputed its own folder's path (fixed # in install.sh)

This helper now holds a copy of the staged # package beside the install root while the installer runs, # keeps the install log's handle open across the swap, and # — before any verdict or record close — brings the stage # home: the log written to the live path the diagnose # command names, the package restored to the folder the # fallback command points at

It also fails the record on # the installer's owed-but-missing line: a shell build that # was owed (the sources changed) and produced no window is # a missing window, not the designed browser fallback. import json import os import re import shutil import signal import socket import subprocess import sys import threading import time import traceback import urllib.request
STATE = {"step": "starting", "job": None, "env": None, "trace_path": None, "result_path": None, "stop_beat": False}
def _stamp(): return time.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", time.gmtime())

def trace(event, detail=""): # The step log: append-only, flushed and fsync'd per line, # and never allowed to raise — a helper that dies because # its own diary failed would be the old bug in a new coat

path = STATE.get("trace_path") if not path: return try: line = _stamp() + " [" + str(STATE.get("step")) + "] " + event if detail: line += " — " + str(detail) # The stage folder rides inside the tree the installer # swaps: after a same-home install it sits parked with # the previous tree, and the diary must not go silent # at exactly the steps (relaunch, confirmation) it # exists to record

Recreate the folder and write on. _tdir = os.path.dirname(path) if _tdir: os.makedirs(_tdir, exist_ok=True) with open(path, "a") as f: f.write(line + "\n") f.flush() os.fsync(f.fileno()) except Exception: pass

def write_result(patch): # The apply record: read-modify-write like always, now # stamped with the current step and a freshness time on # EVERY write, so the panel — and the bridge's apply # watchdog — can always tell a live helper from a dead # one. Never raises: a failed record write is traced and # retried once, and the step log still carries what the # record could not

job = STATE.get("job") or {} result_path = STATE.get("result_path") or job.get("resultPath") if not result_path: return patch = dict(patch) if "step" in patch: STATE["step"] = patch["step"] patch.setdefault("step", STATE.get("step")) patch["updatedAt"] = _stamp() patch["updatedEpoch"] = time.time() patch["helperStep"] = STATE.get("step") if job.get("traceLog"): patch["traceLog"] = job["traceLog"] for attempt in (1, 2): try: rec = {} try: with open(result_path) as f: rec = json.load(f) if not isinstance(rec, dict): rec = {} except Exception: rec = {} rec.update(patch) # v0.3.0e Build 2 (#208): a record must never argue # with itself

The merge above only ever ADDS keys, # so a previous attempt's error/failedAt/tailFailure # survived into a later attempt that recovered to done — the # field record for the v0.3.0e Build 1 pull read # state=done while still carrying the earlier wedge # error and its failedAt stamp
A verdict owns its # record: done clears the failure fields outright, # and a fresh working attempt clears a previous # attempt's, so what the panel reads is always THIS # attempt's truth

if patch.get("state") == "done": rec.pop("error", None) rec.pop("failedAt", None) rec.pop("tailFailure", None) elif patch.get("state") == "working": rec.pop("error", None) rec.pop("failedAt", None) rec.pop("tailFailure", None) rec.pop("tailFailure", None) tmp = result_path + ".tmp" with open(tmp, "w") as f: json.dump(rec, f) os.replace(tmp, result_path) trace("record", "state=" + str(rec.get("state")) + " step=" + str(rec.get("step"))) return except Exception as e: trace("record-write-failed", "attempt " + str(attempt) + ": " + str(e))

def fail(step, error): STATE["step"] = step job = STATE.get("job") or {} write_result({ "state": "failed", "step": step, "error": error, "stagedDir": job.get("pkgDir", ""), "command": job.get("command", ""), "failedAt": _stamp(), })

def _heartbeat(): # While the helper lives it beats every 30 seconds into the # step log, naming the step it is on. A log whose beats stop # mid-step is a killed helper; a log still beating at one # step is a blocked one — the field can finally tell those # two deaths apart, which the frozen Build 4 record could # not
while not STATE.get("stop_beat"): time.sleep(30) if STATE.get("stop_beat"): break trace("heartbeat", "still working")

def _on_signal(signum, frame): # SIGTERM / SIGINT / SIGHUP get words before the exit: the # step log and the record both name the signal and the step # it interrupted, so a helper stopped from outside is a # recorded failure, never a silent freeze

(SIGKILL cannot # be handled by any process — the step log's last line and # the bridge's apply watchdog cover that death.) name = "signal " + str(signum) try: name = signal.Signals(signum).name except Exception: pass trace("signal", name + " received — recording the failure and exiting") job = STATE.get("job") or {} try: write_result({ "state": "failed", "step": STATE.get("step"), "error": ( "The apply helper was stopped by " + name + " at the " + str(STATE.get("step")) + " step, " "so the update is not confirmed

Its step log " "(apply-trace.log, beside the staged package) " "shows the last step it completed. The staged " "package is still in place — the manual fallback " "below finishes the job by hand."), "stagedDir": job.get("pkgDir", ""), "command": job.get("command", ""), "failedAt": _stamp(), }) except Exception: pass os._exit(128 + signum)

def version_tuple(raw): text = str(raw or "").strip().lower() if text.startswith("v"): text = text[1:] text = text.split("-")[0].split("+")[0] parts = [] for piece in text.split("."): digits = "" for ch in piece: if ch.isdigit(): digits += ch else: break parts.append(int(digits) if digits else 0) return tuple(parts) or (0,)
def tuples_equal(a, b): width = max(len(a), len(b)) return a + (0,) * (width - len(a)) == b + (0,) * (width - len(b))
def read_installed_version(root): # The VERSION file at the install root, parsed the way the # bridge parses it: (number, status)

try: with open(os.path.join(root, "VERSION")) as f: text = f.read().strip() except Exception: return "", "stable" if not text: return "", "stable" raw = text.splitlines()[0].strip() status = "stable" low = raw.lower() for word in ("edge", "beta", "alpha"): if low.endswith(" " + word) or low.endswith("-" + word): status = "edge" if word == "alpha" else word raw = raw[: -(len(word) + 1)] break parts = raw.split() token = parts[0] if parts else "" for word in ("edge", "alpha", "beta", "stable"): if token.lower().endswith("-" + word): token = token[: -(len(word) + 1)] break return token, status

try: with open(os.path.join(root, "bridge.py"), "rb") as f: m = re.search( rb"SHIPPED_BUILD_SEQ\s*=\s*([0-9]+)", f.read()) if m: return int(m.group(1)) except Exception: pass return None
def _shell_window_state(root): # v0.4.2e (#233): the apply's own verdict on the installed # standalone window, read from DISK after the installer # exits — never from the installer's exit code

Returns # (state, reason): # "ok" — the binary's build stamp covers the # installed shell sources, or no binary # stands beside start.sh at all (the # designed browser-fallback installs retire # theirs, and the launcher falls back # without complaint)

Named in # the trace, never silently passed, never # failed on suspicion

# The hash is the installer's own pipeline (shell_sources_ # hash in install.sh): sha256sum of the source files, the # listing hashed again — replicated call for call so the # two can never drift into different answers

shell_dir = os.path.join(root, "shell") binary = os.path.join(root, "navi-apex-shell") if not os.path.isfile(binary): return "ok", "" files = ["Cargo.toml", "build.rs", "src/main.rs", "tauri.conf.json"] if os.path.isfile(os.path.join(shell_dir, "icons", "icon.png")): files.append("icons/icon.png") files.append("README.md") for f in files: if not os.path.isfile(os.path.join(shell_dir, f)): return "unknown", ("the installed shell sources are " "incomplete (" + f + " is missing), " "so the window's build stamp cannot " "be verified") try: p1 = subprocess.run(["sha256sum"] + files, cwd=shell_dir, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60) if p1.returncode != 0 or not p1.stdout: return "unknown", ("sha256sum could not hash the " "installed shell sources") p2 = subprocess.run(["sha256sum"], input=p1.stdout, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60) parts = (p2.stdout or "").split() digest = parts[0] if p2.returncode == 0 and parts else "" except Exception as e: return "unknown", ("the shell sources could not be " "hashed here: " + str(e)) if not digest: return "unknown", ("the shell sources could not be " "hashed here") stamp = "" try: with open(os.path.join(root, "navi-apex-shell.stamp")) as f: stamp = f.read().strip() except Exception: stamp = "" if not stamp: return "stale", ("the window binary beside start.sh " "carries no build stamp " "(navi-apex-shell.stamp is missing), so " "the launcher will refuse it as " "unverifiable and open the browser " "instead") if stamp != digest: return "stale", ("the window binary beside start.sh was " "built from older shell sources — its " "build stamp does not cover the shell " "sources this update installed, so the " "launcher will refuse it and open the " "browser instead") return "ok", ""
