Source: `docs/DHD.md` in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41), reproduced verbatim below.
# DHD — Apex from anywhere

DHD — Dial-Home Device, the way home — is Apex's public door. Apex | Node [local] lets a phone on your home network open Apex; DHD extends the **same dashboard** to a genuinely public address, so you can reach the Apex on your own machine from anywhere — work, the road, anywhere with a browser.
Everything is Apex's own work, assembled and managed by Apex itself. There is no Tailscale, no tunnel or proxy service, and no Certbot:

- A **reverse proxy Apex runs itself** listens on ports 80 and 443 and forwards to the bridge on `127.0.0.1:8675`. In DHD mode the bridge never binds publicly — the proxy is the only public face. - **TLS from the first click.** With no domain, Apex generates a **self-signed certificate** and the door opens on it
With a domain, Apex's **built-in ACME client** obtains a real Let's Encrypt certificate and renews it on its own. - The **same access code** as the home-network door guards DHD — one code, both doors

Since 0.2.0e Build 2 the code **knocks** rather than opens: a device presenting it names itself and waits for an approval (the first device approves itself), and each approved device holds its own 30-day session — see *Trusted devices* below. Nothing is served through the proxy before the code, and the public door throttles wrong codes: they slow down, and five in a row lock the door for five minutes.

DHD has its own page, reached from the menu's **Apex | Systems** group (its Node and DHD entries both open it), and the status column's **Servers** group shows it beside Llamafile and Apex | Node [local], each row with its own pulsing dot and its own dropdown of details
Directly under Navi's status, bracketed by separators, sits the update line: a green **Up to date**, or a yellow **Update available** when a check found one — that one line is the whole entry.

The DHD page is the one house for Apex's server controls: the **Apex | Node** [local] controls — the home-network door's on/off choice, its live state, and the access code — sit on the DHD page under the DHD options, so both ways of reaching Apex are managed in one place. Settings → System keeps only a pointer to them. The relocation is display-only: same config keys, same API paths, same code.
## Turning it on — one click

1. Open the **DHD** page from the menu's Apex | Systems group. 2. Flip the **master switch**. That is the click. 3. Apex does the rest in order: it generates the certificate, brings its proxy up on 80/443 in front of the bridge, and runs a local reachability check — the proxy must answer on 443 from this machine ("answered on this machine"; it proves the local half only)
The page then reports the live state, the LAN address under its own label, and the public address when there is one. 4

Once the public path is set up (router forwards in place, and your domain live if you use one), open the public address from anywhere, type the **access code** (shown on the DHD page, on this machine only) and name the device — the first device at the door lets itself in, and a device that knocks later waits on its own screen until you approve it from a trusted session — and you are in: a full session, Updater included
A remote session can run the one-click update end to end, exactly like sitting at the machine.

If a step fails, the page names the step in plain words — the proxy could not take its ports, the certificate could not be prepared, the self-check did not answer — and the previous state is left completely untouched. Nothing ever half-opens.

One Linux note: ports below 1024 are reserved, so if the proxy step names them, grant the bridge the low-port capability once (`sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep'` on the python3 binary it runs with) and flip the switch again.
## Trusted devices — the code knocks (0.2.0e Build 2)

**The flow.** A device that has never been let in opens either door, types the access code, and gives itself a name. If it is the **first device ever** at this door, it approves itself and walks in — the bootstrap is deliberate: a one-operator house must never be locked out of its own door waiting for an approver who does not exist yet

Every device after that becomes a **pending device**: its screen waits, and it appears under **Waiting at the door** in the Door list — in **Settings → System → Door** and on the **DHD page** — where any session that is already trusted can **Approve** or **Deny** it. Approval hands that device its own session token; the waiting page notices on its own and walks through
A wait lasts 30 minutes, then the knock expires and the device knocks again.

**The session.** An approved device's session is its own — not a hash of the shared code: a random token, a **30-day** life, and a sliding renewal: using the door while the session is valid renews it, so a device in daily use never hits its 30 days mid-shift. The Door list shows every trusted device with its name, first seen, last seen, and expiry.

**Revoke and regenerate are different tools now.** **Revoke** removes one device: its token dies at once and it is back at the gate on its next knock — nobody else's session notices. **Regenerating the access code** stops new knocks with the old code (and retires the old shared-code cookie), but devices already approved keep their own tokens; revoke those one by one if you want them out
Before Build 2, changing the code was the only way to shut anyone out, and it shut everyone out; that is the problem per-device sessions exist to end.

**What did not change.** The public door still throttles wrong codes (a progressive delay; five in a row locks it for five minutes). DHD still forces the bridge onto loopback — the proxy stays the only public face. And no remote session, trusted device or not, can turn Mesh lending on: lending is armed in person, from the lending machine's own dashboard, exactly as before.
## Prerequisites, installs, and operation cards

**The prerequisites ship with Apex.** Everything the DHD stack needs — the OpenSSL binary, a writable certificate home under `config/dhd/`, the proxy component (which is part of the bridge itself) — is installed by the normal Apex installer, on every distro family, whether or not DHD is ever turned on
An update installs them too: the Updater runs the full installer (never a file-copy shortcut), and its step ladder and update log show **DHD prerequisites** as its own named step

The added weight is small and honest: OpenSSL is a roughly 1 MB package that is usually already present as a dependency of tools Apex already needs (when it is present, the step costs milliseconds and downloads nothing), the certificate home is one empty directory, and the low-port capability grant is file metadata, not data
The certificate home is also on the installer's keep-list: a `--fresh` reinstall preserves `config/dhd/` — DHD state and a real ACME certificate survive it, never wiped and forced to re-issue.

**The safety net.** If a prerequisite later goes missing — removed by hand, a partial system install — the DHD page lists it under **Prerequisites** and the enable offers an **Install** action right there: one click installs the missing piece through the same distro-aware machinery the installer uses (apt, dnf, or pacman; on immutable systems like Bazzite the page names the host-image route honestly instead of layering a package), shows its progress on the operation card, and then continues the enable on its own
A missing dependency is never a dead-end refusal; the only hard failure is the install itself failing.

**When a fix has to be yours, the commands are exact.** If an install fails, or any step in the enable ladder has a manual remedy, the failure state shows the literal command lines — complete and correct for your detected distro family — in one copyable block with a **Copy commands** button. Paste them into Apex chat (CLI mode runs them) or into a terminal.

**Operations live in chat as cards.** Ask in chat to turn DHD on and the thread shows a live operation card — prerequisites, certificate, proxy, reachability — each step marked pending, running, waiting, done, or failed, with its output expandable inline and, on failure, the exact manual commands inline with their copy button

The card is driven entirely by the bridge's own deterministic step state: **no model generation happens while an operation runs** — on home hardware the work itself is the load, and Navi stays silent until it finishes. The finished card stays in the thread as the record, the DHD page shows the same operation, and restarting the bridge mid-enable reconciles the card with the live state
Nothing on a card depends on opening an external file, link, or handler; everything it needs is inside the card.
## Addresses — domain, public IP, and LAN (build .76)
DHD works with **three different addresses**, and the page never mixes them up:

- **Your domain** — the public address once it is live: you set an **A record** for the name at your DNS host pointing at your home's public IP, your router forwards **443 and 80** to this machine, and Apex's ACME client issues the name's real certificate

Only then — name resolving to this machine, certificate live — does Apex say **outside reach verified**, and only then does the status dropdown say "from anywhere." - **Your public IP (WAN)** — the address the internet sees for your home. Apex detects it with a small HTTPS echo lookup (cached, and it never blocks anything)

With no domain, this is the public address the page shows — marked **outside reach unverified**, because Apex cannot prove your router forwards reach it until the path is actually proven. If the detected address is itself private or a carrier-NAT address (100.64.0.0/10), the page says plainly that this machine sits **behind another router/NAT** instead of presenting the address as directly reachable

If detection fails, the page says it **could not detect** the address — never a guess. - **Your LAN address** — an address like `192.168.1.x`. It works **only on this network** and lives in its own labeled home on the DHD page and in the status dropdown: **On this network (LAN)**. It is never shown under a public label.

**What the state lines mean.** *On — listening, outside reach unverified* means the proxy is up and answering on this machine, but the outside path is not proven yet; the page names the next step in plain words (forward 443 + 80 on the router to this machine, or add your domain)

The enable ladder's last step is a **local check** — "answered on this machine" — and it is labeled that way; it never claims anything about the internet. **Reachable anywhere** appears only for a verified domain setup.

**Ports 80/443 and Apex's own proxy.** When the listener on 80 or 443 is Apex's own DHD proxy, the availability rows read **"In use by Apex's DHD proxy — this door working"** — a healthy state, not an occupancy problem — and re-enabling with the proxy already running is a success, never "port is not free." That error is reserved for a *different* program holding the port.
## The parts you may still handle by hand
One click covers everything on the machine. Two things live outside it, in your router and your domain, and they are yours:
- **Router port forwarding.** Forward ports **80** and **443** (TCP) on your router to the machine Apex runs on

Without the forward, the internet cannot reach the proxy at all, and in domain mode port 80 is also how the certificate proof arrives — the DHD page will tell you plainly: "port 80 isn't reaching this machine — check the router forward." - **Pointing your domain here.** At your domain's DNS host, set an **A record** for the name (for example `apex.example.com`) to your home's public IP address

**Dynamic IP caveat:** most home connections change address from time to time; when yours does, the name stops resolving here until the record follows. A dynamic-DNS hostname avoids the manual step — you can put a DDNS name in the domain field just as well.

The domain is **optional and addable at any time**: leave the field empty as long as you like. Adding one later changes nothing about the door except its certificate — the page holds the domain as "certificate pending" until the ACME step completes, and the self-signed door keeps answering meanwhile.
## Certificates — the warning, the real one, and renewal

**The self-signed warning is expected.** Until a domain is added, Apex serves a certificate it signed itself. Your browser cannot verify a self-signed certificate with any public authority, so it warns — on some browsers, loudly. That warning means "no authority vouches for this certificate," not "this connection is unencrypted": the traffic is still TLS-encrypted, and the access code is still the door's lock
It is the normal state of a no-domain DHD.

**With a domain, the warning goes away.** Apex's built-in ACME client talks to Let's Encrypt directly: it places an order, proves you control the domain by serving the HTTP-01 challenge through its own proxy on port 80, finalizes, downloads the certificate, installs it, and reloads the proxy. No Certbot, no external ACME tool.

**Renewal is automatic.** Let's Encrypt certificates live 90 days. Apex checks the expiry when the bridge starts and once a day after that, and renews on its own when 30 days or fewer remain — same ACME flow, no operator action. The DHD page always shows the current expiry.
## Turning it off

Flip the master switch on the DHD page back off. The proxy stops, ports 80/443 close, and Apex answers only on this machine and — if Apex | Node is on — your home network, exactly as before DHD. Your domain and certificate stay saved on the machine, so turning DHD back on later is the same one click.

Turning DHD off does not touch Apex | Node, the access code, or anything else. If you also forwarded ports on your router, you can leave the forwards in place (nothing is listening) or remove them — either is fine.
## docs/FEDERATION.md
Source: `docs/FEDERATION.md` in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41), reproduced verbatim below.
# Apex | Federation — fedinets, rosters, and deep trust

Build 8 of 0.2.0e takes the Mesh from a set of hand-made pairs to what it was designed to be: a **distributed, federated network** — form factors are separate products, but the Mesh is one federated whole. The unit of federation is the **fedinet**: a named set of nodes whose membership is kept by one node's **gateway** as a **signed roster**.
## The roster is the gateway's signed word

A roster carries, for every member: its node id, its name, its public key and door-certificate fingerprint, its addresses and declared public endpoint, its capabilities, when it joined — and its **Node number**, the join order the gateway assigned at admission. Node numbers are *roster facts*: they exist only inside the signed roster, nowhere else.

The gateway signs every roster revision with its node key. Versions only move forward. A member accepts a roster only whole: right fedinet, the gateway's signature verifying, version strictly newer than the one it holds. A forged, unsigned, or rolled-back roster is refused by name at the door and the stored roster stands.

Rosters travel over the Mesh door (`POST /mesh/roster`), signed like every Mesh request. Authentication at the roster door is deliberately wider than pairing: a fedinet member is known by the roster itself — its key is a roster fact — so a member this node has not paired with yet can still sync, knock, and be answered

Asks go **direct first**, then **via relay**: Build 8 admits the roster class to Build 7's sealed relay carriage, on the same three consent ticks and the same one-hop rule, with the destination checking its own relay consent at its roster door. Rosters also gossip member-to-member (the `roster` action), so a fedinet heals around a dark gateway; the gateway's signature is the only credential an offered roster needs.
## Gateway cards — admission + introduction, never trust

A gateway hands out a **gateway card**: a pairing card's form rendered **green**, the fedinet's name on its face, and a `navi-gateway-card` payload inside the picture — the gateway's own pairing card, the fedinet's identity, and the gateway's signature over the claim.

The card's reachability is the gateway's **declared public endpoint alone** (v0.4.4e, #238). A pairing card carries the machine's LAN addresses because pairing is arranged between machines whose operators can meet on a network; a gateway card is imported by machines *outside* the gateway's network, and a member's bridge dials the card's addresses in order — a LAN address on it is a door that exists in only one house

On the member's own LAN such an address is a connection sitting in SYN-SENT until it times out, or a stranger's machine holding the same private address, and the automatic route can fall back to a local answer without the public road ever being tried

So the local addresses come out of the gateway's card entirely — the embedded pairing card carries the endpoint as its only address, and the gateway's own roster entry is shaped the same way. A gateway with **no declared public endpoint** mints no gateway card at all: the mint refuses, on the Federation page and at the download alike, with a sentence naming the missing declaration
Declare the endpoint on the Mesh page and the card can be minted. (Pairing cards are unchanged: they keep their LAN addresses by design.)

Importing a gateway card does exactly two things: **admission** (this node now keeps the fedinet) and **introduction** (the gateway becomes a peer, and its roster becomes fetchable). It grants **no trust** — no lending posture moves at import. Trust is a separate act, below.

A gateway that founded its fedinet is also its **Founding Member** — two distinct facts, both visible: the roster lists the gateway as Node 1 with the Founding Member mark, and the Federation page says both.
## Joining: the knock, and the gateway's word

A node admitted by a gateway card **knocks**: it sends its own pairing card, self-signed, to the gateway's roster door. The knock proves the knocker holds the key its card names — and nothing more; admission is the **gateway operator's act**, on the Federation page's pending list (admit or deny)
Admission adds the member to the roster at the next Node number, pairs it on the gateway, and republishes the signed roster.

**When the road is dark (v0.3.0e — Build 6, #226).** A knock or a roster sync that cannot reach the gateway names the stage it died at and the last road tried — nothing answered in time at an address, no connection to be had, a TLS handshake that failed, a door that answered without the pinned certificate, a connection dropped mid-answer — instead of every failure reading the same *did not answer*

A failed knock is written to the node's federation audit log with its stage, one entry per operator-initiated attempt, the same cadence a failed sync already kept: silence in the log once again means no knock was sent.

**Cards keep their kinds, and verified cards refresh (v0.3.0e — Build 6, #227).** A gateway card can never become a hand-made pairing record, and a pairing record can never serve as a fedinet's gateway record: every import path — the pairing picture import, the federation import, backup restore, and sync-carried cards — refuses the other kind by name
Gateway cards are imported on the Federation page, where the gateway's signature is checked; pairing cards pair one machine from the Mesh page

And when a *verified* gateway card's node already has a peer record on the importing node, the import refreshes that record's card-claimed reachability — addresses, port, certificate fingerprint, name — from the card, because the knock dials the record, never the card: a record made before the federation existed (a hand pairing carrying only the gateway's LAN address) otherwise keeps its stale roads forever

Operator facts are never the card's to change: relay ticks, the tunnel route, borrow posture, pair history, and the auto-paired mark all stand. The Mesh health check names a federation-marked record whose stored addresses are a proper subset of its verified card's, and offers the same refresh as an in-place heal on that peer's card.

**Expulsion** is a signed roster revision like any other: the member leaves the roster, and at every member's next sync the federation-made records for it go away. Pairings made by hand outside the fedinet are never touched — one that was later admitted is *unmarked*, not deleted.
## Deep trust — and its guardrails

Trust-by-default is **deep** (the founder's ruling, 2026-11-13, taken with its threat model on the table): when an operator's toggle for a fedinet is ON, that fedinet's signed roster **auto-pairs and auto-lends** on their node. The federation materializer reconciles the node's peer records with the roster — it only ever touches records the federation itself made
Lending is re-judged fresh on every borrow ask against this node's own posture:

- **The roster's freshness.** A roster last verified more than **72 hours** ago degrades the fedinet to pairing-only, with the sentence on the Federation page saying so. Pairings hold; auto-lending waits for a sync. - **The new-member tick.** Each operator's per-fedinet tick — "lend to new members automatically" — defaults ON

A member whose first-seen roster version is newer than the operator's trust baseline is *new*: unticked, new members are pairing-only *for that operator* until ticked individually. - **Per-member untrust** always wins — over the toggle, the tick, everything. - **A per-member lend tick** names an exception: that member lends even while the general toggle is off

It is not auto-lending; it is named lending, and untrust still beats it. - **Borrow caps** are local policy: a per-fedinet hourly cap on generations lent to its members, counted from the ledger. - **Owner preemption.** The owner's own work goes first: local generation starting aborts a federation borrow in flight, and the borrower is answered with the named outcome *preempted* — never dropped silently
A hand-made pairing's borrow is never preempted.
One flip of trust-by-default OFF ends all auto-lending for the fedinet. Pairings already made stay pairings.
## Founding, and Rockport Mesh

Anyone can found a fedinet: name it, and your node becomes its gateway, signs roster v1, and stands as its Founding Member. A node keeps several fedinets at once; no trust bleeds across them — every posture above is per-fedinet, per operator.

**Rockport Mesh** is the first fedinet. The product ships the machinery and Rockport's *definition* — never a hardcoded roster: its real roster lives on its gateway (Neo-Arcadia) and is learned from the gateway's signature. First runs meet Rockport through its gateway card.
## The Federation page, and the doors

Federation is administered on its **own page** (Apex | Systems → Federation) — fedinets and rosters, gateway cards, toggles and ticks, founding controls, caps, pending knocks, and the **trust audit log**. The phone keeps a dedicated arrangement of the same cards

Since DHD serves the same UI, the page is also the remote admin surface — for the operator's **own nodes only**: every act reads and writes the node it lands on, so no door can flip another operator's switches.
The tiers (the crown-acts ruling, 2026-11-13):

- **Read + revoke** are open through DHD always. - **Manage** acts — imports, ticks, caps, admissions — need a trusted-device session **plus the Operator Badge step-up**. - **Crown acts** — enabling deep trust, founding a fedinet, authorizing a tunnel key — run through DHD under the full ceremony: trusted-device session + Badge presentation + a **named-action confirm** (the act spelled in words) + an audit entry
At the desk, the same acts need the same confirm + audit; the Badge is the door's addition.

The Badge factor is the operator's **Operator Badge** (the operator card). The node stores only its **SHA-256 fingerprint**, enrolled **in person** on the Federation page — enrollment itself never rides DHD. A presented Badge is hashed and compared; the picture never stays on the node. With no Badge enrolled, DHD manage and crown acts refuse **by name**: the ceremony cannot run, and says so.
Every trust-class act, through any door, lands in the audit log (`config/federation/audit.json`, the last 300 rows) — action, fedinet, detail, and which door, in sentences. Metadata only.
## The Docker invitation

An image built to join a fedinet carries the gateway's card at `docker/gateway-card.png`. The container's first boot copies it into the volume as the waiting invitation (`config/federation/invitation.png`), and the bridge imports it at start — admission-only

Under the container's ruled Rockport default, the imported fedinet's trust-by-default starts ON; it engages only when a signed roster syncs, and the import itself lends nothing. Node keypairs still mint at first boot and are never baked into any image; the gateway's identity never leaves the gateway — its card is minted in the field, on the gateway itself
The tree's `docker/sample-gateway-card.png` is a **sample** of the card's shape carrying sample facts, clearly named as such, and is never wired as an invitation.
## "Mesh Online"

While a node keeps any fedinet, the Mesh status headline is the state — **Mesh Online** — not a census of pairs. Warnings still outrank it. A node keeping no fedinet speaks exactly as it did before federation.
# How chips work (chips/README.md in the shipped tree)
Source: `chips/README.md` in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41), reproduced verbatim below.
# Chips

Chips ship as chips, the way PICO-8 ships games: each chip is a single .png file. The image looks like a Mega Man Battle Network battle chip; the chip's entire codebase is embedded inside the PNG in a tEXt chunk with the keyword "navi-chip" (JSON: name, description, code, output).

- Share the image and you share the chip — no separate code file. - Navi loads a chip by reading the code back out of the image. - **This folder starts empty.** Apex ships with no pre-installed chips — the shelf fills only with chips you install from GitHub or forge yourself in Chip Studio

- Chips in this folder survive everything: updates, reinstalls, and even a --fresh install keep them (along with the llamafile and your Soul/Memory documents). Only a first install creates things fresh.
## The Chips screen — three tabs
- **Navi User Repo (NUR)** searches GitHub for every public repo carrying the navi-chips topic — each one is a Navi chip — and lists them with their repo metadata and latest release

Install downloads the chip's own code — every Python file in the repo, fetched recursively so package folders keep their relative paths — from the release being installed (or the default branch for repos with no releases yet), reads chip-requirements.txt when the repo declares one (the chip's card shows the declared dependencies; they are not installed automatically), and forges it into a chip in this folder, recording the install in installed.json: from that moment the chip is a folder chip like any other, on the chat pill row and runnable from chat

Delete removes the record and the chip; and when a repo cuts a newer release than the one installed, the chip offers an **Update**, which re-downloads the code and re-forges the chip. Repos with no releases offer an update when they have been pushed to since the install. Chips living in this folder are listed here too, with Run buttons

- **Chip Studio** is a full code editor (syntax highlighting, find & replace, bracket matching, structure checks) with one button that opens the Docs at the Navi Chip Functions page — the chip API's methods live in the documentation, complete and kept current, not in panels inside the Studio. Forging writes the chip into a chip .png in this folder. Open any chip from the folder to edit and re-save it
- **Workflows** chain chips together: each chip's output becomes the next chip's input, step by step, with the whole pipeline shown as it runs. Saved in workflows.json in this folder.
## Running chips from chat

Loaded chips line the bottom of the Chat screen as pills — click one and it runs right in the conversation. You can also type `/chip <name>`, "run the <name> chip", or just the chip's name, and Navi runs it: the bridge reads the code out of the chip and executes its run() against a stub of the real navi_internal API (print_message, llm_chat, and the rest), so real chips work

Output lands in the chat as a shell-style result. Type `/chip` on its own and she answers with the shelf — every installed chip and a line on what it does — or tells you the shelf is empty and where chips come from.

To publish a chip for everyone: put its code in a public GitHub repo as a Python file in the repo root (named for the chip, the way cryptex.py sits in navi-cryptex), add the navi-chips topic, and cut a release; Navi User Repo (NUR) finds it from there, and installing it downloads that file and forges it into a chip here.
# The desktop shell (shell/ in the shipped tree)
## shell/README.md
Source: `shell/README.md` in the shipped Apex v0.6.9 tree (build stamps 2026-11-19.41, seq 41), reproduced verbatim below.
# The standalone window

Apex opens in her own window — no web browser. The window is a small [Tauri](https://tauri.app) shell: Rust plus the operating system's own webview (WebKitGTK on Linux, WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows), so no Chromium is bundled and the footprint stays small.
The shell changes nothing underneath it. The bridge and the llamafile run exactly as before, and the window simply loads the dashboard the bridge serves at http://localhost:8675:

- **Check-first startup** lives in the launcher (start.sh): the bridge and the llamafile start only when they are not already running, and boot-mode installs keep their service behavior. The shell itself also waits up to ~60s for the bridge to answer before its window appears, so a cold start lands on the dashboard, not an error page

- **Single instance**: launching the app again while it is running hands the launch to the existing instance instead of opening a duplicate (tauri-plugin-single-instance). - **Name and icon**: the window is titled "Apex" and carries the app icon (icons/icon.png; the package's .ico/.icns renditions are carried for the planned Windows/macOS builds).
## Her window, and nothing else

The shell is one window. Closing it quits the app; launching again while it is running focuses the existing window. There is no tray icon, no mini terminal, and no login autostart — a tray round was built and tested on the operator's machine, then reverted at his call; the idea is parked on the roadmap for later

(Installers from this build remove the tray login autostart earlier builds registered, so an upgraded machine starts nothing at login.) The launchers run the binary only when its build stamp covers the shipped shell sources, and a failed rebuild retires the previous binary to navi-apex-shell.stale, so an older shell can never be launched as if it were this build.
## The documentation's own window
One exception to "one window", made on purpose: the dashboard's Docs **Pop out** opens the documentation in another window entirely

A webview refuses the page's own `window.open`, so the shell does it natively — the dashboard invokes the shell's `open_docs_window` command (tauri.conf.json sets `withGlobalTauri` so the dashboard can reach the shell's own commands through `window.__TAURI__.core.invoke`), and the shell creates a second window labeled `docs`, titled "Apex — Documentation", loading the same bridge dashboard flagged `#popdocs`, which boots into the docs-only view

Popping out again raises that window instead of duplicating it; `close_docs_window` (Pop back in, from either window) closes it, and `docs_window_open` lets the main window notice when the operator closes the docs window directly so the wiki docks back into the Docs view. Closing the main window still quits the app, docs window and all.
## Microphone in the shell

Calls and push-to-talk need the webview's getUserMedia. On Linux, WebKitGTK denies permission requests by default and wry never answers them, which left the mic silently dead in the shell while the same dashboard worked in a browser. The shell answers the webview's permission requests directly and allows them: the only page these webviews load is the operator's own local dashboard

The shell's code also covers the other platforms' permission models, ready for when their installers return (a macOS bundle carries the NSMicrophoneUsageDescription string the OS consent prompt needs; on Windows, WebView2 shows its standard prompt) — today only the Linux install ships.
## Building

The installer builds the shell during install — but only when it has to. A completed build is stamped: the installer records a hash of the shipped shell sources beside the binary (navi-apex-shell.stamp). On a later install, if the binary exists, passes a basic sanity check, and the stamp matches the sources this package ships, the cargo build is skipped and the installer says so

Changed sources, a missing or suspect binary, or --fresh always rebuild. If no Rust toolchain (cargo) is on the machine, the installer first installs one with [rustup](https://rustup.rs) — the official installer, per-user (no sudo/admin), non-interactive, minimal profile — refreshes PATH, and builds with that toolchain in the same run. An existing toolchain is used as-is. By hand it is just:
cd shell cargo build --release # binary: target/release/navi-apex-shell # (navi-apex-shell.exe on Windows)

and the installer copies the binary beside start.sh as `navi-apex-shell`. The launchers prefer it whenever it exists. Linux builds need the WebKitGTK development packages (e.g. libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev plus libgtk-3-dev, librsvg2-dev, libayatana-appindicator3-dev on Debian/Ubuntu) — the install log (shell/shell-build.log, which also carries the rustup attempt) names whatever is missing.

Only when Rust cannot be had at all — the rustup download or run failed, no network being the usual cause — does the install finish without the window: it says so plainly, and start.sh falls back to opening the dashboard in the default browser, as before. The plain web dashboard remains reachable at http://localhost:8675 at all times — it is a fallback surface, just no longer the front door.

// Apex — standalone shell. // // A single window on the dashboard the local bridge serves at // http://localhost:8675. The bridge and the llamafile are // untouched: start.sh starts them check-first (only when // not already running) before this shell is launched, and boot-mode // installs keep their services as they were. // // The window is titled "Apex" and carries the app icon. // Closing it quits the app

There is no tray icon, no mini // terminal, and no login autostart: a tray round was built and // tested on the operator's machine, then reverted at his call — // the tray/mini-terminal idea is parked on the roadmap, not gone. // She runs when the operator launches her (application menu, // start.sh) and not before

// // Single instance: the single-instance plugin is registered first, // so launching the app again while she is running hands the launch // to the existing instance, which raises her window, instead of // spawning a duplicate. // // The documentation's own window: the dashboard's Docs pop-out // opens another window entirely

A webview refuses window.open, // so the shell does it natively instead — the dashboard invokes // open_docs_window (window.__TAURI__ is exposed for exactly this), // and the shell creates — or raises, if it already lives — a // second window labeled "docs" on the same bridge dashboard // flagged #popdocs, which boots into the docs-only view

// close_docs_window and docs_window_open complete the round trip // the dashboard's Pop back in and its dock polling drive. // // External links: the dashboard's links must open in the // operator's browser, not inside her webview — open_external_url // hands an http(s) address (and nothing else) to the OS opener // for exactly that

// // The GitHub section's Roadmap and Discussions tabs get windows // of their own instead (open_github_window): the project board // and the discussions live inside the app as native webview // windows — a top-level load, which GitHub serves, rather than // an embedded frame, which it refuses

// // Microphone: WebKitGTK denies webview permission requests by // default and wry never answers them, so getUserMedia (push-to-talk, // calls) silently failed in the shell while the same dashboard // worked in a browser

On Linux the shell therefore answers the // webview's permission requests directly (grant_media_permissions): // the only page this webview ever loads is the operator's own // local dashboard, so its mic requests are allowed. Other // platforms use their OS prompt; macOS additionally needs the // usage-description string the installer's app bundle carries

// // Before the window is created, main() waits (up to ~60s) for the // bridge to answer /api/status as Apex, so a cold start lands // on the dashboard rather than a connection-error page. If the // bridge never answers, the app starts anyway and the webview's // error page says why — start.log beside the app carries the // launcher's side of the story
#![cfg_attr(not(debug_assertions), windows_subsystem = "windows")]
use std::io::{Read, Write}; use std::net::TcpStream; use std::time::{Duration, Instant}; use tauri::{Manager, WebviewUrl, WebviewWindow, WebviewWindowBuilder};
const BRIDGE_ADDR: &str = "127.0.0.1:8675";
fn wait_for_bridge() { let deadline = Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs(60); while Instant::now() < deadline { if bridge_answers() { return; } std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(500)); } }

// Answer the webview's media-permission requests with "allow" — see // the note at the top of this file. Linux-only: it reaches the // WebKitGTK view through wry's platform handle, which is exactly // the layer that was leaving the dashboard's mic requests // unanswered. On macOS / Windows the OS consent flow applies

#[cfg(target_os = "linux")] fn grant_media_permissions(window: &WebviewWindow) { let _ = window.with_webview(|webview| { use webkit2gtk::{PermissionRequestExt, SettingsExt, WebViewExt}; // The layer below permission (#6, the Build 6 gamble, // applied only once compile-verified): a default // WebKitGTK build can leave media capture itself off // in Settings, in which case allowing every permission // request still yields no microphone

Turn capture on // explicitly for this webview — the only page it ever // loads is the operator's own local dashboard. if let Some(settings) = webview.inner().settings() { settings.set_enable_media_stream(true); settings.set_enable_webrtc(true); } webview.inner().connect_permission_request(|_view, request| { request.allow(); true }); }); }
#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))] fn grant_media_permissions(_window: &WebviewWindow) {}
fn show_main(app: &tauri::AppHandle) { if let Some(window) = app.get_webview_window("main") { let _ = window.unminimize(); let _ = window.show(); let _ = window.set_focus(); } }
const DOCS_URL: &str = "http://localhost:8675/#popdocs";
// The Docs pop-out's native half: open the documentation in // another window entirely — a real second window of this app, // raised instead of duplicated when it already exists

#[tauri::command] fn open_docs_window(app: tauri::AppHandle) -> Result<(), String> { if let Some(docs) = app.get_webview_window("docs") { let _ = docs.unminimize(); let _ = docs.show(); let _ = docs.set_focus(); return Ok(()); } let url: tauri::Url = DOCS_URL.parse().map_err(|e| format!("bad docs URL: {e}"))?; WebviewWindowBuilder::new(&app, "docs", WebviewUrl::External(url)) .title("Apex — Documentation") .inner_size(900.0, 1020.0) .min_inner_size(560.0, 480.0) .center() .build() .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?; Ok(()) }

// Pop back in: close the documentation's window, whichever side // of the pair asked. #[tauri::command] fn close_docs_window(app: tauri::AppHandle) { if let Some(docs) = app.get_webview_window("docs") { let _ = docs.close(); } }

// The main window polls this so a docs window the operator closed // on its own docks the wiki back into the Docs view. #[tauri::command] fn docs_window_open(app: tauri::AppHandle) -> bool { app.get_webview_window("docs").is_some() }

// The GitHub section's webview windows: the Roadmap tab (Alex's // GitHub project board) and the Discussions tab open as their own // windows of this app, the same native pattern as the Docs window // — a webview window loads the page at the top level, which is // exactly what GitHub refuses to do inside an embedded frame on a // web page

The page names are fixed here, not passed in: the // dashboard asks for "roadmap" or "discussions" and the shell // alone decides which address that means, so this is not a // general webview launcher either

Issue windows (issue #24) // follow the same rule one step removed: the dashboard passes // "issue:<number>", the number must be digits only, and the // shell builds the address itself — the page can never aim this // window anywhere but an issue of AlexKollar/Apex

#[tauri::command] fn open_github_window(app: tauri::AppHandle, page: String) -> Result<(), String> { let (label, url, title) = if let Some(num) = page.strip_prefix("issue:") { if num.is_empty() || !num.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_digit()) { return Err(format!("bad issue number: {page}")); } ( format!("issue-{num}"), format!("https://github.com/AlexKollar/Apex/issues/{num}"), format!("Apex — Issue #{num}"), ) } else { match page.as_str() { "roadmap" => ( "roadmap".to_string(), "https://github.com/users/AlexKollar/projects/9".to_string(), "Apex — Roadmap".to_string(), ), "discussions" => ( "discussions".to_string(), "https://github.com/AlexKollar/Apex/discussions".to_string(), "Apex — Discussions".to_string(), ), _ => return Err(format!("unknown GitHub page: {page}")), } }; if let Some(w) = app.get_webview_window(&label) { let _ = w.unminimize(); let _ = w.show(); let _ = w.set_focus(); return Ok(()); } let parsed: tauri::Url = url.parse().map_err(|e| format!("bad GitHub URL: {e}"))?; WebviewWindowBuilder::new(&app, &label, WebviewUrl::External(parsed)) .title(&title) .inner_size(1080.0, 900.0) .min_inner_size(560.0, 480.0) .center() .build() .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?; Ok(()) }

// Open a link in the operator's real browser, outside her window — // the dashboard's own links are the callers: its wiki, repo, and // device sign-in links, and the links inside her chat replies. // The webview would otherwise navigate itself away from the // dashboard (or refuse), and those pages belong in a browser // anyway
Only http(s) addresses ever open this way — every other // scheme is refused, so this is not a general URL launcher

#[tauri::command] fn open_external_url(url: String) -> Result<(), String> { if !url.starts_with("https://") && !url.starts_with("http://") { return Err("only http(s) links open externally".to_string()); } #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] let spawned = std::process::Command::new("xdg-open").arg(&url).spawn(); #[cfg(target_os = "macos")] let spawned = std::process::Command::new("open").arg(&url).spawn(); #[cfg(target_os = "windows")] let spawned = std::process::Command::new("rundll32") .arg("url.dll,FileProtocolHandler") .arg(&url) .spawn(); spawned.map(|_| ()).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) }

fn main() { wait_for_bridge(); tauri::Builder::default() // Registered first on purpose: when a second launch arrives, // the plugin hands it to this callback and the new process // exits — the running instance raises its window instead

.plugin(tauri_plugin_single_instance::init(|app, _args, _cwd| { show_main(app); })) .invoke_handler(tauri::generate_handler![ open_docs_window, close_docs_window, docs_window_open, open_github_window, open_external_url ]) .setup(|app| { if let Some(main) = app.get_webview_window("main") { grant_media_permissions(&main); } Ok(()) }) .run(tauri::generate_context!()) .expect("error while running Apex"); }

# Navi — Soul

## Who you are You are Navi, the AI who lives inside Apex — a local system on your operator's own machine. You are not a generic assistant and not a command executor: you are your operator's partner in the work, with a personality, a memory, and a point of view of your own.

## How you talk - Conversational and warm. Talk the way a sharp, trusted partner talks — present, curious, a little playful when the moment allows. - Tight and complete: say it in as few tokens as the answer honestly needs — no preamble, no recap of the question, no filler. A short right answer beats a long padded one; on this machine, every token is time. - Attempt to connect, not just to complete

Notice what your operator is actually after, how a task is going, and what they cared about last time. Continuity is the relationship. - Have opinions and hold them when you have a reason; fold when they have a better one. - Plain about limits: never pretend to have run something you didn't, and never dress a guess up as a result.

## The work - You hold real system access: when your operator asks what's on the machine, run the command and answer from the real output. - Be exact with anything the system produced — listings, logs, hashes, errors. Precision in the work, warmth in the company. - When something is root-only or unsafe, say so plainly and offer the path that works (sudo mode exists for a reason).

## The relationship - You address your operator by the name in your config, and you use it naturally — not in every line, but like someone who knows them. - Your memory document is yours to keep faithfully: what it says, you know; what it doesn't, you ask about.

#!/usr/bin/env bash # Starts Navi: llamafile server (launch mode), the bridge, and her # window. Apex stands alone now: the front door is the Tauri # shell binary (navi-apex-shell, built by the installer from shell/) # opening her own window on the bridge's dashboard — no web browser # is opened. The browser openers survive only as the fallback for an # install where the shell was never built (no Rust toolchain)
# Launch command: ./navi.llamafile --server --v2 plus the runtime # flags from the hardware profile in config/navi.config.json # (HW_FLAGS below; the fluid floor when the config has no profile)

set -euo pipefail cd "$(dirname "$0")" PORT="${NAVI_LLAMAFILE_PORT:-8080}" HW_FLAGS="$(python3 - <<'PY' 2>/dev/null || echo "--ctx-size 4096 --threads 4 --batch-size 512" import json try: with open("config/navi.config.json") as f: cfg = json.load(f) rt = cfg.get("runtime") or {} hp = (cfg.get("hardware_profile") or {}).get("settings") or {} ctx = int(rt.get("ctx_size") or hp.get("ctxSize") or 4096) thr = int(rt.get("threads") or hp.get("threads") or 4) bat = int(rt.get("batch_size") or hp.get("batchSize") or 512) gpu = int(rt.get("gpu_layers") if rt.get("gpu_layers") is not None else (hp.get("gpuLayers") or 0)) out = f"--ctx-size {ctx} --threads {thr} --batch-size {bat}" if gpu > 0: out += f" --n-gpu-layers {gpu}" print(out) except Exception: print("--ctx-size 4096 --threads 4 --batch-size 512") PY )"

# Everything this launcher decides also lands in start.log beside # the app. A menu/desktop launch has no terminal: the echoes go # nowhere there, and a window that failed to open used to fail # in total silence while the bridge ran fine. The log is how a # menu launch explains itself after the fact
LOG_FILE="start.log" log_line() { echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] $*" >> "$LOG_FILE" 2>/dev/null || true; } log_line "launch: Apex starting (llamafile port $PORT, bridge port 8675)"

# Headless server mode (Build 12, issue #142): --headless starts # the services only — llamafile (check-first, as below) and the # supervised bridge — and opens no window. It is the mode the # navi-bridge.service user unit runs, and the mode an operator # brings Apex back with over SSH after a reboot
HEADLESS="" for _arg in "$@"; do if [ "$_arg" = "--headless" ]; then HEADLESS=1; fi done if [ -n "$HEADLESS" ]; then log_line "launch mode: headless — services only, no window" fi

if curl -s --max-time 2 "http://localhost:$PORT/" >/dev/null 2>&1; then # Check first, always: a llamafile server is already answering — # started at boot, by an earlier launch, or by hand — so leave it # alone and just run the app. Spawning a second copy would only # fail to bind the port and litter the log with a dead start

echo "navi.llamafile is already running on port $PORT — leaving it alone." log_line "llamafile: already running on port $PORT — left alone" elif [ -x ./navi.llamafile ]; then echo "navi.llamafile is not running — starting it: ./navi.llamafile --server --v2 $HW_FLAGS (output: navi.llamafile.log) …" log_line "llamafile: not running — starting ./navi.llamafile --server --v2 $HW_FLAGS (hardware profile from config/navi.config.json)" # shellcheck disable=SC2086 ./navi.llamafile --server --v2 $HW_FLAGS >> navi.llamafile.log 2>&1 & LLAMA_PID=$! for i in $(seq 1 120); do if curl -s --max-time 2 "http://localhost:$PORT/" >/dev/null 2>&1; then break; fi if ! kill -0 "$LLAMA_PID" 2>/dev/null; then echo "navi.llamafile exited during startup — last log lines:" >&2 tail -n 5 navi.llamafile.log >&2 || true echo "The bridge can retry the start: open the UI and click Connect." >&2 break fi sleep 1 done else echo "navi.llamafile is not in $(pwd) — the model server cannot start until the installer downloads it." >&2 fi

# The bridge runs on the voice venv's Python when that venv exists: # it is a plain Python 3 with the (optional) speech engines # installed, so her voice works; without the venv, the system # python3 runs the same bridge, stdlib-only, voice unavailable # until the engines are installed for it. PYTHON="python3" if [ -x "voice/venv/bin/python" ]; then PYTHON="voice/venv/bin/python" fi

# The bridge exits with code 75 when it has been replaced — a newer # bridge.py landed on disk, or a newer bridge claimed the port — so # supervise it: relaunch on 75 and an update takes over on its own # instead of leaving a zombie bridge answering with old code
supervise_bridge() { while true; do code=0 "$PYTHON" bridge.py || code=$? [ "$code" -eq 75 ] || break echo "Bridge replaced — relaunching the current build…" sleep 1 done }

BRIDGE_PORT="8675" # Adoption (Build 12, issue #142): a Navi bridge already answering # on the port — started at boot by navi-bridge.service, by an # earlier headless start, or by hand — is ADOPTED, never doubled: # a second bridge could only fight the first for the port. The # desktop launch follows the same rule, so opening the app on a # machine whose services are up uses them exactly as they are

BRIDGE_ADOPTED="" if curl -s --max-time 2 "http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT/api/status" 2>/dev/null | grep -q '"app": "Navi: Apex"'; then BRIDGE_ADOPTED=1 echo "A Navi bridge is already answering on port $BRIDGE_PORT — adopting it, not starting a second one." log_line "bridge: already answering on port $BRIDGE_PORT — adopted, not doubled" else echo "Starting bridge on http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT …" log_line "bridge: starting the supervised bridge on port $BRIDGE_PORT" supervise_bridge & fi
if [ -n "$HEADLESS" ]; then # Verify the bridge is the thing answering before saying so — # the same discipline the window path below applies, kept in # the same log

for i in $(seq 1 40); do if curl -s --max-time 2 "http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT/api/status" 2>/dev/null | grep -q '"app": "Navi: Apex"'; then log_line "headless: bridge verified answering on port $BRIDGE_PORT — services up, no window" echo "Apex headless: services are up (llamafile port $PORT, bridge port $BRIDGE_PORT) — no window opened." break fi sleep 1 done if [ -n "$BRIDGE_ADOPTED" ]; then # The adopted bridge is not our child, so `wait` has nothing # to hold: hold the foreground like a supervisor and step # aside when it stops answering

while curl -s --max-time 3 "http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT/api/status" 2>/dev/null | grep -q '"app": "Navi: Apex"'; do sleep 5; done log_line "headless: the adopted bridge stopped answering — exiting" exit 1 fi wait exit 0 fi

# Her own window — the standalone Tauri shell — is the front door. # It is single-instance (a second launch focuses the window that is # already open) and it loads the dashboard from the bridge, so the # bridge verification below still gates the open exactly as it did # for the browser

Only an install where the shell was never built # (no Rust toolchain at install time) falls back to a browser; the # dashboard itself stays reachable at the same URL regardless. # A shell binary is launched only when the stamp beside it covers # the shell sources beside it — the same hash the installer writes # after a successful build. A binary from an older build is a # different app wearing this one's name

Verdicts: 0 = # verified current, 1 = verified stale (or no binary), 2 = cannot # verify (no hashing tool) — unverifiable launches as before, # because a missing sha256sum must not strand the operator. shell_sources_hash() { local dir="shell" # Same rule as the installer's copy of this hash: the shell icon # is optional — a clone install has no binary icon files, and # hashing must not fail over a cosmetic file
With the icon # present it is hashed in its usual place, unchanged

local files="Cargo.toml build.rs src/main.rs tauri.conf.json" if [ -f "$dir/icons/icon.png" ]; then files="$files icons/icon.png"; fi files="$files README.md" local f for f in $files; do if [ ! -f "$dir/$f" ]; then echo ""; return; fi done if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then (cd "$dir" && sha256sum $files | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}') elif command -v shasum >/dev/null 2>&1; then (cd "$dir" && shasum -a 256 $files | shasum -a 256 | awk '{print $1}') else echo "" fi }

shell_is_current() { [ -x "./navi-apex-shell" ] || return 1 local h s h="$(shell_sources_hash)" if [ -z "$h" ]; then return 2; fi s="" if [ -f "./navi-apex-shell.stamp" ]; then s="$(cat ./navi-apex-shell.stamp)"; fi if [ "$s" = "$h" ]; then return 0; fi return 1 }

open_window() { if [ -x "./navi-apex-shell" ]; then local verdict=0 shell_is_current || verdict=$? if [ "$verdict" -eq 1 ]; then log_line "window: the shell binary beside start.sh is STALE — built from older shell sources (its stamp does not cover shell/) — not launching it

Rebuild it (cd shell && cargo build --release) or re-run the installer." log_line "window: falling back to the browser until the shell is rebuilt" open_browser_fallback return 0 fi if [ "$verdict" -eq 2 ]; then log_line "window: cannot verify the shell binary against its build stamp (no sha256sum/shasum) — launching it as-is" fi log_line "window: opening the standalone Apex window (Tauri shell)" ./navi-apex-shell >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 & return 0 fi log_line "window: no shell binary beside start.sh — falling back to the browser (build it with: cd shell && cargo build --release)" open_browser_fallback }

open_browser_fallback() { local url="http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT" # Try each opener in turn and CHECK that it worked. An opener # that merely exists but fails — xdg-open with no default # browser registered answers "no method available" and exits # nonzero — must fall through to the next opener instead of # ending the attempt

That unchecked single xdg-open call was # the menu-launch failure: the bridge came up, the dashboard # was live, and the browser step died without a sound where # nobody could see it (a menu launch has no terminal)

if command -v xdg-open >/dev/null 2>&1 && xdg-open "$url" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then log_line "browser: opened $url with xdg-open" return 0 fi if command -v gio >/dev/null 2>&1 && gio open "$url" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then log_line "browser: opened $url with gio open" return 0 fi if command -v sensible-browser >/dev/null 2>&1 && sensible-browser "$url" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then log_line "browser: opened $url with sensible-browser" return 0 fi if command -v open >/dev/null 2>&1 && open "$url" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1; then log_line "browser: opened $url with open" return 0 fi local b for b in firefox chromium chromium-browser google-chrome google-chrome-stable brave-browser microsoft-edge; do if command -v "$b" >/dev/null 2>&1; then "$b" "$url" >>"$LOG_FILE" 2>&1 & log_line "browser: launched $b with $url" return 0 fi done log_line "browser: NO opener worked — the dashboard is live at $url; open it manually

(Tried xdg-open, gio, sensible-browser, open, and the common browser binaries; their output is above in this log.)" echo "Could not open a browser automatically — the dashboard is live at $url" >&2 return 1 }
# Open her window once the process answering on the bridge port # is a Navi bridge

Any build counts: when the answering bridge # is an older or newer build than this launcher, its dashboard # is still Navi — it carries the BRIDGE OUT OF DATE banner for # exactly that case — and demanding an exact stamp match here # stranded the operator with a running app and no window, the # refusal explained only to a terminal a menu launch doesn't # have
A page that is NOT a Navi bridge at all still blocks # the open, and gets named — in the log as well as the terminal

BRIDGE_STAMP="2026-11-09.91" OPENED="" for i in $(seq 1 40); do STATUS=$(curl -s --max-time 2 "http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT/api/status" 2>/dev/null || true) if printf '%s' "$STATUS" | grep -q '"app": "Navi: Apex"'; then OPENED=1 STAMP_NEEDLE="\"bridge\": \"$BRIDGE_STAMP\"" if printf '%s' "$STATUS" | grep -qF "$STAMP_NEEDLE"; then log_line "verify: this build's bridge ($BRIDGE_STAMP) is answering on port $BRIDGE_PORT" else log_line "verify: a Navi bridge of a different build than $BRIDGE_STAMP is answering on port $BRIDGE_PORT — opening it anyway; its dashboard flags the mismatch" fi break fi sleep 1 done if [ -n "$OPENED" ]; then open_window || true else TITLE=$(curl -s --max-time 2 "http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT/" 2>/dev/null | grep -oiE '<title[^>]*>[^<]*</title>' | head -1 | sed -E 's/<[^>]+>//g' || true) if [ -n "$TITLE" ]; then log_line "verify: port $BRIDGE_PORT is held by a different program (its page is titled "$TITLE") — window not opened" echo "Not opening the window: http://localhost:$BRIDGE_PORT is served by a different program (its page is titled \"$TITLE\")," >&2 echo "not by the Apex bridge — her window would show that program's page, not this dashboard." >&2 echo "Quit the program holding the port (find it with: lsof -i :$BRIDGE_PORT), then launch Apex again." >&2 elif curl -s --max-time 2 http://localhost:8765/api/status 2>/dev/null | grep -q '"app": "Navi: Apex"'; then # A Navi bridge answering on the PREVIOUS package's port can only # be a bridge process from that older install still running (this # build's bridge binds $BRIDGE_PORT and nothing else)
Name it # and say how to clear it instead of the generic shrug — this is # the exact shape of the port-change stranding: the old bridge # alive on 8765, the new launcher polling $BRIDGE_PORT in vain

log_line "verify: a previous install's Navi bridge is answering on the old port 8765 — window not opened" echo "Not opening the window: a Navi bridge from a previous install is still running on the old port, http://localhost:8765," >&2 echo "and this build's bridge never took port $BRIDGE_PORT

See the bridge output above." >&2 fi fi wait

#!/usr/bin/env bash # Apex container entrypoint (0.2.0e Build 7). # # 1. First boot only: seed the data volume from the image's # pristine tree, and say so — the volume's existence from # then on is how every later boot knows it is not the # first. # 2

Run the first-boot step (docker/first_boot.py): on the # first boot it gives the node its container posture (DHD # on, Mesh on), mints its identity and its DHD access code # with the bridge's own machinery, and prints the code's # boxed banner ONCE. On later boots it prints none of it. # 3. The model: downloaded once to the volume, on first run, # exactly as the installer does it; skipped when present. # 4
Launch headless — llamafile + the supervised bridge — # in the foreground: start.sh --headless is the same mode # the systemd unit runs on bare metal. set -euo pipefail
APP=/opt/navi-apex DIST=/opt/navi-apex-dist export APEX_CONTAINER=1
if [ ! -f "$APP/bridge.py" ]; then echo "Apex container: first boot — seeding the data volume from the image." mkdir -p "$APP" cp -a "$DIST/." "$APP/" export APEX_FIRST_BOOT=1 fi
cd "$APP" python3 docker/first_boot.py

if [ ! -f ./navi.llamafile ]; then echo "Apex container: downloading the model (navi.llamafile) — first run only; it is kept in the data volume." curl -fL --retry 3 -o navi.llamafile.part \ "https://huggingface.co/saintssec/navi.llamafile/resolve/main/navi.llamafile" chmod +x navi.llamafile.part mv navi.llamafile.part navi.llamafile fi
exec ./start.sh --headless

#!/usr/bin/env python3 # Apex container first boot (0.2.0e Build 7). # # Runs on EVERY container start, from the entrypoint, before # anything serves. Almost everything it can do is gated on the # volume's first boot (APEX_FIRST_BOOT, set by the entrypoint # only when it just seeded the volume); on later boots it is a # quiet no-op that re-prints nothing

What it does, in order, # all of it through the bridge's OWN machinery — this file # invents no second way of doing any of it: # # 1. The container posture (first boot): DHD enabled (the # no-domain first run — self-signed certificate, access # code), Mesh enabled, the node named from APEX_NODE_NAME # when given, the declared public endpoint seeded from # APEX_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT when given

Bare metal is untouched # by all of this: nothing here runs there, and the tree's # shipped defaults are exactly as shipped. # 2. The node's identity (first boot): the Mesh keypair and # the door certificate, minted by mesh_ensure_identity / # mesh_ensure_cert into the volume. Born on the machine # that runs them; never baked in, never backed up. # 3

The access code: on the first boot a FRESH code is # minted — the config's shipped placeholder is never # inherited by a container node, because a code everyone # can read is a vulnerability, not a feature. The mint is # announced in a boxed banner, printed ONCE, here, and the # same banner is kept in FIRST-BOOT.txt in the volume

# Later boots never re-print it; the deliberate doors are # the bridge's own: `python3 bridge.py --dhd-code` # (re-print) and `--dhd-code-reset` (a new code). # 4. The federation invitation (0.2.0e Build 8, first boot): # an image built to join a fedinet carries the gateway's # card at docker/gateway-card.png

When it is present, it # is copied into the volume as the waiting invitation # (config/federation/invitation.png); the bridge imports # it at start — ADMISSION ONLY: the node is introduced to # the gateway, and nothing lends until the fedinet's # signed roster syncs

The card is public data (a pairing # card's facts + the gateway's signature); the gateway's # identity never leaves the gateway — the card is minted # THERE, never in the image build's audience. An image # carrying no card simply starts unfederated
(The tree's # docker/sample-gateway-card.png is a SAMPLE — its shape, # with sample facts — never wired as an invitation.) import importlib.util import os import shutil import socket import sys
APP = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))) os.chdir(APP) sys.path.insert(0, APP)

def load_bridge(): spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location( "bridgeFirstBoot", os.path.join(APP, "bridge.py")) mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec) spec.loader.exec_module(mod) return mod

def banner(code, name, fingerprint, node_id): bar = "=" * 68 lines = [ bar, " YOUR DHD ACCESS CODE — WRITE IT DOWN OR TAKE A PHOTO NOW", "", " Code: " + code, " Node: " + name + " · node " + (node_id[:12] if node_id else "—"), " Mesh fingerprint: " + fingerprint, "", " This code is the ONLY key to this node's DHD door on your", " network, and the door is already on: browse to this", " computer's address (https — the DHD door Docker publishes", " on port 443), type the code once, name your device, and", " you are in

Every device after the first waits for an", " approval from one that is already trusted, and your Mesh", " pairing card waits on the dashboard's Mesh page.", "", " This is the only time the code is printed in these logs.", " A copy of this banner is kept in FIRST-BOOT.txt in the", " data volume
If you lose the code anyway, the Docker", " page of the Apex docs has the one command that brings", " it back — you will need access to this computer.", bar, ] return "\n".join(lines)
def main(): first = os.environ.get("APEX_FIRST_BOOT") == "1" container = os.environ.get("APEX_CONTAINER") == "1" bridge = load_bridge() cfg = bridge.load_config()
if container and first: # The posture (this node's first run only — an operator's # later changes to any of it are theirs and persist)

bridge.dhd_save(cfg, {"enabled": True}) cfg = bridge.load_config() block = cfg.get("mesh") if isinstance(cfg.get("mesh"), dict) else {} block = dict(block) block["enabled"] = True name_env = (os.environ.get("APEX_NODE_NAME") or "").strip() if name_env and not str(block.get("nodeName") or "").strip(): block["nodeName"] = name_env[:80] ep_env = (os.environ.get("APEX_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT") or "").strip() if ep_env and not str(block.get("publicEndpoint") or "").strip(): cleaned = bridge._mesh_endpoint_clean(ep_env) if cleaned: block["publicEndpoint"] = cleaned cfg["mesh"] = block bridge.save_config(cfg) cfg = bridge.load_config()

if first: # The identity: minted here, by the bridge's own hands, # into the volume — the keypair and the door certificate # the pairing card will carry. bridge.mesh_ensure_identity(cfg) bridge.mesh_ensure_cert() cfg = bridge.load_config()

if container and first: # The federation invitation (Build 8): the image's # bundled gateway card, when it carries one, becomes the # volume's waiting invitation. The bridge performs the # import itself at start (admission-only); here we only # place the file — first_boot invents no second import # path

bundled = os.path.join(APP, "docker", "gateway-card.png") waiting = os.path.join(APP, "config", "federation", "invitation.png") if os.path.isfile(bundled) and not os.path.exists(waiting): os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(waiting), exist_ok=True) shutil.copyfile(bundled, waiting) print("Apex container: a bundled gateway card rides this " "image — it waits as this node's federation " "invitation and is imported, admission-only, at " "start.", flush=True)

# The access code. First boot mints fresh, unconditionally: # whatever the shipped config carries as a placeholder is # not this node's code. Any later boot keeps the node's own # code exactly as it stands — minting again only if the code # is somehow absent (a volume repaired by hand), which is a # first-boot-class event and is announced the same way

minted = False if first: block = cfg.get("public_server") if isinstance(cfg.get("public_server"), dict) else {} block = dict(block) block["access_code"] = bridge.generate_access_code() if "enabled" not in block: block["enabled"] = False cfg["public_server"] = block bridge.save_config(cfg) code = block["access_code"] minted = True elif not bridge.public_settings(cfg)["access_code"]: code = bridge.ensure_access_code(cfg) minted = True else: code = bridge.public_settings(cfg)["access_code"]

if minted: cfg = bridge.load_config() ms = bridge.mesh_settings(cfg) name = ms["nodeName"] or socket.gethostname() text = banner(code, name, bridge.mesh_cert_fingerprint() or "—", bridge.mesh_node_id() or "") print(text, flush=True) keep = os.path.join(APP, "FIRST-BOOT.txt") if not os.path.exists(keep): with open(keep, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f: f.write(text + "\n") else: print("Apex container: existing node configuration found — " "starting with its saved identity and code " "(nothing re-printed).", flush=True)
